subtopic_detail: Neonatal jaundice phototherapy threshold
stem: A term boy born at 39+4 weeks is 54 hours old and jaundiced to the chest. He has fed 8 times in 24 hours and is alert with normal tone.

data_table.Examination: Jaundice to the chest; no hepatosplenomegaly; 4 per cent weight loss
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 278 micromol/L; conjugated 8 micromol/L; DAT negative; reticulocytes not raised
data_table.Threshold: RCH phototherapy line at 54 hours: 280 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop breastfeeding and give formula for 24 hours to clear the bilirubin
Single overhead phototherapy with a repeat bilirubin in 6 hours
Urgent transfer for intensive multiple-light phototherapy and fluids
A split bilirubin and thyroid function, with gastroenterology referral
Continue breastfeeding, repeating the bilirubin in 12 to 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Prolonged jaundice and biliary atresia recognition
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 4-week-old exclusively breastfed girl for a well-child check. Her mother mentions the yellow tinge has not resolved and she noticed the nappy stools look pale over the last week.

Birth was at 39 weeks with normal weight and no early jaundice. She has regained birth weight and is above the 25th centile. Examination reveals visible scleral icterus, a soft abdomen with a liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin, and normal tone.

Antenatal serology was negative, newborn screening was normal, and vitamin K was given intramuscularly at birth. You send investigations. Total serum bilirubin 148 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 62 micromol/L, ALT 92 U/L, GGT 310 U/L, INR 1.0, and the stool colour chart shows a pale colour matching the abnormal range.

data_table.History: Antenatal serology negative; newborn screen normal; IM vitamin K at birth
data_table.Examination: Scleral icterus; liver edge 2 cm below costal margin; normal tone
data_table.Investigations: TSB 148 micromol/L; conjugated 62 micromol/L; ALT 92 U/L; GGT 310 U/L; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Same-day referral to a tertiary paediatric hepatology service for urgent workup including hepatobiliary imaging
Attribute the appearance to breast milk jaundice and review again in 4 weeks with a repeat total bilirubin
Arrange outpatient thyroid function tests and metabolic screen and review in 2 weeks with results
Prescribe oral ursodeoxycholic acid and phototherapy at home while awaiting a routine paediatric appointment
Reassure the family and repeat total bilirubin, LFTs, and INR in 2 weeks if the yellow tinge persists

subtopic_detail: Exchange transfusion threshold and IVIG in severe hyperbilirubinaemia
stem: A 32-hour-old term infant is on intensive phototherapy for rapidly rising jaundice, with maternal anti-c antibodies detected antenatally. He feeds poorly with intermittent lethargy but has normal tone and no retrocollis.

data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 445 micromol/L, up 24 micromol/L over 2 hours of intensive lights; direct antiglobulin test positive; Hb 118 g/L
data_table.Thresholds: Exchange line at 32 hours (term, high risk) 425 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Withhold feeds, give albumin and repeat bilirubin in six hours
Continue intensive phototherapy and repeat bilirubin in four hours
Give a single-volume top-up transfusion of packed red cells
Commence intravenous dextrose and add oral phenobarbital
Give immunoglobulin and prepare for double-volume exchange

subtopic_detail: Investigating constipation with faltering growth and iron deficiency in a school-aged child
stem: A 7-year-old girl has had hard, infrequent stools for two years. She is pale and tired, and her height has fallen from the 50th to the 15th centile since she started school.

data_table.Examination: Thin; mild abdominal distension; palpable faecal loading; neurological examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 71 fL, ferritin 8 microgram/L, thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total immunoglobulin A level
Thyroid stimulating hormone with a free thyroxine level
Serum lead level with a repeat full blood count in one month
Plain abdominal radiograph to assess the degree of faecal loading
Sweat chloride test at an accredited paediatric respiratory unit

subtopic_detail: Maintenance therapy and encopresis relapse prevention
stem:
You are the GP reviewing a 7-year-old girl 3 months after successful oral macrogol disimpaction for functional constipation. She has been on maintenance macrogol producing one soft stool most days with two episodes of soiling per week.

Her parents ask about stopping the medication because a family friend told them long-term laxatives cause dependence. She sits on the toilet after breakfast and dinner most days as advised. Diet is varied with adequate fluid intake, and physical activity is age-appropriate.

Growth remains on the 50th centile. Abdominal examination is soft with no palpable stool mass, and school reports the soiling continues to disrupt her class.

data_table.Symptoms: One soft stool most days; two soiling episodes per week
data_table.Growth: 50th centile stable
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen; no palpable stool mass

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to paediatric gastroenterology for anorectal manometry and biofeedback therapy under specialist supervision
Reassure the family and taper the macrogol dose by half over 2 weeks now that the soiling frequency has fallen
Stop macrogol and start a high-fibre diet with 4 servings of fruit and lactulose only if constipation recurs
Add oral senna daily and reduce the macrogol dose to avoid excessive stool frequency over the medium term
Titrate the maintenance macrogol dose upward and continue therapy for at least 6 months of full symptom control

subtopic_detail: Kawasaki disease diagnostic criteria and IVIG timing
stem: A 3-year-old girl is on day 6 of daily fever. She is irritable and refusing to eat.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis sparing the limbus; cracked red lips with strawberry tongue; macular truncal rash; swollen red hands and feet; 2 cm cervical node
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 612 x10^9/L; CRP 148 mg/L; ALT 78 U/L; sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg for 3 days, then reassessment
Repeat echocardiogram and inflammatory markers at 48 hours before committing
Empirical intravenous flucloxacillin and ceftriaxone for toxin-mediated illness
Intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as a single infusion, with aspirin
Oral aspirin at anti-inflammatory dose with review in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: IVIG resistance in Kawasaki disease
stem: A 2-year-old boy with Kawasaki disease diagnosed on day 6 received intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and aspirin. He remains febrile 48 hours after the infusion, with conjunctival injection and swollen hands.

data_table.Investigations: CRP 132 mg/L (pre-treatment 148), sodium 128 mmol/L, ALT 92 U/L, platelets 604 x10^9/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A second dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg with methylprednisolone
Continue the current aspirin and repeat inflammatory markers in 24 hours
Switch aspirin to clopidogrel and start therapeutic enoxaparin
Intravenous infliximab alone, stopping aspirin during the infusion
Add intravenous ciclosporin and retest for resistance in 72 hours

subtopic_detail: SUFE recognition in the obese adolescent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 13-year-old boy brought by his mother for 5 weeks of intermittent left knee pain that has become constant over 3 days.

He walks with an out-toed limp. He is on the 97th centile for weight and 50th for height. There is no history of trauma, fever, or recent viral illness. He can weight bear but refuses to sprint.

Hip examination shows loss of internal rotation of the left hip, and obligatory external rotation of the hip when the knee is flexed passively toward the chest. Distal neurovascular examination is normal. CRP and WCC are within normal limits. Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral pelvis x-rays are ordered.

data_table.Growth: 97th centile weight; 50th centile height
data_table.History: 5 weeks intermittent left knee pain; 3 days constant; no trauma; no fever; no viral prodrome
data_table.Examination: Out-toed antalgic gait; loss of left hip internal rotation; obligatory external rotation on passive hip flexion; normal distal neurovascular status
data_table.Investigations: CRP and WCC within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: AP and frog-leg lateral pelvis x-rays ordered

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform hip joint aspiration under fluoroscopy to exclude septic arthritis before further planning
Prescribe simple analgesia and physiotherapy, with GP follow-up in 2 weeks for reassessment
Arrange outpatient MRI hip within 2 weeks and continue partial weight bearing as tolerated in the meantime
Non-weight-bearing precautions and urgent orthopaedic referral for percutaneous in situ screw fixation
Trial 48 hours of oral ibuprofen and observed rest with return precautions if symptoms progress

subtopic_detail: Perthes vs transient synovitis discrimination
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy with 8 weeks of intermittent left hip pain and a limp. Symptoms started insidiously and have not resolved.

He had a mild upper respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago that has since resolved. He is well grown and afebrile. He can weight bear but tires more quickly than his peers.

Examination shows an antalgic gait, restriction of abduction and internal rotation of the left hip, and a positive Trendelenburg sign on the left. There is no rash, no lymphadenopathy, and no other joint involvement. WCC, CRP, and ESR are within normal limits, and hip x-ray shows increased density of the left femoral epiphysis with subchondral lucency and preserved joint space.

data_table.History: 8 weeks intermittent left hip pain; mild URTI 4 weeks ago resolved; no persistent fever
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait; restricted left hip abduction and internal rotation; positive Trendelenburg on left; no rash; no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: WCC, CRP, ESR within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: AP pelvis x-ray: increased density of left femoral epiphysis with subchondral lucency; preserved joint space

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Transient synovitis of the hip
Legg-Calve-Perthes disease
Slipped upper femoral epiphysis
Septic arthritis of the hip
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis

subtopic_detail: Kocher criteria and irritable hip pathway
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 4-year-old girl brought in refusing to bear weight on the right leg for 24 hours. She had a runny nose 5 days ago that has settled.

She screams on passive movement of the right hip. She lies with the hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. There is no rash, no other joint involvement, no recent trauma, and no unwell contacts.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.6. WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (5-15), CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 45 mm/hr, blood cultures pending. Right hip x-ray is unremarkable. Bedside ultrasound shows a right hip effusion of 5 mm.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 98/60, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.History: 24 hours refusal to weight bear; URTI 5 days ago resolved; no trauma
data_table.Examination: Hip held flexed, abducted, externally rotated; screams on passive movement; no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L (5-15); CRP 42 mg/L; ESR 45 mm/hr; blood cultures pending
data_table.Imaging: Right hip x-ray unremarkable; ultrasound shows 5 mm right hip effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose transient synovitis and discharge home with GP review in 48 hours and simple analgesia
Admit for observation with paracetamol and ibuprofen and repeat inflammatory markers in 12 hours
Urgent orthopaedic consultation for hip aspiration in theatre with intravenous flucloxacillin after cultures
Arrange urgent MRI hip and defer antibiotics until imaging confirms osteomyelitis or septic arthritis
Start oral cefalexin as an outpatient with orthopaedic outpatient clinic review scheduled in 1 week

subtopic_detail: Paediatric acute asthma escalation ladder
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 6-year-old girl with known asthma presents with 4 hours of worsening shortness of breath and cough after her parents ran out of preventer 2 weeks ago.

She usually inhales salbutamol via spacer at home for exacerbations. On arrival she cannot speak in full sentences, uses accessory muscles, and has an audible wheeze.

Vital signs: pulse 138, blood pressure 102/68, respiratory rate 42, SpO2 90% room air, temperature 37.1. Auscultation reveals bilateral polyphonic wheeze with prolonged expiration. She has received salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer with mask 20 minutes ago at triage with only partial improvement and is now on 2 L nasal prong oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 102/68, RR 42, SpO2 90% room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Cannot speak full sentences; accessory muscle use; audible wheeze; bilateral polyphonic wheeze with prolonged expiration
data_table.Treatment given: Salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer with mask 20 minutes ago; 2 L nasal prong oxygen
data_table.History: Preventer ran out 2 weeks ago; usually uses spacer at home

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous magnesium sulfate 25 to 50 mg per kg over 20 minutes now as the next escalation step
Commence nebulised salbutamol 5 mg back-to-back and start intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg
Repeat salbutamol 12 puffs via spacer with mask, add ipratropium 8 puffs via spacer, and give oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg
Add intravenous aminophylline loading dose of 5 mg per kg over 20 minutes with cardiac monitoring
Trial high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L per kg per minute and reassess bronchodilator response

subtopic_detail: Life-threatening asthma escalation to IV magnesium
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar continuing to manage the 6-year-old girl with severe acute asthma. She has now received back-to-back salbutamol via spacer plus ipratropium in the first hour and oral prednisolone.

One hour on, she is drowsy, silent on auscultation, and using significant accessory muscles. She responds only to voice with brief eye opening.

Vital signs: pulse 168, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 12, SpO2 88% on 6 L via Hudson mask, temperature 37.2. Venous blood gas: pH 7.30, pCO2 55 mmHg, pO2 not applicable, HCO3 25 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. She has intravenous access.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168, BP 96/58, RR 12, SpO2 88% on 6 L Hudson, temperature 37.2
data_table.Mental state: Drowsy; brief eye opening to voice
data_table.Examination: Silent chest; significant accessory muscle use
data_table.Treatment so far: Back-to-back salbutamol via spacer plus ipratropium in first hour; oral prednisolone given
data_table.Venous blood gas: pH 7.30; pCO2 55 mmHg; HCO3 25 mmol/L; lactate 4.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 40 mg per kg (up to 2 g) infused over 20 minutes with continuous cardiac monitoring
Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation with ketamine induction and rocuronium paralysis
Intravenous salbutamol infusion 5 mcg per kg per minute without loading dose and observe for 20 minutes
High-flow nasal cannula at 2 L per kg per minute and heliox 70:30 while awaiting critical care review
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 through the Hudson mask while preparing intubation kit

subtopic_detail: Early-onset neonatal sepsis empirical antibiotics
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a 12-hour-old term male infant on the postnatal ward. The midwife noticed grunting and poor colour.

Mother had prolonged rupture of membranes for 22 hours and an intrapartum temperature of 38.4. Group B streptococcus swab was positive at 36 weeks but she declined intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis.

Vital signs: pulse 176, blood pressure 58/32, respiratory rate 78, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 36.1. The infant is mottled with delayed capillary refill of 4 seconds and mild subcostal recessions. He has intercostal recessions and grunting. Blood culture, full blood count, and CRP are collected, an umbilical venous catheter is being placed, and lumbar puncture is planned once he is stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 176, BP 58/32, RR 78, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 36.1
data_table.Maternal history: Prolonged rupture of membranes 22 hours; intrapartum temperature 38.4; GBS positive at 36 weeks; declined intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis
data_table.Examination: Mottled; capillary refill 4 seconds; intercostal recessions and grunting
data_table.Investigations: Blood culture, FBC, CRP collected; UVC being placed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin plus gentamicin at neonatal doses with fluid resuscitation as needed
Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin at neonatal early-onset sepsis doses
Intravenous cefotaxime plus vancomycin at neonatal doses with lumbar puncture prior to first dose
Intravenous amoxicillin plus aciclovir plus gentamicin at neonatal doses given maternal fever
Intravenous meropenem monotherapy pending cultures with vancomycin added at 48 hours if unresponsive

subtopic_detail: Late-onset neonatal sepsis with HSV cover indications
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar in the emergency department. A 14-day-old term girl presents with 12 hours of poor feeding and lethargy.

She was born at 39 weeks vaginally after an uncomplicated pregnancy. Mother has no known genital herpes but recalls a painful ulcer near delivery that resolved without swabbing.

On examination the infant is grunting with a bulging fontanelle, and there is a cluster of small vesicles at the base of the scalp overlying the vertex. Vital signs: pulse 188, blood pressure 62/38, respiratory rate 66, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.0.

Investigations: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L (5-19), platelets 82 x10^9/L (150-400), ALT 340 U/L, INR 1.8. Blood cultures and lumbar puncture are being obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 188, BP 62/38, RR 66, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 36.0
data_table.Maternal history: No known genital herpes; painful ulcer near delivery unswabbed and resolved
data_table.Examination: Grunting; bulging fontanelle; cluster of small vesicles at base of scalp overlying vertex
data_table.In progress: Blood cultures and lumbar puncture being obtained

lead_in: What is the single best empirical treatment regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin at neonatal doses and admit for observation over 48 hours
Intravenous cefotaxime plus vancomycin plus intravenous aciclovir at neonatal doses after cultures and lumbar puncture
Intravenous flucloxacillin plus gentamicin plus oral aciclovir at neonatal doses and admit to the ward
Intravenous cefotaxime plus vancomycin without aciclovir; add aciclovir only if HSV PCR positive
Intravenous meropenem plus vancomycin plus intravenous aciclovir and defer lumbar puncture indefinitely

subtopic_detail: Fever under 3 months investigation and empirical treatment
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 24-day-old term boy in the emergency department with a temperature of 38.4 at home and now 38.6 in triage.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery. He is feeding, has appropriate wet nappies, and there are no unwell contacts other than his 3-year-old sister with a runny nose.

He is alert with normal tone, no rash, and no focal signs on examination. Anterior fontanelle is soft. Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 46, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.6. Urine sample by catheter has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 78/48, RR 46, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.History: Term uncomplicated birth; feeding well; adequate wet nappies; sibling with URTI
data_table.Examination: Alert; normal tone; no rash; no focal signs; soft anterior fontanelle

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urine culture only and discharge home on paracetamol with 24 hour telephone follow up given viral contact
Blood culture, FBC, CRP, and urine only; defer lumbar puncture unless the infant appears unwell
Full septic workup including blood, urine, and CSF sampling followed by intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
FBC and CRP only, then admit for observation with intravenous antibiotics only if inflammatory markers are raised
Nasopharyngeal viral swab and observe on the ward for 4 hours before deciding on further investigations

subtopic_detail: Croup severity assessment and dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy brought in at 10 pm with a barking cough and noisy breathing that started after a runny nose earlier in the day.

He is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. On examination he has stridor audible only when he becomes upset, mild sternal recession at rest, and no cyanosis or drooling.

Vital signs: pulse 128, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.6. There is no history of foreign body, no immunocompromise, and immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/60, RR 32, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.6
data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable; stridor only when upset; mild sternal recession at rest; no cyanosis; no drooling
data_table.History: Barking cough and noisy breathing after URTI; no foreign body; immunisations up to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg per kg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 with 3 hour observation
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg per kg as a single dose then observe for at least 30 minutes before discharge
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose with discharge home immediately after the treatment
Steam inhalation and humidified air with as-needed paracetamol and no corticosteroid at this stage
Admission for a lateral neck x-ray to exclude epiglottitis and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone

subtopic_detail: Paediatric anaphylaxis IM adrenaline banded dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to resus for a 4-year-old girl who developed hives, lip swelling, and vomiting 10 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit at a birthday party.

She has a known peanut allergy prescribed an EpiPen Jr, which her parents did not have with them.

On arrival she is drowsy with widespread urticaria, audible wheeze, and mild stridor. She weighs an estimated 17 kg based on parental report. Vital signs: pulse 158, blood pressure 78/40, respiratory rate 38, SpO2 92% room air, temperature 36.8. Intravenous access has not yet been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 158, BP 78/40, RR 38, SpO2 92% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.History: Known peanut allergy; ingested peanut biscuit 10 minutes ago
data_table.Examination: Drowsy; widespread urticaria; audible wheeze; mild stridor

lead_in: What is the single best immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 4 mg per kg and oral loratadine 5 mg while waiting for adrenaline to be drawn up
Intramuscular adrenaline 300 mcg to the mid-outer thigh, call for help, and give supplemental oxygen by mask
Intramuscular adrenaline 150 mcg to the mid-outer thigh, call for help, and lay the child flat with legs elevated
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 while intravenous access is being obtained for an adrenaline infusion
Intravenous adrenaline 10 mcg per kg bolus once intravenous access is secured then commence a maintenance infusion

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis low-flow oxygen and HFNC escalation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9-month-old girl with 3 days of coryza followed by cough, poor feeding, and increased work of breathing.

She is alert, mildly tachypnoeic, and taking about 40% of her usual feeds. She has no comorbidity and no risk factors for severe disease.

On examination there is moderate subcostal recession, widespread fine crackles, and expiratory wheeze. Vital signs: pulse 152, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 58, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.9. A nasopharyngeal swab has been sent and intravenous fluids have not yet been commenced.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 92/58, RR 58, SpO2 88% room air, temperature 37.9
data_table.History: 3 days coryza then cough, poor feeding, increased work of breathing; taking 40% of usual feeds; no comorbidity
data_table.Examination: Alert; moderate subcostal recession; widespread fine crackles; expiratory wheeze
data_table.Investigations: NPA sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial respiratory support?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg per kg and nebulised hypertonic saline 3% every 4 hours
High-flow nasal cannula at 2 L per kg per minute from the outset given hypoxia below 90%
Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back-to-back with observation of respiratory response
Low-flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L per minute titrated to maintain SpO2 at or above 90%
Non-invasive ventilation with CPAP 8 cm H2O in the paediatric high dependency unit

subtopic_detail: Failed nasogastric rehydration in gastroenteritis
stem: An 18-month-old girl with gastroenteritis and 6 percent weight loss has had nasogastric rehydration solution running for 2 hours. She has vomited large volumes twice in the last hour and her abdomen has changed.

data_table.Examination: Distended tympanic abdomen, absent bowel sounds, capillary refill 3 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop nasogastric fluid, check electrolytes and rehydrate intravenously
Halve the nasogastric rate and give a second dose of ondansetron
Continue the same nasogastric rate and reassess the abdomen in one hour
Replace the nasogastric tube and restart the same hourly volume
Give an intravenous fluid bolus and continue nasogastric fluid

subtopic_detail: Paediatric UTI imaging cascade under 24 months
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 15-month-old girl 48 hours after commencing oral cefalexin for a first culture-proven E coli urinary tract infection. The urine was collected by catheter.

She has defervesced within 24 hours, is drinking well, and her mother reports she is back to her usual behaviour.

Her birth was at term after antenatal care that included a normal 20 week morphology ultrasound. She has no family history of vesicoureteric reflux or renal disease. Examination is unremarkable with a soft non-tender abdomen, normal external genitalia, and no palpable bladder or masses. Her weight is on the 60th centile and her blood pressure is at the 50th centile for age.

data_table.History: First UTI (E coli, catheter sample); defervesced within 24 hours of oral cefalexin
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen; normal external genitalia; no palpable bladder or masses
data_table.Growth and BP: 60th centile weight; blood pressure at 50th centile for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: Urgent renal tract ultrasound during this admission to exclude an obstructive uropathy or renal abscess
Renal tract ultrasound within 6 weeks of the acute illness and outpatient paediatric review
DMSA scan at 4 to 6 months to detect renal scarring plus micturating cystourethrogram to assess for reflux
No routine renal tract imaging; provide return precautions for recurrent UTI, poor response, or systemic features
MRI urogram at 3 months of age plus continuous prophylactic trimethoprim until the imaging result is available

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA initial fluid resuscitation
stem: A 9-year-old girl weighing 30 kg has three days of thirst, polyuria and vomiting. She is alert with warm peripheries, dry mucous membranes and deep sighing breathing.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130 /min, BP 98/62 mmHg, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 26 mmol/L, venous pH 7.15, ketones 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid plan?

options.text: A 20 mL/kg saline bolus, then deficit rehydration over 24 hours
A 10 mL/kg saline bolus over 30 to 60 minutes, then rehydration over 48 hours
Intravenous insulin at 0.1 units/kg/hour now with 0.45% saline
Sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg over 30 minutes, then saline maintenance
A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with a 3% hypertonic saline infusion

subtopic_detail: Cerebral oedema in paediatric DKA
stem: A 7-year-old girl is 5 hours into treatment for diabetic ketoacidosis, on 48-hour rehydration with insulin from hour 2. She has developed severe headache and become difficult to rouse.

data_table.Investigations: pH 7.10 to 7.24, glucose 32 to 12 mmol/L, corrected sodium 141 to 144 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the best immediate intervention?

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3% 5 mL/kg over 15 minutes, slowing the fluid rate
A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with 5% dextrose added to current fluids
Stop insulin and arrange an urgent non-contrast CT brain scan
Intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg with the bed laid flat
Intubate and hyperventilate to a target PaCO2 of 25 mmHg

subtopic_detail: Potassium management in paediatric DKA
stem: A 12-year-old boy weighing 40 kg has new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis. He has had a 10 mL/kg saline bolus, rehydration fluid is prescribed, and insulin has not yet started. He has not passed urine since arrival.

data_table.Investigations: pH 7.10, bicarbonate 6 mmol/L, glucose 30 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 78 micromol/L
data_table.ECG: Sinus tachycardia with normal T waves

lead_in: Which potassium prescription is most appropriate?

options.text: Add 40 mmol/L potassium chloride now, regardless of urine output
Withhold potassium until urine output is documented, then add 40 mmol/L
Add 20 mmol/L potassium chloride and recheck in six hours
Give intravenous calcium gluconate and nebulised salbutamol
Add 60 mmol/L potassium chloride for total body depletion

subtopic_detail: First unprovoked seizure workup
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a previously well 8-year-old boy in the emergency department 90 minutes after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure. His mother describes stiffening followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs for around 90 seconds, with post-event confusion for 10 minutes.

He has since returned to baseline, is playing on the tablet, and complains only of a mild frontal headache. He has no history of head injury, no fever, no rash, and no family history of epilepsy. Development is age-appropriate and school reports are normal.

Vital signs within normal limits and neurological examination is unremarkable including tone, power, reflexes, gait, and fundi. Point-of-care glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8) and a bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with a corrected QT of 400 ms.

data_table.Examination: Fully recovered; normal tone, power, reflexes, gait, fundi
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); ECG sinus rhythm, QTc 400 ms
data_table.Event: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure ~90 sec; post-ictal 10 min; no fever, no head injury

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent non-contrast CT brain in the emergency department before discharge from the emergency department
Start sodium valproate 15 mg/kg per day and arrange outpatient neurology follow-up in 6 weeks for further review
Discharge with safety advice, arrange outpatient EEG and MRI brain, and refer to paediatric neurology for outpatient review
Perform a lumbar puncture for cell count, protein, glucose, and herpes simplex virus PCR before disposition
Admit for 24 hour cardiac monitoring and prolonged video EEG telemetry to characterise the event before discharge

subtopic_detail: Infantile spasms recognition
stem: A 6-month-old boy has three weeks of brief movement clusters, now 15 to 30 a day, mostly on waking. Video shows his arms drawing in and knees drawing up in clusters of 20. He no longer reaches for objects or laughs.

data_table.Examination: Axial hypotonia, three hypopigmented trunk macules, head circumference fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Outpatient electroencephalogram in six weeks and a metabolic screen
Reassure that this is benign sleep myoclonus of infancy
Oral omeprazole for suspected Sandifer syndrome, review in a month
Same-day neurology referral with electroencephalogram within 24 hours
Oral phenobarbital with outpatient neurology review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Childhood absence epilepsy recognition and treatment
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 7-year-old girl has been referred by her school after her teacher reported multiple episodes each hour when she seems to stare and stop what she is doing for a few seconds before continuing.

Her parents had thought she was daydreaming until they noticed it happening several times during a single meal. There is no post-event confusion, no incontinence, and no witnessed limb jerking. Development is age-appropriate and she is in a mainstream class.

In the room, you ask her to hyperventilate for 3 minutes by blowing on a paper windmill. During this, she stops speaking mid-sentence, stares blankly for about 8 seconds with eyelid fluttering, then resumes exactly where she left off with no post-event drowsiness. Neurological examination is otherwise unremarkable and vital signs within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Age-appropriate development; unremarkable neurological examination
data_table.Event characteristics: Multiple daily 8-second staring episodes with eyelid fluttering; no post-event drowsiness; provoked by hyperventilation
data_table.History: No incontinence, no limb jerking, no post-ictal confusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line antiseizure medication?

options.text: Ethosuximide, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
Carbamazepine, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
Sodium valproate, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
Levetiracetam, titrated to therapeutic dose over 1 to 2 weeks
Lamotrigine, titrated slowly to therapeutic dose over 4 to 6 weeks

subtopic_detail: MMR contraindications and precautions
stem:
You are the GP registrar in a suburban practice. A mother brings her 12-month-old son for his routine immunisations. He was born at term and has been well.

He received the standard 2 month, 4 month, and 6 month vaccines uneventfully. Six weeks ago he was admitted to hospital for a febrile illness and received a single unit of packed red cells after an accident in which he lost blood.

He is now afebrile and eating well. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination is unremarkable. His mother has no history of immunosuppression and there is no household contact with immunocompromised individuals. She asks whether he can have his 12 month vaccines today.

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; systemically well
data_table.History: Packed red cells 6 weeks ago; on time for prior vaccines; no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immunisation plan today?

options.text: Give the meningococcal ACWY and pneumococcal 13v today but defer MMR for a further 4 months
Give all three scheduled vaccines today because 6 weeks is a sufficient washout after packed red cells
Defer all three scheduled 12 month vaccines for a further 6 months given the recent packed red cell transfusion
Give MMR intramuscularly today and hold the meningococcal ACWY and pneumococcal 13v until next month
Check measles serology today and give MMR only if antibody titre is negative and 6 months have elapsed

subtopic_detail: Post-exposure prophylaxis for chickenpox
stem:
You are the ED registrar. A 5-year-old immunocompetent boy who attends kindergarten was in close contact with a schoolmate who developed a widespread vesicular rash 2 days ago and was diagnosed with chickenpox. His parents present today, 72 hours after the exposure, asking what should be done.

He is a full-term, previously healthy child. He had a single varicella-containing vaccine dose at 18 months and no boosters since. He is currently well with no fever, no rash, and no respiratory symptoms.

He has no history of eczema and is not on any medication. His younger sister is 6 weeks old, exclusively breastfed, and his mother reports she herself had chickenpox as a child. Vital signs within normal limits and examination unremarkable.

data_table.Examination: Well; no rash; no respiratory symptoms
data_table.Vaccination history: Single varicella dose at 18 months; no boosters
data_table.Exposure: Close contact 3 days ago with schoolmate who has chickenpox
data_table.Household: 6-week-old sister; mother had chickenpox in childhood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the 5-year-old?

options.text: Give a second dose of varicella-containing vaccine today as post-exposure prophylaxis for the schoolmate contact
Give varicella zoster immunoglobulin (VZIG) intramuscularly today as post-exposure prophylaxis for the school contact
Commence oral aciclovir 20 mg/kg four times daily for 7 days as post-exposure prophylaxis for the school contact
Reassure the parents that no action is needed today because he had a varicella vaccine at 18 months of age
Isolate at home for 21 days without vaccination and swab any new vesicular lesions with viral PCR if they appear

subtopic_detail: Catch-up schedule for the incomplete traveller child
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who has recently arrived in Australia from overseas with her family. Her interpreter-supported history is that she received BCG at birth and one dose of DTP-HiB-HepB-IPV as an infant.

She is otherwise well, developing appropriately, and attends kindergarten now that she has settled in. There are no documented allergies. Her family plans to travel back to visit relatives in 6 months.

Vital signs within normal limits. Examination is unremarkable. She has no current fever or rash. She has not received any measles-mumps-rubella containing vaccine. The mother has brought a paper immunisation record from her country of origin which corroborates the history.

data_table.Examination: Well; growth and development age-appropriate
data_table.Previous immunisation: BCG at birth; single DTP-HiB-HepB-IPV in infancy; no MMR
data_table.Documentation: Paper record from country of origin corroborates history

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her catch-up schedule today?

options.text: Serology for measles, mumps, rubella, hepatitis B, and varicella today, then commence catch-up only if seronegative
Give only tetanus-diphtheria vaccine today and refer to a public health service for the remainder of the schedule
Restart the entire NIP schedule from birth today, ignoring the paper record from her country of origin
Delay all catch-up vaccinations until she has been in Australia for 6 months and has established a Medicare number
Give catch-up vaccines today using the online Handbook calculator, prioritising MMR and DTP-containing vaccines

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - non-organic red flags
stem: An 11-month-old boy's weight has drifted from the 50th centile at birth to the 3rd centile since 4 months. He is playful, meets his milestones and interacts warmly with his mother.

data_table.Growth: Weight 7.2 kg, length 25th centile, head circumference 50th centile
data_table.Examination: No dysmorphism, organomegaly or rash
data_table.Feeding: Grazes on bottled cow's milk all day with minimal solids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Dietitian input, three meals and two snacks with cup-only milk
Coeliac serology, full blood count, electrolytes and thyroid function
Admit for supervised feeding and structured observation
A high-energy formula supplement 150 mL twice daily, reviewing growth
Notify child protection services today because of the growth pattern

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - organic red flags requiring investigation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 22-month-old girl is referred by her GP for weight loss and poor growth over the last 4 months.

Her weight has dropped from the 50th centile at 12 months to the 5th centile now, with length falling from the 50th to the 15th centile over the same period. Her head circumference remains on the 50th. Her mother describes intermittent loose stools, a distended tummy after meals, and irritability at mealtimes.

She eats a varied family diet without cow's milk overuse, was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, and was previously well. Vital signs within normal limits. Examination shows a distended abdomen without organomegaly, mild wasting of the buttocks, and pale conjunctivae. Her older sibling has type 1 diabetes mellitus.

data_table.Growth: Weight 50th to 5th centile over 4 months; length 50th to 15th; head circumference 50th
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen; no organomegaly; buttock wasting; pale conjunctivae
data_table.History: Loose stools, abdominal distension after meals, irritability; varied diet; no cow's milk excess
data_table.Family history: Older sibling with type 1 diabetes mellitus

lead_in: What is the single most useful initial investigation?

options.text: Full blood count, ferritin, C-reactive protein, and thyroid function tests as an initial screening panel
Faecal calprotectin and stool microscopy, culture, and sensitivity as first-line for gastrointestinal symptoms
Anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with a total serum IgA level, on a gluten-containing diet, as first-line
Urine microscopy, culture, and sensitivity plus urea and electrolytes for occult renal or urinary tract cause
Empirical trial of a strict gluten-free diet for 6 weeks before any further blood, stool, or urine investigation

subtopic_detail: Failure to thrive - short stature discrimination
stem: A 5-year-old boy has been the shortest in his class for a year. He was born at term on the 50th centile and is otherwise well.

data_table.Growth: Height 3rd centile since age 2, growth velocity 6 cm/year
data_table.Examination: Well proportioned, no dysmorphism
data_table.History: Father 165 cm (5th centile), mother 155 cm (10th centile)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for growth hormone stimulation testing and consider replacement
Commence recombinant growth hormone and review the response in 3 months
Order thyroid function, coeliac serology and a karyotype today
Arrange a bone age radiograph of the non-dominant hand and wrist
Reassure the parents, calculate mid-parental target height and review in 6 months

subtopic_detail: Pyloric stenosis recognition
stem: A 5-week-old formula-fed boy has two weeks of vomiting after every feed. His mother describes non-bilious vomits that shoot across the room minutes after feeding, and he takes the next bottle avidly.

data_table.Growth: 3.5 kg at birth, 3.3 kg today
data_table.Examination: Alert, dry mucous membranes, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Na 135 mmol/L, K 3.1 mmol/L, Cl 92 mmol/L, HCO3 32 mmol/L, pH 7.48

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Abdominal ultrasound today with intravenous fluid and electrolyte correction
Reassure as posseting and advise thickened feeds with review
Urgent laparotomy without preoperative imaging or optimisation
Oral omeprazole for reflux with outpatient review in two weeks
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study with nasogastric decompression

subtopic_detail: Intussusception - imaging and treatment
stem: A 9-month-old girl has 12 hours of screaming episodes with leg drawing every 20 minutes, and is sleepy between episodes. She has vomited three times, the last two green, and her nappy contained stool mixed with red jelly.

data_table.Examination: HR 148 /min, capillary refill 3 seconds, palpable long thin mass in the right upper abdomen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Air-contrast enema in the emergency department before resuscitation
Theatre for open manual reduction without imaging or resuscitation
Oral ondansetron, discharge home and outpatient review in 24 hours
Resuscitate with 20 mL/kg saline, urgent ultrasound and surgical consult
Nuclear medicine Meckel scan today to find the lead point first

subtopic_detail: GORD versus surgical vomiting discrimination
stem: A 3-week-old girl has vomited after feeds for a week. The vomits are effortless and variable in volume; one yesterday looked green-tinged, the rest milky. Stools are soft and yellow.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well perfused, feeds hungrily; abdomen soft and non-distended; no visible peristalsis
data_table.Growth: 2.9 kg at birth to 3.4 kg today, tracking the 25th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with reassurance and review at the routine 6 week check
Urgent upper gastrointestinal contrast to define the duodenojejunal junction
Abdominal ultrasound today to measure the pyloric channel and thickness
A 4 week trial of thickened feeds and omeprazole 1 mg/kg daily
Contrast enema today to exclude Hirschsprung disease as the cause

subtopic_detail: Developmental delay red flags and referral
stem: An 18-month-old boy is seen for routine developmental review. He cruises and takes one to two steps with hand-holding. He babbles but has no clear words, does not point to show interest, and rarely responds to his name.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral serous middle ear effusions with no acute infection
data_table.Hearing history: Passed newborn hearing screen, not tested since

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Chromosomal microarray and Fragile X testing before any referral
Reassure that boys often talk later and review at two years
Refer to audiology and to community paediatric services
Insert bilateral tympanostomy tubes now for the effusions
Prescribe amoxicillin for the effusions and review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: M-CHAT-R interpretation and next steps
stem: A 20-month-old boy has a few single words but rarely uses them to request or share, lines up his toy cars, is distressed by changes in routine, and often does not respond to his name. Audiology last month was normal.

data_table.Screening: M-CHAT-R score 8 of 20, failing pointing, showing, response to name, pretend play and joint attention

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Community speech pathology referral for expressive language delay
Repeat the M-CHAT-R follow-up interview before referral
Reassure, give parent advice and rescreen at the 2 year check
Chromosomal microarray, Fragile X and metabolic screening
Autism assessment referral and NDIS early childhood approach

subtopic_detail: Global developmental delay etiologic workup
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar seeing a 2-year-old girl for delay across all developmental domains. She was born at term after an uneventful pregnancy.

She sits unsupported but does not yet walk. She has no words and does not point. She can hold a spoon briefly but cannot self-feed. Her mother and father are unrelated and there is no family history of intellectual disability or genetic disorders.

Vital signs within normal limits. She has broad-based gait with a hand-held examiner, and a widely-spaced upper central incisor pattern. Head circumference is on the 3rd centile (was on 10th at 6 months). Formal hearing and vision assessment 2 months ago were both normal. She has been referred to the NDIS Early Childhood Approach.

data_table.Examination: Not walking; head circumference 3rd centile (down from 10th at 6 months); broad-based gait with support; widely-spaced upper incisor pattern
data_table.Development: Delay across gross motor, fine motor, expressive language, social
data_table.Recent tests: Formal hearing and vision normal 2 months ago
data_table.Family history: Unrelated parents; no known intellectual disability or genetic disorders

lead_in: What is the single most useful first-line investigation for aetiology?

options.text: Blood ammonia, lactate, plasma amino acids, and acylcarnitine profile as a metabolic screen for global delay
Standard G-banded karyotype from peripheral blood to detect chromosomal aneuploidy and balanced rearrangements
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with sedation for structural aetiology in unexplained global delay
Chromosomal microarray from peripheral blood to detect copy number variants as first-tier genetic testing
Electroencephalogram from a routine 20 minute recording to detect epileptic encephalopathy contributing to delay

subtopic_detail: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder recognition
stem: A 5-year-old boy is referred by his kindergarten teacher for behavioural difficulties. He cannot sit still, struggles with two-step instructions, becomes explosive when redirected and misses social cues. His mother drank heavily through the first two trimesters of pregnancy.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference 2nd centile, height and weight 25th; short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin vermilion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange formal cognitive assessment through the school psychology service
Commence methylphenidate and review the response in four weeks
Reassure the family that behaviour will settle with more structure
Refer to a geneticist for microarray and Fragile X testing
Refer to a specialist multidisciplinary developmental clinic

subtopic_detail: Mandatory reporting in NSW
stem: A 26-year-old woman at 32 weeks gestation has drunk about six standard drinks daily since before she knew she was pregnant, stopping two weeks ago. She now has morning tremor when she does not drink.

data_table.Examination: Engaged, not intoxicated; no jaundice or tenderness
data_table.History: No other children; not known to drug and alcohol or child protection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action today?

options.text: Report only after the birth, once features are documented
A prenatal Report of Concern plus perinatal drug and alcohol referral
Motivational counselling alone, deferring reporting as she came voluntarily
Outpatient diazepam home detoxification and review in one week
Police contact for involuntary admission for the safety of the pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Antipyretic advice for the well febrile toddler
stem:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to your general practice on the second day of a fever. He has a runny nose and a loose cough, and his 4-year-old sister had the same illness last week.

He is alert, playing with the toys in your room, drinking well and has had five wet nappies today. Examination of his ears, throat, chest and abdomen is unremarkable and there is no rash.

His mother has been giving paracetamol whenever the thermometer reads above 38 degrees Celsius and asks whether she should also add ibuprofen overnight so that his temperature never climbs high enough to cause a fit.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 94/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about antipyretic use?

options.text: Alternate paracetamol and ibuprofen four-hourly overnight to hold the temperature below 38 degrees Celsius.
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) six-hourly only when the fever is making him uncomfortable.
Give ibuprofen 10 mg/kg (maximum 400 mg) six-hourly regularly for five days to prevent a febrile convulsion.
Withhold all antipyretics so that the true fever pattern can be documented before his next review.
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg regularly and add tepid sponging every two hours until the temperature settles.

subtopic_detail: Urine testing in the febrile young infant with a positive viral swab
stem:
A 6-week-old boy born at 39 weeks is brought to the emergency department with three days of a runny nose and a wet cough. His mother says he now stops part way through feeds to catch his breath and is taking about two thirds of his usual volume.

On examination he has mild subcostal recession with widespread crackles and expiratory wheeze. He has had four wet nappies in the last 12 hours and is alert between coughing bouts.

A nasopharyngeal swab has returned positive for respiratory syncytial virus, and his temperature has been recorded at 38.4 degrees Celsius on two separate occasions in the department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158/min, blood pressure 78/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 58/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius

lead_in: In addition to supportive care, which investigation is most important now?

options.text: Chest radiograph to identify a bacterial focus before any antibiotic is commenced.
Venous blood gas and lactate to grade the severity of his respiratory illness.
Full blood count with C-reactive protein to decide whether empirical antibiotics are required.
Catheter urine specimen sent for microscopy, culture and antimicrobial sensitivity testing.
Repeat nasopharyngeal testing for pertussis and adenovirus to look for viral co-infection.

subtopic_detail: Parent-recorded fever that has settled before arrival in a young infant
stem:
A 5-week-old girl born at term is brought to the emergency department at 2 am. Her parents recorded axillary temperatures of 38.3 and 38.5 degrees Celsius two hours apart at home using a digital thermometer, and they have not given any medicine.

She fed poorly during the evening but has since taken a full 90 mL bottle in the waiting room. She is alert, has a soft fontanelle, no rash, and a normal cardiorespiratory and abdominal examination.

Her temperature in triage is 37.2 degrees Celsius and the resident asks whether the workup can be stood down now that she is afebrile and feeding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the documented home temperature as fever and proceed with the young infant evaluation.
Observe in the short stay unit for six hours and investigate only if the fever returns.
Reassure the parents that axillary readings overestimate and arrange a general practice review tomorrow.
Send a bag urine specimen and discharge her home if the dipstick shows no nitrites at all.
Request a full blood count and C-reactive protein and take cultures only if either is abnormal.

subtopic_detail: Fever without source in the fully immunised toddler aged 3 to 36 months
stem:
A 14-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department with two days of fever reaching 39.6 degrees Celsius. There is no cough, rash, vomiting or loose stools, and her appetite for solids is reduced but she is drinking well.

She is fully immunised for age and has never been unwell before. In the cubicle she is pulling books off the shelf and objects to examination vigorously.

Ears, throat, chest, abdomen and skin are all normal, and after 40 minutes of observation and a careful second look you have still not identified a focus for the fever.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 30/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take blood cultures and commence intravenous ceftriaxone while the culture results are awaited.
Arrange a chest radiograph to look for an occult bacterial focus in the lower airway.
Send a catheter or clean catch urine specimen for microscopy, culture and sensitivities.
Prescribe oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg three times daily and review him in 48 hours.
Discharge home with antipyretic advice alone and no further investigation on this visit.

subtopic_detail: Fever in the asplenic child on penicillin prophylaxis
stem:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to a regional emergency department four hours after his mother recorded a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius. He vomited once in the car, has a mild sore throat and is otherwise complaining of nothing.

He is alert and chatty, his peripheries are warm with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, and examination of his chest, abdomen, skin and joints is unremarkable.

He had a splenectomy two years ago for hereditary spherocytosis, has received all the recommended additional vaccines, and his mother confirms she gave his twice daily phenoxymethylpenicillin this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care blood glucose 5.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase the phenoxymethylpenicillin to four times daily and review him again in 24 hours.
Send a throat swab and blood film and await both results before giving any antibiotic.
Prescribe oral amoxicillin and arrange review by his general practitioner the next morning.
Observe him in the department for four hours and discharge if he stays alert and afebrile.
Take blood cultures and give intravenous ceftriaxone now, then admit him for observation.

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of fever in the child returned from a malarious region
stem:
A 9-year-old girl presents with three days of fever reaching 39.2 degrees Celsius, associated with shaking chills, headache and two episodes of vomiting. She returned ten days ago from three weeks visiting family in eastern Indonesia.

She has no cough, no dysuria, no diarrhoea and no rash. Her abdomen is soft with a spleen tip palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin, and the rest of the examination is normal.

Her mother says the atovaquone with proguanil tablets were started late and several doses were missed during the trip.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), white cell count 4.8 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), bilirubin 28 micromol/L (2-20)

lead_in: Which investigation is most important now?

options.text: Blood culture with abdominal ultrasound looking for a hepatic or splenic collection.
Thick and thin blood films with a rapid diagnostic test, repeated 12 to 24 hourly.
Dengue NS1 antigen with paired serology sent to the state reference laboratory.
Enteric fever serology with stool culture and a full blood count taken today.
Epstein-Barr virus serology with liver function tests and a repeat full blood count.

subtopic_detail: Empirical therapy for prolonged fever after travel to South Asia
stem:
An 11-year-old boy has had seven days of fever that has climbed a little higher each evening, now reaching 39.4 degrees Celsius. He has a dull headache, abdominal discomfort and was constipated for four days before passing loose stools yesterday.

He returned eight days ago from six weeks staying with relatives in rural Uttar Pradesh. Three sets of thick and thin films have been negative and a rapid antigen test for malaria is negative.

His abdomen is mildly distended with a spleen tip palpable, and his pulse is 88 per minute while his temperature is 39.4 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 3.4 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), platelets 128 x10^9/L (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 92 U/L (5-40), C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical treatment?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 15 mg/kg (maximum 750 mg) twice daily for seven days from today.
Oral amoxicillin 25 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) three times daily for fourteen days from today.
Oral metronidazole 10 mg/kg (maximum 400 mg) three times daily for seven days from today.
Intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) once daily for fourteen days from today.
Oral azithromycin 20 mg/kg (maximum 1 g) once daily for three days only from today.

subtopic_detail: Blood culture sampling in the febrile child with a central venous access device
stem:
A 7-year-old girl on maintenance chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is brought in by her father after a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius at home, now 38.9 degrees Celsius in the department.

She is alert and talking, her peripheries are warm with a capillary refill of 2 seconds, and there is no cough, dysuria, rash or abdominal tenderness. The exit site of her double lumen tunnelled central line is clean and non-tender.

Her full blood count taken on arrival shows a neutrophil count of 3.2 x10^9/L, and the nurse is drawing up the first antibiotic dose while you decide how blood should be collected.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 106 g/L (115-155), white cell count 5.6 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), neutrophils 3.2 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to blood culture collection?

options.text: A single set drawn from the lumen most recently used to deliver her chemotherapy.
A single peripheral set only, since the exit site shows no redness, discharge or tenderness.
Cultures deferred until her temperature again exceeds 39 degrees Celsius on repeat measurement.
One set from a single lumen plus surface swabs from the exit site and nares.
Paired sets from a peripheral vein and from each lumen of her central venous line.

subtopic_detail: Stopping empirical antibiotics after a viral cerebrospinal fluid result in an infant
stem:
A 6-week-old boy was admitted two days ago with a temperature of 38.5 degrees Celsius and marked irritability. A full evaluation including lumbar puncture was performed on arrival and he was started on intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin.

He has now been afebrile for 18 hours, is taking full feeds, settles easily in his mother's arms and has a soft fontanelle with a normal neurological examination.

The laboratory has telephoned to report that blood, urine and cerebrospinal fluid cultures remain sterile at 36 hours and that the cerebrospinal fluid enterovirus polymerase chain reaction is positive.

data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 46 x10^6/L (0-5) with 90% lymphocytes, red cells 4 x10^6/L, protein 0.55 g/L (0.15-0.45), glucose 3.2 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 5.0 mmol/L, Gram stain no organisms seen
data_table.Blood: White cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (5.0-19.5), C-reactive protein 12 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intravenous cefotaxime to complete a seven day course and then reassess him.
Change to oral amoxicillin for five days and discharge him with community nurse review.
Cease antibiotics and discharge him with general practice review within the next 24 hours.
Add intravenous aciclovir and repeat the lumbar puncture within the next 24 hours for review.
Continue antibiotics until cultures have remained sterile for a full 72 hours before stopping.

subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia detected during paediatric septic shock resuscitation
stem:
A 3-year-old boy weighing 15 kg is brought in by ambulance with two days of fever and a day of refusing all fluids. He is difficult to rouse, his knees and hands are mottled and his capillary refill is 4 seconds centrally.

Intraosseous access has been secured in the proximal tibia, blood cultures have been drawn, intravenous ceftriaxone has been given and a 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride has run over eight minutes.

His conscious state has not improved after the bolus and the bedside glucose meter reads 2.0 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 182/min, blood pressure 82/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 96% on 8 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.4 mmol/L (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 2.0 mmol/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Give 2 mL/kg of 10% glucose intravenously and recheck the blood glucose in 15 minutes.
Start a maintenance infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride with 5% glucose and recheck hourly.
Give 5 mL/kg of 10% glucose intravenously and recheck the blood glucose in 30 minutes.
Give intramuscular glucagon 0.5 mg and recheck the blood glucose again in 15 minutes.
Give a further 20 mL/kg bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride over 10 minutes and reassess him.

subtopic_detail: Escalation to intraosseous access when cannulation fails in a shocked infant
stem:
A 4-month-old girl weighing 6 kg is brought to a district emergency department with 12 hours of fever and reduced feeding. She is mottled to the elbows and knees, her capillary refill is 5 seconds and she responds only to painful stimulus.

The sepsis pathway has been activated, oxygen is running and the drugs are drawn up. Her temperature is 38.8 degrees Celsius and her blood pressure is 62/34 mmHg.

Three attempts at peripheral cannulation by two clinicians over the past two minutes have all failed and no further visible or palpable veins remain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 198/min, blood pressure 62/34 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO2 94% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 4.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to deliver resuscitation?

options.text: Persist with further peripheral attempts while giving intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg now.
Insert an intraosseous needle and give the fluid bolus and first antibiotic through it.
Request an ultrasound guided femoral central line from the retrieval intensive care team.
Pass a nasogastric tube and give oral rehydration solution while vascular access is sought.
Perform a venous cutdown on the long saphenous vein at the ankle under anaesthetic.

subtopic_detail: Induction agent selection for intubation in paediatric septic shock
stem:
A 5-year-old girl weighing 18 kg has received 40 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid and is on a peripheral adrenaline infusion for septic shock. Blood cultures were taken and ceftriaxone was given within 30 minutes of arrival.

Her work of breathing has increased over the last 20 minutes, she is now grunting, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score has fallen from 13 to 9. The retrieval team is 90 minutes away and the consultant has decided to intubate her here.

Her blood pressure is 72/38 mmHg and her venous lactate has risen from 3.9 to 5.6 mmol/L over the last hour.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168/min, blood pressure 72/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 92% on 15 L/min via reservoir mask, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 5.6 mmol/L (less than 2.0), pH 7.21, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22-32), bedside glucose 5.8 mmol/L

lead_in: Which induction agent is most appropriate?

options.text: Propofol 2 mg/kg intravenously with fentanyl 1 microgram/kg as the induction sequence.
Thiopentone 4 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
Midazolam 0.2 mg/kg intravenously with suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
Ketamine 1 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.
Etomidate 0.3 mg/kg intravenously with rocuronium 1 mg/kg as the induction sequence.

subtopic_detail: Ward recognition of deterioration in a febrile child already under observation
stem:
You are the paediatric resident asked to review a 2-year-old boy on the ward. He was admitted eight hours ago with fever and reduced oral intake and has been having hourly observations.

Two hours ago he was given paracetamol and took 10 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution without vomiting. His temperature has now settled to 37.8 degrees Celsius but his heart rate has not come down with it.

He was chatting to his mother at the last review and now has to be repeatedly roused for observations, with cool knees and a central capillary refill of 4 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Difficult to rouse, cool peripheries to the knees, central capillary refill 4 seconds, no rash, moist mucous membranes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Escalate on the sepsis pathway with cultures, lactate and intravenous antibiotics now.
Repeat the paracetamol dose now and reassess his heart rate again in a further hour.
Arrange an urgent chest radiograph to identify the source before any antibiotic is given.
Give a further 10 mL/kg of oral rehydration solution and continue hourly observations.
Request an urgent full blood count and C-reactive protein before starting any treatment.

subtopic_detail: Vasoactive selection in vasodilated fluid refractory septic shock
stem:
An 8-year-old girl weighing 26 kg has had three days of fever and is now hypotensive. Blood cultures were taken, ceftriaxone was given within 25 minutes and she has received 60 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid in 20 mL/kg aliquots over 40 minutes.

Her chest remains clear, her liver edge is not palpable and there is no gallop rhythm. She is drowsy but rousable and her urine output over the last hour was 0.3 mL/kg/hour.

Her hands and feet are warm to the touch with bounding pulses and a capillary refill under 1 second, and her blood pressure remains 78/30 mmHg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, blood pressure 78/30 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 3.8 mmol/L (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L, base excess -7 mmol/L

lead_in: Which vasoactive agent is most appropriate now?

options.text: Adrenaline infusion started at 0.05 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
Dobutamine infusion started at 5 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
Noradrenaline infusion at 0.05 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
Milrinone infusion started at 0.25 microgram/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.
Vasopressin infusion started at 0.0003 units/kg/min through a large peripheral cannula.

subtopic_detail: Carriage clearance for the index case after treated invasive meningococcal disease
stem:
A 14-year-old boy is on day five of intravenous benzylpenicillin for invasive meningococcal disease confirmed by blood polymerase chain reaction. He has been afebrile for 48 hours, his rash has faded and he is eating normally.

The public health unit has already contacted his household and all four members have taken their clearance antibiotics. His school has been notified and no further cases have occurred.

He is ready for discharge this afternoon and his mother asks whether he himself needs to take anything before going home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 18 mg/L (less than 5), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action before he is discharged?

options.text: No further antibiotic is required because he has completed a full treatment course.
Give rifampicin 10 mg/kg once daily for five days before he leaves the ward today.
Repeat a nasopharyngeal swab and treat only if meningococci are subsequently grown.
Give a further 48 hours of intravenous benzylpenicillin before discharge is considered.
Give ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose before he leaves the ward today.

subtopic_detail: Fever without source in the incompletely immunised toddler
stem:
A 15-month-old boy presents with 36 hours of fever peaking at 39.9 degrees Celsius. He is miserable when the fever climbs but settles, smiles and accepts a bottle after paracetamol.

Examination of his ears, throat, chest, abdomen, skin and joints is normal, his neck is supple and his fontanelle has closed. He has had four wet nappies today and his capillary refill is 2 seconds.

His parents have declined all childhood vaccinations, so he has never received a conjugate pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae type b dose.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148/min, blood pressure 94/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 39.6 degrees Celsius

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge with antipyretic advice and general practitioner review in 48 hours if unwell.
Perform a lumbar puncture now because he has never been immunised against Haemophilus.
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg now and arrange review in the department tomorrow.
Take blood culture and catheter urine, then reassess in the department after four hours.
Perform a chest radiograph and start oral amoxicillin if any consolidation is demonstrated.

subtopic_detail: Obtaining cerebrospinal fluid in a febrile child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt
stem:
A 5-year-old girl with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted at 4 months for post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus presents with two days of fever to 38.8 degrees Celsius. She has vomited four times today and complains that her head hurts when she lies down.

She is irritable but rousable and orientated, her neck is supple, her fontanelle has long closed and there are no focal neurological signs. The skin over the shunt tract is intact, flat and not tender.

Her shunt was revised 6 weeks ago for a distal catheter blockage and she has had no abdominal pain since.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126/min, blood pressure 100/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.6 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5); computed tomography shows ventricles unchanged from her baseline study

lead_in: What is the most appropriate way to obtain cerebrospinal fluid?

options.text: Bedside lumbar puncture at the L3 to L4 interspace given the reassuring computed tomography.
Shunt reservoir aspiration done by the neurosurgical team under a strict aseptic technique.
External ventricular drain insertion in theatre to allow continuous drainage and sampling.
Bedside lumbar puncture at the L4 to L5 interspace done by the medical registrar today.
Cisternal puncture done under image guidance by the interventional radiology service today.

subtopic_detail: Parenteral therapy for severe imported falciparum malaria in a child
stem:
A 12-year-old boy weighing 38 kg returned from three weeks in Papua New Guinea twelve days ago and has had four days of fever. Over the last six hours he has become progressively drowsy and has vomited twice.

He opens his eyes to voice, is confused in conversation and localises to pain. His neck is supple, there is no rash and his chest is clear. His spleen is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.

Thick and thin films report Plasmodium falciparum with a parasitaemia of 6% and no other species seen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (130-170), platelets 48 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 110 micromol/L (45-90), bilirubin 60 micromol/L (2-20), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 3.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 hours, then once daily thereafter.
Oral artemether with lumefantrine as a six dose regimen given over the next three days.
Intravenous quinine 20 mg/kg as a loading dose then 10 mg/kg every eight hours.
Oral atovaquone with proguanil at treatment dose once daily for the next three days.
Intravenous doxycycline 2 mg/kg twice daily with oral primaquine given as radical cure.

subtopic_detail: Sequencing antibiotics and imaging when raised intracranial pressure is suspected
stem:
A 4-year-old girl presents with 12 hours of fever, headache and three episodes of vomiting. Her mother says she has become harder and harder to wake over the last hour.

She opens her eyes to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds and localises the painful stimulus. Her neck is stiff and there is no rash anywhere on her body.

Her right pupil measures 5 mm and responds sluggishly to light while the left measures 3 mm and is brisk, and her respiratory pattern has become irregular.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 62/min, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min and irregular, SpO2 97% on 8 L/min oxygen, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 9 (E2 V2 M5), right pupil 5 mm sluggish, left pupil 3 mm brisk, neck stiffness present
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 6.1 mmol/L, coagulation profile pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture now to obtain cerebrospinal fluid before starting antibiotics.
Arrange computed tomography of the brain first and give the antibiotics once she returns.
Give dexamethasone then ceftriaxone now and defer the lumbar puncture until later.
Give mannitol 0.5 g/kg and arrange urgent transfer without antimicrobial therapy for now.
Intubate for airway protection and observe her before commencing any antimicrobial therapy.

subtopic_detail: Interpreting a traumatic cerebrospinal fluid specimen in a febrile neonate
stem:
A 3-week-old boy born at term was admitted last night with a temperature of 38.6 degrees Celsius and poor feeding. Blood and catheter urine cultures were taken and he was started on intravenous cefotaxime, benzylpenicillin and aciclovir.

The lumbar puncture required three attempts and the fluid was heavily blood stained in all three bottles. Twelve hours later he is afebrile, feeding 80 mL every three hours and neurologically normal.

The registrar proposes applying a red cell to white cell correction ratio to the result and stopping antibiotics if the corrected count falls within the normal range.

data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: Red cells 8600 x10^6/L, white cells 42 x10^6/L (0-20 in neonates) with 60% neutrophils, protein 1.4 g/L (0.4-1.2 in neonates), glucose 2.6 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 5.4 mmol/L, Gram stain no organisms seen
data_table.Blood: White cell count 11.8 x10^9/L (9.0-30.0), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5), cultures negative at 12 hours

lead_in: How should this cerebrospinal fluid result be used?

options.text: Apply a red cell to white cell correction ratio and cease antibiotics if it normalises.
Treat the cell count as uninterpretable and continue antibiotics pending the culture results.
Regard the specimen as normal because the Gram stain showed no organisms in the fluid.
