Treat as proven bacterial meningitis and commit him to a full 21 day intravenous antibiotic course.
Repeat the lumbar puncture immediately to obtain a clean and interpretable specimen today.

subtopic_detail: Corticosteroid decision in bacterial meningitis in the first month of life
stem:
A 3-week-old girl born at 39 weeks was brought in with a temperature of 38.7 degrees Celsius, a high pitched cry and refusal of two consecutive feeds. Her anterior fontanelle was full and she was irritable on handling.

Blood and urine cultures were taken and a lumbar puncture was performed atraumatically before intravenous cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin were commenced within 40 minutes of arrival.

The laboratory has telephoned to report gram positive cocci in chains on the cerebrospinal fluid Gram stain and the consultant asks you what you plan to do about corticosteroid.

data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 1840 x10^6/L (0-20 in neonates) with 88% neutrophils, red cells 6 x10^6/L, protein 2.4 g/L (0.4-1.2 in neonates), glucose 1.1 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 5.2 mmol/L, gram positive cocci in chains seen
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178/min, blood pressure 68/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 56/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius

lead_in: Which one of the following is the most appropriate corticosteroid decision?

options.text: Do not give any corticosteroid; continue the intravenous antibiotics alone.
Give dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg six-hourly intravenously for four days from now.
Give dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg twelve-hourly intravenously for two days from now.
Give hydrocortisone 1 mg/kg six-hourly intravenously for four days from now.
Give methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg daily intravenously for three days from now.

subtopic_detail: Treatment duration and repeat sampling in neonatal gram negative meningitis
stem:
A 2-week-old boy has completed 36 hours of intravenous cefotaxime after presenting with fever, lethargy and a full fontanelle. He is now afebrile, feeding fully and has a normal neurological examination.

Both blood and cerebrospinal fluid cultures have grown Escherichia coli that is sensitive to cefotaxime, gentamicin and meropenem. His mother had no antenatal complications and there were no perinatal risk factors.

The consultant asks you to write the antimicrobial plan including any further investigations before he is stepped down to the ward.

data_table.Cerebrospinal fluid: White cells 920 x10^6/L (0-20 in neonates) with 80% neutrophils, protein 2.8 g/L (0.4-1.2 in neonates), glucose 0.9 mmol/L with paired plasma glucose 4.8 mmol/L, culture Escherichia coli
data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142/min, blood pressure 72/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein falling from 190 to 96 mg/L (less than 5), cranial ultrasound shows no collection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antimicrobial plan?

options.text: Continue cefotaxime for a total of 10 days and discharge without repeat sampling.
Change to oral trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole at day 7 to complete 14 days in total.
Continue cefotaxime for 14 days and image the brain only if the fever returns later.
Add intraventricular gentamicin and complete 14 days of intravenous cefotaxime alongside it.
Continue cefotaxime for 21 days and repeat the lumbar puncture now to confirm clearance.

subtopic_detail: Distribution of petechiae in the febrile child with a non-blanching rash
stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department because his mother noticed tiny red dots on his face and upper chest that did not fade when she pressed a glass against them. He has had two days of a runny nose and a harsh cough with several bouts of coughing until he vomited.

In the department he is running between the chairs, drinking juice and objecting loudly to examination. His peripheries are warm, his capillary refill is 2 seconds and there is no neck stiffness or photophobia.

The non-blanching spots are confined to his face, neck and chest above the nipples, with none on his limbs, lower trunk or mucous membranes, and none has appeared in the three hours since arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 11.2 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), neutrophils 5.4 x10^9/L (1.5-8.0), platelets 285 x10^9/L (150-400), C-reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), coagulation profile within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg now and admit him for 48 hours of observation.
Take blood cultures with meningococcal polymerase chain reaction and then discharge him.
Give a single dose of intramuscular benzylpenicillin 60 mg/kg and review him tomorrow.
Observe in the department for four hours, then discharge with written return advice.
Admit for lumbar puncture and intravenous antibiotics until all cultures are negative.

subtopic_detail: Halting bolus escalation when fluid overload emerges during septic shock resuscitation
stem:
A 2-year-old boy weighing 12 kg presented with two days of fever and eight hours of drowsiness. Blood cultures were taken, intravenous ceftriaxone was given at 18 minutes and he has received 40 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid in 20 mL/kg aliquots over the last 25 minutes.

He remains difficult to rouse with cool mottled peripheries and a central capillary refill of 4 seconds, and his blood pressure has barely moved. His bedside glucose is 5.6 mmol/L and his lactate has fallen only slightly.

Since the second bolus his liver edge has moved from 1 cm to 4 cm below the right costal margin, there are new fine crackles at both bases with a gallop rhythm, and his oxygen saturation has drifted from 98% to 90% on 8 L/min.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 186/min, blood pressure 76/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 90% on 8 L/min oxygen, temperature 39.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Difficult to rouse, cool mottled peripheries, central capillary refill 4 seconds, liver 4 cm below costal margin, gallop rhythm, bibasal fine crackles
data_table.Investigations: Venous lactate 4.9 mmol/L falling from 5.4 (less than 2.0), bedside glucose 5.6 mmol/L, haemoglobin 104 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a third 20 mL/kg bolus of balanced crystalloid over 10 minutes and reassess him.
Give 10 mL/kg of 4% albumin over 20 minutes and then reassess his perfusion afterwards.
Stop the boluses and start adrenaline at 0.05 microgram/kg/min, then call retrieval.
Give intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg and continue boluses towards a total of 60 mL/kg.
Give a 10 mL/kg bolus of packed red cells and withhold vasoactive support.

subtopic_detail: Empirical antimicrobial change in tropical northern Australian sepsis failing pathway therapy
stem: A 13-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes presents in Darwin in February after a week wading through flooded paddocks. He has four days of fever and cough. Twenty hours after intravenous ceftriaxone he remains febrile and noradrenaline dependent.

data_table.Investigations: CRP 340 mg/L, creatinine 128 micromol/L; blood cultures growing gram negative bacilli
data_table.Imaging: Right upper lobe consolidation with a 2 cm cavity

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to antimicrobial therapy?

options.text: Change to intravenous meropenem in place of ceftriaxone
Change to intravenous piperacillin with tazobactam
Add intravenous gentamicin to the current ceftriaxone
Add intravenous azithromycin to the current ceftriaxone
Change to intravenous ciprofloxacin in place of ceftriaxone

subtopic_detail: Umbilical granuloma after cord separation distinguished from omphalitis and umbilical remnants
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-week-old boy, born at term and fully breastfed. His mother says the cord came away on day 9 and since then there has been a small moist pink lump at his belly button that keeps staining his singlet with clear yellowish fluid.

He feeds every three hours, has eight wet nappies a day and regained his birth weight by day 10. He has had no fever and no vomiting. His mother has been cleaning the area with cooled boiled water.

data_table.Examination: 5 mm soft pink pedunculated lesion arising from the umbilical base, no surrounding erythema or induration, no urine and no faeculent material expressed on gentle pressure, abdomen soft with no palpable mass
data_table.Growth: Weight on the 50th centile, tracking since birth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral cefalexin and review the umbilicus in 48 hours
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to assess the urachal remnant
Apply silver nitrate cautery to the lesion and review in one week
Refer to paediatric surgery for excision under general anaesthetic
Take a swab for culture and start topical mupirocin three times daily

subtopic_detail: Prolonged evening crying in a thriving six week old with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6-week-old boy whose parents say he cries inconsolably for about three hours most evenings, drawing his knees up and going red in the face, starting around 5 pm and settling by nine. It began at 3 weeks and is worse on some days than others.

His mother is exclusively breastfeeding and has already cut dairy from her own diet for a fortnight with no change. He feeds eagerly, has eight wet nappies a day, and passes soft yellow stool with no blood or mucus. His father says they are exhausted and have been told to try three different formulas.

data_table.Examination: Alert and settled during the consultation, abdomen soft and non-tender with no mass or organomegaly, no inguinal or scrotal swelling, no anal fissure, normal tone and reflexes, no corneal abrasion and no hair tourniquet on digits
data_table.Growth: Birth weight on the 50th centile, current weight on the 50th centile, length and head circumference tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the pattern, teach settling techniques and arrange early review
Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and review in two weeks
Commence an oral proton pump inhibitor and review him in four weeks
Prescribe simethicone drops to be given before each evening feed
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to exclude a structural abnormality

subtopic_detail: Easily reducible umbilical defect in a well toddler with a low risk of incarceration
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing an 18-month-old girl whose parents point out a bulge at her belly button that has been present since the early weeks of life. It pushes out when she cries or strains and flattens when she lies quietly.

They have read that it can twist and are asking whether she needs an operation before she starts childcare. She has never vomited, has a good appetite and opens her bowels daily. They have been taping a coin over it at night on a relative's advice.

data_table.Examination: Soft symmetrical umbilical protrusion with a 12 mm fascial defect, completely and easily reducible with one finger, skin over it normal with no erythema or tenderness, abdomen otherwise soft with no distension
data_table.Growth: Weight and height both on the 75th centile and tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for elective surgical repair before she commences childcare
Apply a compression dressing over the defect until it has closed
Request an abdominal ultrasound to measure the fascial defect size
Reassure, advise stopping the taping and review at 4 years of age
Refer urgently to the surgical team for assessment within 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Vulval soreness with scant discharge in a prepubertal girl with no bleeding or foreign body features
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-year-old girl whose mother reports 6 weeks of on and off soreness and itch around the vulva, worse after swimming lessons and when she has been in her leotard all afternoon. There is a small amount of thin discharge on her underwear but no blood.

She wipes herself after using the toilet and often forgets to wash her hands. She has no urinary frequency or dysuria, no bedwetting, no weight loss and no behavioural change. Her mother has been using a bubble bath and a scented soap at bath time.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema of the vulval skin and posterior fourchette with no excoriation, no bruising, no laceration and no bleeding, hymen intact and unremarkable on separation, no visible foreign material, no inguinal lymphadenopathy, no rash elsewhere
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for nitrites, leucocytes and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a 7 day course of oral cefalexin and review after treatment
Advise hygiene measures with a barrier ointment and review in 4 weeks
Apply topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for two weeks and review
Refer to a paediatric gynaecologist for examination under anaesthetic
Refer to the child protection unit for a formal forensic assessment

subtopic_detail: Laryngomalacia complicated by faltering growth requiring airway endoscopy rather than observation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old boy referred with noisy breathing that began at 4 weeks of age. His mother describes a high pitched noise as he breathes in, worse when he lies on his back and when he feeds, and much quieter when he is on his tummy.

Feeds now take 45 minutes, during which he repeatedly pulls off the breast and goes red in the face. His weight has fallen from the 50th centile at birth to the 3rd centile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 136 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor audible at rest, mild suprasternal recession, no barking cough, chest clear on auscultation, no cutaneous haemangioma on the head or neck, no dysmorphic features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review when he is 12 months of age
Commence a proton pump inhibitor and thicken feeds for 6 weeks
Give oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and observe for 3 hours
Arrange a chest radiograph to look for a vascular ring
Refer for flexible laryngoscopy and paediatric airway assessment

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal perianal itch in a school aged child requiring treatment of the whole household
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother reports 3 weeks of intense itching around his bottom, always after he goes to bed, waking him most nights and leaving him irritable at school. She looked with a torch two nights ago and saw what she describes as small moving white threads.

His 4-year-old sister has started scratching too. He has had no diarrhoea, no weight loss, no fever and no blood in the stool. The family has not travelled.

data_table.Examination: Perianal excoriation from scratching with no fissure, no fistula and no perianal erythema suggesting streptococcal infection, abdomen soft and non-tender, no rash elsewhere
data_table.Growth: Weight and height tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the whole household and repeat the dose after two weeks
Treat the index child only with a single dose and review at 4 weeks
Send three stool specimens for microscopy before starting any treatment
Apply a topical corticosteroid nightly for one week and review after
Advise hygiene measures alone and treat only if symptoms persist

subtopic_detail: Positional plagiocephaly distinguished from lambdoid craniosynostosis by head shape and ear position
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 5-month-old boy whose parents noticed flattening at the back of his head from about 3 months of age. He sleeps supine, dislikes tummy time, and was treated with physiotherapy for a right sided head tilt at 8 weeks.

His parents want to know whether he needs an operation. He is smiling, rolling front to back and reaching for objects with both hands.

data_table.Examination viewed from above: Right occipital flattening with the right ear displaced anteriorly and mild right frontal prominence, giving a parallelogram outline
data_table.Skull examination: Anterior fontanelle open and soft, no palpable ridge over any suture, no bulging behind the ear
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile and tracking

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the skull with 3 dimensional views
Refer urgently to the craniofacial unit for surgical assessment
Advise repositioning and tummy time with physiotherapy review
Refer for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted this month
Request skull radiographs to assess the lambdoid suture

subtopic_detail: Distal radial buckle fracture treated with a removable splint rather than cast immobilisation
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 7-year-old boy who fell from the monkey bars onto an outstretched right hand two hours ago. He is holding the wrist and says it hurts when he tries to turn a doorknob.

He has been able to move all his fingers since the fall and there is no other injury. His parents are asking how long he will be in plaster.

data_table.Examination: Minimal swelling over the distal radius with no deformity, no tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox or over the distal ulna, full finger movement, capillary refill under 2 seconds, normal sensation in median, ulnar and radial distributions
data_table.Radiograph: Buckling of the dorsal cortex of the distal radial metaphysis with the volar cortex intact, no angulation, distal radioulnar joint congruent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Below elbow backslab and fracture clinic review within one week
Full below elbow cast for 6 weeks with repeat radiographs at 3 weeks
Closed reduction under procedural sedation then apply a cast
Sling for comfort and repeat radiographs in 10 days to reassess
Removable wrist splint for 3 to 4 weeks without routine follow up

subtopic_detail: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy and a positive Gowers sign requiring creatine kinase measurement
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred because he walks on his toes most of the time. His parents were told at his 3 year check that it was habit and that he would grow out of it.

He walked independently at 17 months, still falls several times a day, and climbs stairs one foot at a time holding the rail. He speaks in full sentences and is toilet trained. He was born at term with no perinatal problems.

data_table.Gait and lower limb examination: Walks on the toes of both feet with intermittent heel contact, bulky firm calves bilaterally, ankle dorsiflexion 5 degrees beyond neutral with the knee extended
data_table.Neurological examination: Rises from the floor by turning prone and pushing up on his own thighs, normal tone, reflexes present and symmetrical, no ankle clonus, plantar responses downgoing, no spinal dimple or hairy patch

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for a serial casting program of both ankles
Measure the serum creatine kinase and review the result urgently
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spinal cord
Refer for orthopaedic tendo Achilles lengthening assessment now
Request nerve conduction studies of both lower limbs this week

subtopic_detail: Craniocervical junction stenosis in achondroplasia presenting with central apnoea and long tract signs
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 9-month-old boy with genetically confirmed achondroplasia in the growth clinic. Over the past 6 weeks his parents have noticed pauses in his breathing during sleep, each ending with a snort, and they feel he has become floppier when they pick him up.

He is not yet sitting unsupported. His head circumference is tracking along the 75th centile of the achondroplasia specific chart.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128 beats per minute, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Neurological examination: Central hypotonia with head lag on pull to sit, brisk knee and ankle reflexes, four beats of sustained ankle clonus on the right, plantar responses upgoing bilaterally
data_table.Upper airway examination: Tonsils small, no adenoidal facies, no stridor at rest

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that hypotonia and delayed motor milestones are expected
Arrange overnight oximetry at home and review in three months
Refer for adenotonsillectomy to treat obstructive sleep apnoea
Arrange craniocervical junction imaging and a polysomnogram
Request cervical spine radiographs in flexion and extension

subtopic_detail: Segmental facial infantile haemangioma with persistent stridor indicating subglottic airway involvement
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3-month-old girl whose parents report two weeks of a harsh cough and noisy breathing. She was treated for croup by her general practitioner four days ago with a single dose of oral dexamethasone, with no improvement.

She has a flat red patch covering her chin, lower lip and the front of her neck that was first noticed at 3 weeks of age and has been enlarging since. She has remained afebrile throughout and is feeding more slowly than usual.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 80/46 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor audible at rest with intercostal and suprasternal recession, confluent bright red plaque over the chin, lower lip and anterior neck, chest clear on auscultation, no drooling and no toxic appearance

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg and observe
Refer urgently for flexible laryngoscopy of the upper airway
Commence oral propranolol at home with weekly phone review
Arrange a chest radiograph and treat for bacterial tracheitis
Arrange ultrasound of the neck lesion and review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Right sided varicocele that fails to decompress when supine as a marker of retroperitoneal pathology
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 13-year-old boy who noticed a dull ache in his right scrotum after football and told his mother it feels like a bag of worms above his right testicle. The ache has been present for about six weeks and is worse at the end of the day.

He has had no fever, no urinary symptoms and no weight loss. He is in Tanner stage 3 and his height is tracking along the 50th centile.

data_table.Scrotal examination: Soft non-tender mass of distended veins above the right testis that persists unchanged when he lies flat, left hemiscrotum normal, both testes 12 mL and equal in size and consistency
data_table.Abdominal examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable mass or organomegaly, no inguinal hernia, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure and review in 12 months with testicular volume measured
Refer for varicocele embolisation by interventional radiology
Arrange a scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and review the result
Refer to urology for elective varicocelectomy within 6 months
Arrange abdominal imaging to exclude a retroperitoneal mass

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic neonate with pulmonary venous congestion and a normal cardiac silhouette in whom prostaglandin is harmful
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar at a regional hospital 400 kilometres from the nearest paediatric cardiac surgical centre, where there is no echocardiography available overnight. A term male infant born 6 hours ago by normal vaginal delivery has developed worsening respiratory distress and cyanosis.

He was given 100 per cent oxygen by headbox 20 minutes ago with no change in his saturations. The consultant is driving in. Your resident has drawn up prostaglandin E1 and is asking you to confirm the infusion.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 178 beats per minute, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 80 breaths per minute, SpO2 78 percent right hand and 77 percent right foot, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked subcostal and intercostal recession with grunting, liver edge 3 cm below the costal margin, no murmur audible, femoral pulses present and equal to brachial pulses
data_table.Chest radiograph: Normal cardiac silhouette with cardiothoracic ratio 0.52, diffuse ground glass opacification of both lung fields with septal lines, no pneumothorax
data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.18, PaCO2 38 mmHg, PaO2 32 mmHg on 100 percent oxygen, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L, lactate 6.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intubate and ventilate and arrange urgent cardiac surgical transfer
Commence prostaglandin E1 at 10 nanogram per kilogram per minute
Give a 20 mL per kilogram sodium chloride 0.9 percent fluid bolus
Commence nasal CPAP with intravenous furosemide and fluid restriction
Arrange urgent echocardiography before starting any other treatment

subtopic_detail: Tender concentric subareolar breast tissue in a pubertal boy with symmetrical testes and normal pubertal progression
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14-year-old boy brought in by his father because both his breasts have become swollen and sore over the past six months. He has stopped swimming with his friends and keeps his shirt on at the beach, and his father wants to know whether an operation is needed.

He takes no medication, uses no protein powders or muscle building supplements, and does not use cannabis or alcohol. He has grown 8 cm in the past year and his voice has begun to deepen.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, a firm mobile tender disc of tissue about 3 cm across lying concentrically beneath each areola, no nipple discharge or skin tethering, no axillary lymphadenopathy, Tanner stage 3 pubic hair with testicular volume 10 mL on both sides and no testicular mass, no hepatomegaly, visual fields full to confrontation
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Measure beta human chorionic gonadotrophin, testosterone and oestradiol today
Refer to a paediatric surgeon for bilateral subcutaneous mastectomy of the tissue
Reassure with an explanation of the natural history and review him in six months
Commence tamoxifen to reduce the glandular tissue over the next three months
Arrange a scrotal ultrasound scan and a karyotype to look for a syndromic cause

subtopic_detail: Inward pointing feet in a toddler with normal hip rotation and an inwardly rotated thigh foot axis
stem:
You are the registrar in a general paediatric clinic reviewing a 2-year-old girl whose parents say both her feet point inwards when she walks and that she trips over more than other children at her playgroup. They have been told by a relative that she needs special boots before the bones set.

She walked at 13 months, has no pain, and keeps up with her older brother in the park. She sits on the floor with her legs out in front rather than between her heels.

data_table.Examination: Feet point inwards symmetrically during gait, hip internal rotation 45 degrees and external rotation 45 degrees bilaterally in the prone position, thigh foot axis 20 degrees internal on both sides, forefoot border straight, no leg length difference and full painless knee and ankle movement
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review her gait at the next routine visit
Prescribe a night time derotation brace to be worn until school age
Request standing radiographs of both lower limbs to measure the torsion
Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of a tibial derotation osteotomy
Advise she avoid sitting in the W position and start corrective footwear

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs and wrist swelling in a prolonged breastfed toddler with a raised alkaline phosphatase and symmetrical metaphyseal change
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 18-month-old girl referred because her legs have become increasingly bowed since she started walking at 16 months. Her mother says her wrists look knobbly and that she is slower to get up off the floor than her cousin of the same age.

She was breastfed as her only milk until 14 months and now drinks small amounts of cow's milk. Her mother has deeply pigmented skin, wears clothing covering her arms and legs outdoors, and takes no supplements. There are no bruises anywhere on the child, and the family has no history of bone disease or fractures.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened painless wrists and costochondral junctions, anterior fontanelle closed, no bruising or skin injury, normal tone and power
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20-2.65), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20-1.80), alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (110-320), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (greater than 50), parathyroid hormone elevated, urea creatinine and electrolytes within normal limits, wrist radiograph shows symmetrical metaphyseal cupping and fraying at both distal radii

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Start oral calcitriol and repeat the calcium in two weeks
Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of the lower limb deformity
Give intravenous calcium gluconate and admit for cardiac monitoring
Arrange a skeletal survey and notify child protection services
Start oral colecalciferol with supplemental dietary calcium

subtopic_detail: Repeated nosebleeds from one nostril in a school aged child with normal platelets and normal coagulation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy brought in because he has had nosebleeds most weeks through the winter. His mother says blood comes from the right side only, it stops within about five minutes when she pinches the soft part of his nose, and it usually happens after he has been picking at it.

He has eczema treated with a moisturiser and uses no other medications. He has never bled from his gums or had bleeding after a dental extraction, and no one in the family bruises easily or has needed treatment for bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Prominent dilated vessels on the anterior right nasal septum with a small area of adherent crust, no septal perforation, no facial or oral petechiae, no bruising or lymphadenopathy, spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), platelets 286 x10^9/L (150-400), white cell count within normal limits, prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for examination under anaesthesia
Apply an antiseptic nasal cream to the affected nostril for two weeks
Cauterise the bleeding point with a silver nitrate stick at this visit
Request von Willebrand factor assays and a platelet function analysis
Prescribe oral tranexamic acid to be taken through the winter months

subtopic_detail: Midline translucent membrane fusing the labia minora in a preschool girl who voids normally
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the opening between her lips looks closed over and is worried that she has been born with something missing.

The child is toilet trained, passes a normal stream without straining or dribbling afterwards, and has never had a urinary infection or a fever without a cause. She has no itch, no discharge and no pain, and her mother has not seen her scratching or touching the area.

data_table.Examination: Labia minora fused in the midline by a thin translucent membrane with a visible pale line along the fusion, a patent opening anteriorly through which the urethral meatus is seen, vulval skin otherwise normal with no erythema, excoriation, whitening or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a topical oestrogen cream along the fusion line each night
Separate the adhesion manually during this consultation
Refer for surgical division of the adhesion under general anaesthesia
Reassure the parents and review at the next scheduled health check
Apply a topical betamethasone ointment along the fusion line nightly

subtopic_detail: Ballooning of the foreskin on voiding in a preschool boy with a healthy pink preputial opening
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4-year-old boy whose father has asked for a referral for circumcision. He says the foreskin puffs up like a balloon when the boy passes urine and then the urine comes out in a normal stream, and that the foreskin has never pulled back.

The boy has had no urinary infections, no fevers without a cause and no pain when he passes urine. His father has been pulling the foreskin back a little each bath time because he was told it would loosen it.

data_table.Examination: Foreskin non retractile with a soft pink preputial opening that pouts on gentle traction, no white scarring or thickened ring at the tip, glans not visible, no erythema, discharge or tenderness of the prepuce
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure about normal non retractility and advise against retraction
Apply a topical corticosteroid ointment to the preputial tip for six weeks
Refer to a paediatric surgeon for circumcision on the current waiting list
Teach the father a graded daily retraction routine with a lubricant
Prescribe an oral antibiotic and arrange a renal tract ultrasound scan

subtopic_detail: Fevers recurring on a fixed monthly cycle with oral ulceration and a neutrophilia measured during an episode
stem: A 4-year-old boy has had four-day fevers every 26 to 28 days for eight months, predictable within two days, with sore throat and mouth ulcers. Between episodes he is well and grows along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: During today's episode: T 39.4 degrees C, two aphthous ulcers, injected pharynx, tender cervical nodes
data_table.Investigations: Taken today: neutrophils 11.2 x10^9/L (1.5 to 8.0), CRP 68 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Full blood counts twice weekly for six weeks
Tonsillectomy as definitive treatment of the episodes
Long term oral phenoxymethylpenicillin prophylaxis
Genetic testing for the Mediterranean fever gene
A single oral prednisolone dose at the next onset

subtopic_detail: Painless limp of several weeks in a school aged boy with restricted hip abduction and normal inflammatory markers
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 7-year-old boy whose parents say he has walked with a limp for about six weeks. He complains mostly of an ache in the front of his right thigh and in his knee after football training, and he has been reluctant to run at school.

He has had no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss, and no viral illness in the months before the limp began. He is otherwise well, takes no medication, and has never had a hip problem or a significant injury.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 per minute, blood pressure 102/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Antalgic gait on the right, right hip internal rotation 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the left, abduction restricted to 25 degrees, no groin or knee effusion, knee ligaments stable, no spinal tenderness and no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 7.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 8 mm/h (less than 15)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate investigation?

options.text: Ultrasound of the right hip with aspiration of any effusion identified
Plain radiographs of both hips including frog leg lateral projections
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis under general anaesthesia
No imaging, with simple analgesia and clinical review in two weeks
Blood cultures with an urgent orthopaedic review for joint washout

subtopic_detail: Absent red reflex on one side in an infant whose family noticed a pale pupil in flash photographs
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-month-old girl at her immunisation visit. Her mother shows you three photographs taken over the past two months in which the left pupil looks pale and creamy while the right pupil looks red, and says a friend told her it was just the camera.

The baby was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, has no family history of eye disease or childhood cancer, and is feeding and growing normally. Her mother has noticed the left eye drifting outwards when she is tired.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex present on the right and absent on the left with a white reflex seen instead, left eye intermittently divergent on cover testing, both eyes of normal size with clear corneas, no proptosis, no orbital or lid swelling, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family that this is a photographic artefact and repeat the photographs
Refer routinely for assessment of the divergent eye at twelve months of age
Arrange an orbital ultrasound scan through the local radiology practice first
Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment within the coming week
Refer to a community optometrist for refraction and orthoptic assessment

subtopic_detail: Restricted tongue elevation in a two week old with maternal nipple trauma and weight below birth weight
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14-day-old boy for a weight check. His mother describes cracked painful nipples that hurt through the whole feed, says he feeds for about an hour and wakes within thirty minutes wanting more, and has asked to be referred to have his tongue tie cut today.

She has had no fever, and there is no red wedge shaped area or lump in either breast. She has begun expressing after feeds and getting good volumes into the bottle, which he takes quickly and settles after.

data_table.Examination: Birth weight 3.42 kg, weight today 3.28 kg, tongue tip notched on protrusion with a thin anterior frenulum, tongue elevates to about half the height of the open mouth, palate intact, no cleft, normal suck on a gloved finger with a shallow latch observed at the breast and the nipple emerging compressed and blanched
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin not indicated, no jaundice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a frenotomy at this visit and review the weight in one week
Supply nipple shields and continue direct breastfeeding without other change
Arrange assessment of positioning and attachment with a lactation consultant
Commence formula top ups after each feed and review the weight in one week
Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for frenuloplasty under anaesthesia

subtopic_detail: Months of multifocal bone pain with sterile biopsy and no response to prolonged antistaphylococcal therapy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 10-year-old girl in clinic with four months of pain over her right collarbone and her left ankle. The pain wakes her at night and is worse in the mornings, and she has missed sport but not school.

She was admitted three months ago, had a bone biopsy of the clavicle which grew no organisms on extended culture, and completed six weeks of flucloxacillin with no change in her symptoms. She has had no fevers, no weight loss and no night sweats. Her father has psoriasis affecting his elbows.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 per minute, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Firm non fluctuant swelling and tenderness over the medial right clavicle, tenderness over the left distal tibia, no overlying erythema or warmth, no joint effusions, no rash, no nail pitting
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.9 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5), C reactive protein 14 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 32 mm/h (less than 15), blood cultures negative, clavicular biopsy histology shows a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with no organisms on special stains, radiograph of the clavicle shows sclerosis with periosteal new bone

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Whole body magnetic resonance imaging with short tau inversion recovery sequences
Repeat bone biopsy with prolonged culture for mycobacteria and fungi
Technetium bone scan to identify areas of increased osteoblastic activity
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to exclude leukaemia and neuroblastoma
Computed tomography of the clavicle to define the extent of bone destruction

subtopic_detail: Hypoglycaemia during an intercurrent illness with inappropriately low ketones in a toddler who had no newborn screening
stem:
You are the emergency registrar called to a 16-month-old boy who has been vomiting and refusing food for 24 hours during a gastroenteritis outbreak at his childcare centre. He was born overseas, arrived in Australia at nine months, and his mother says he had no heel prick test as a newborn.

He is drowsy but rousable and has had no seizure. There is no diarrhoea with blood, no rash and no history of possible ingestion. He has had two similar admissions for drowsiness during viral illnesses in the past year, each time recovering quickly after treatment in another emergency department.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 per minute, blood pressure 88/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable to voice, capillary refill 3 seconds, liver edge palpable 3 cm below the costal margin, no rash, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive
data_table.Investigations: Bedside glucose 1.8 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), blood ketones 0.2 mmol/L (rise above 1.0 with fasting hypoglycaemia), venous pH 7.34 with bicarbonate 19 mmol/L (22-28), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), lactate 1.9 mmol/L (less than 2.0), alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give intravenous glucose now and arrange metabolic testing once he has recovered
Give an intramuscular dose of glucagon and repeat the glucose in fifteen minutes
Give oral sucrose by syringe and reassess his conscious state in fifteen minutes
Give intravenous hydrocortisone and take a paired cortisol before treatment starts
Draw the diagnostic blood and urine samples as intravenous glucose is being given

subtopic_detail: Toddler refusing to use an arm after axial traction, held pronated, with no focal bone tenderness and pain only on forearm rotation
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 2-year-old girl who has not used her left arm since her older brother swung her up by both hands at the playground an hour ago. Her mother says she cried for a minute, then settled, and has since been eating and playing one handed.

There was no fall and nothing struck the arm. She lets you touch the whole limb without complaint, and only cries when the forearm is turned.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held slightly flexed and pronated against the trunk, no swelling, bruising or deformity, no focal tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, olecranon, radius or ulna, full passive shoulder movement, resists supination of the forearm, hand warm with radial pulse present and capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling and review her in fracture clinic in seven days
Perform a supination and flexion manoeuvre at the elbow without imaging
Request radiographs of the left elbow before attempting any manipulation
Request radiographs of the left clavicle, humerus and forearm today
Immobilise in an above elbow backslab and review clinically in ten days

subtopic_detail: Limping toddler with focal tibial tenderness after a low energy twisting fall and radiographs reported as normal
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 20-month-old boy who caught his foot at the bottom of a slide yesterday and twisted as he came down. Since then he will crawl and will stand if held, but screams and lifts the right leg whenever he tries to take a step.

He is afebrile, has been well, and has had no recent illness. His mother has seen no swelling and the leg looks straight to her.

data_table.Examination: No effusion, warmth or restriction at the right hip, knee or ankle, full painless passive rotation of the hip, point tenderness over the mid to distal right tibial shaft, no bruising or deformity, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right tibia and fibula reported as no fracture identified; C reactive protein 4 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply an above knee cast or boot and arrange clinical review in two weeks
Arrange an urgent hip ultrasound and review the result the same afternoon
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after taking blood cultures on arrival
Discharge with simple analgesia and advice to mobilise as pain allows
Arrange a whole body bone scan through the radiology department this week

subtopic_detail: Newborn with inturned feet distinguishing a rigid deformity requiring serial casting from one that corrects passively to neutral
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar performing the newborn examination on a term baby girl on day one. The midwife has asked you to look at her feet, which both point inwards, and her parents want to know whether she will need an operation.

The pregnancy was uncomplicated with normal liquor volume and no breech presentation. She is feeding, moving all four limbs and has a normal neurological examination.

data_table.Examination: Both forefeet are adducted and the heels are turned inwards, the right hindfoot is fixed in equinus and cannot be brought past 20 degrees of plantarflexion, the left foot can be brought to a neutral ankle position and the lateral border straightened with gentle pressure, deep medial and posterior creases on the right only, right calf circumference 1 cm less than the left, hips stable with negative Ortolani and Barlow tests, spine intact with no dimple or hair tuft

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management for the right foot?

options.text: Reassure the parents and teach them passive stretching at each nappy change
Refer for serial casting with a view to starting in the first weeks of life
Arrange hip ultrasound at six weeks and orthopaedic review of the feet after that
Refer for surgical soft tissue release to be performed at three months of age
Apply below knee strapping on the ward and review her in clinic at six weeks

subtopic_detail: Napkin area rash involving the skin creases with separate small lesions beyond the main red area after a week of barrier cream
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-month-old boy whose nappy rash has not settled despite a week of zinc barrier paste applied at every change. His mother says the redness now runs right into the skin folds at the tops of his legs, and that there are a few separate red spots on his tummy just above the nappy line.

He finished a course of oral amoxicillin for otitis media ten days ago. He is feeding normally, growing along the 50th centile and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: Confluent beefy red erythema over the perineum and buttocks extending into the inguinal and gluteal creases, a collarette of fine scale at the margin, several discrete red papules and small pustules on skin beyond the main plaque, no vesicles, no honey coloured crust, no ulceration, oral mucosa clear, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Apply a topical imidazole antifungal to the affected area at each nappy change
Continue the barrier paste and add frequent nappy free time each day
Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid ointment twice daily for a week
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review the rash at the end of it
Take a skin scraping for fungal culture and withhold treatment until it returns

subtopic_detail: Preschool girl whose vulval skin appears fused in the midline with a normal urinary stream and no symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the skin between her legs looks joined together, and is worried that something is blocked or that she has been interfered with.

The child passes urine in a single steady stream, is dry by day, has no pain, no itch and no discharge, and has never had a urinary infection. She is thriving, her behaviour is unchanged and there are no child protection concerns raised by the history.

data_table.Examination: The labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent membrane with a visible pale central line, an opening of about 4 mm remains anteriorly, no erythema, no excoriation, no bruising or tears, no discharge, perineum and anus otherwise normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to a paediatric surgeon for division of the membrane under anaesthesia
Separate the adhesion manually in the clinic room using lubricant and traction
Explain the natural history, advise on hygiene, and review her as needed
Prescribe topical oestrogen cream to the midline nightly for six to eight weeks
Refer to the child protection unit for a formal forensic medical examination

subtopic_detail: Flat pink birthmark present from birth covering the forehead and upper eyelid on one side of a newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar asked to review a term newborn boy on day two because of a birthmark that the midwife says has been there since delivery and has not changed.

His parents are distressed and have been told by a relative that it will fade like a stork mark. He is feeding, alert and moving all limbs symmetrically, and there have been no abnormal movements.

data_table.Examination: A flat pink patch with a sharp midline border covering the left forehead, upper eyelid and the skin in front of the ear, not raised and not blanching fully on pressure, red reflex present bilaterally, pupils equal and reactive, no corneal enlargement or cloudiness, anterior fontanelle soft, tone and primitive reflexes symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the parents that this will fade over the first year and arrange no follow up
Start oral propranolol after a baseline heart rate and blood glucose measurement
Refer him for pulsed dye laser treatment to the patch at around twelve months
Refer for ophthalmology review including measurement of intraocular pressure
Arrange a skin biopsy of the edge of the lesion before any specialist referral

subtopic_detail: School aged child with multiple flat brown skin patches and freckling in the armpits and groins referred for a suspected genetic condition
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old girl whose mother has counted more than six flat coffee coloured patches on her trunk and limbs, some present since she was a baby and others appearing since she started school. Her mother has noticed clusters of small freckles under both arms and in the groin creases.

She is performing at the level expected for her year, has had no seizures and no headaches. No family member has a similar skin appearance.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Eight flat light brown macules ranging from 8 to 22 mm on the trunk and limbs, freckling in both axillae and both groins, two small soft skin coloured nodules on the trunk, height and head circumference on the 50th centile, visual acuity 6/6 both eyes, no scoliosis, no bowing of the long bones, neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits within the next month
Refer to a paediatric dermatologist for laser treatment of the pigmented patches
Reassure the family that pigmented patches are common and require no follow up
Send genetic testing and defer any further assessment until the result returns
Begin annual review including blood pressure, vision, spine and development

subtopic_detail: Girl with brief staring episodes reproduced at the bedside by overbreathing and an electroencephalogram showing generalised spike and wave
stem:
You are the general paediatrician reviewing a 7-year-old girl whose teacher reports that she blanks out many times a day, stopping mid sentence and staring for a few seconds before carrying straight on as if nothing happened. Her parents say she never falls, never shakes and is never drowsy or confused afterwards.

In clinic you asked her to blow at a paper windmill for three minutes and reproduced an episode lasting eight seconds with eyelid fluttering and no response to her name. Her development, school progress and neurological examination are normal, and an electroencephalogram showed generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges with a normal background.

data_table.Examination: Neurological examination unremarkable, no focal deficit, no neurocutaneous stigmata, fundi normal
data_table.Investigations: Electroencephalogram generalised 3 Hz spike and wave on a normal background, no photoparoxysmal response

lead_in: Which medication would you start?

options.text: Carbamazepine, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
Ethosuximide, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
Sodium valproate, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
Levetiracetam, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose
Clobazam, titrated over two weeks to a usual maintenance dose

subtopic_detail: Boggy tender scalp swelling with broken hairs and occipital nodes in a child already treated with a topical antifungal cream
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose scalp has developed a soft boggy lump over six weeks. His mother has been applying an antifungal cream prescribed a month ago for what was then a scaly patch, and says the hair in that area now comes out when she washes it.

The family has two guinea pigs that arrived shortly before the rash began. He has had no fever and is otherwise well.

data_table.Examination: A 5 cm boggy tender raised plaque on the vertex with overlying pustules and yellow crust, hairs within the plaque broken close to the surface and epilate painlessly, surrounding scale, two tender occipital lymph nodes, no fluctuance on palpation, no cellulitis of the surrounding scalp
data_table.Investigations: Skin scraping and plucked hairs sent for fungal microscopy and culture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Continue the topical antifungal cream and add a medicated antifungal shampoo
Refer for incision and drainage of the swelling under general anaesthesia
Prescribe oral flucloxacillin for ten days and review the scalp at the end of it
Prescribe an oral antifungal agent and treat household contacts and the pets
Prescribe a potent topical corticosteroid ointment to settle the inflammation

subtopic_detail: Newborn with a limp arm held internally rotated after a difficult delivery with preserved grasp and an intact clavicle
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a term newborn boy on day one whose right arm lies limp by his side. The birth was complicated by difficulty delivering the shoulders after a prolonged second stage, and his birth weight was 4400 g.

His mother is distressed and asks whether he will ever use the arm and whether an operation is needed now. He is feeding well and is otherwise settled.

data_table.Examination: Right arm held adducted and internally rotated at the shoulder with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated, absent right Moro response with an intact left Moro, grasp reflex present and equal in both hands, no crepitus or tenderness over either clavicle, symmetrical chest expansion with no respiratory distress, pupils equal with no ptosis, right biceps and brachioradialis reflexes absent
data_table.Investigations: Chest and clavicle radiograph shows no fracture and no diaphragmatic elevation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immobilise the arm across the chest for three weeks and review after that
Begin gentle passive movement with physiotherapy and review for biceps recovery
Refer immediately for nerve grafting to be performed within the first fortnight
Arrange nerve conduction studies in the first week to determine the prognosis
Arrange urgent ultrasound of the shoulder to exclude a proximal humeral injury

subtopic_detail: Older boy with a foreskin that was previously retractile and now has a firm pale ring at the tip with spraying and recurrent soreness
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy whose father reports that the end of his foreskin has gone pale and hard over the past year. He used to be able to pull it back for washing and now cannot, his urine comes out as a spray that goes everywhere, and the tip balloons when he goes.

He has had three episodes of a red sore tip in the past twelve months, each treated with a topical preparation. He has no other skin or joint problems.

data_table.Examination: A firm white sclerotic ring at the preputial tip with loss of the normal pliability, the foreskin cannot be retracted at all and the meatus is not visible, no active discharge, the shaft skin and scrotum are unaffected, testes descended bilaterally and of equal volume
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the family and teach gentle daily retraction in the bath at home
Prescribe a topical corticosteroid ointment to the tight ring twice daily for six weeks
Refer for circumcision, which is both treatment and gives tissue for diagnosis
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and review the appearance after the course
Arrange a renal tract ultrasound and review him once the imaging is available

subtopic_detail: Toddler with outward bowing of the legs and wide wrists whose biochemistry shows a raised parathyroid hormone with low vitamin D
stem:
You are the general paediatrician seeing a 22-month-old boy whose legs have bowed outwards over the past six months and who his mother says walks like a sailor. He was breastfed until 18 months without any supplement, and now drinks little milk because of a cows milk protein allergy diagnosed in infancy.

He wears long clothing outdoors and the family spends little time in the sun. There is no family history of bone disease or short stature, and both parents have straight legs.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 10th centile having previously tracked the 40th, symmetrical outward bowing of both tibiae, widened wrists, a palpable ridge at the costochondral junctions, frontal bossing, normal tone and power, no fractures
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.10 mmol/L (2.20 to 2.60), phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20 to 1.80), alkaline phosphatase 980 U/L (100 to 400), parathyroid hormone 16.5 pmol/L (1.6 to 6.9), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 24 micromol/L (15 to 40), venous bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22 to 32), wrist radiograph shows cupping and fraying of the distal radial and ulnar metaphyses

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Oral colecalciferol with calcium supplementation and dietary review
Oral phosphate supplements with active vitamin D and endocrine referral
Oral sodium bicarbonate with potassium replacement and nephrology referral
Referral for orthopaedic assessment with a view to guided growth surgery
Reassurance with repeat measurement of leg alignment in six to twelve months

subtopic_detail: Child with a severely restricted food range who stops walking and has bleeding swollen gums with bruising around the hair follicles
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-year-old boy with autism who has stopped walking over the past three weeks and now screams when his legs are moved. His mother says he has eaten only dry biscuits, plain pasta and chicken nuggets for two years, refuses anything with a wet texture, and that his gums bleed when she brushes his teeth.

He has had no fever, no weight loss and no night sweats, and no joint has been swollen or red.

data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear, lies with hips and knees flexed, marked tenderness over both distal femora with no joint effusion or warmth, boggy bleeding gum margins around erupted teeth, scattered bruising and corkscrew hairs surrounded by small haemorrhages over both shins, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no pallor of the conjunctivae
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115 to 135), white cell count 7.2 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0), platelets 380 x10^9/L (150 to 450), blood film shows no blasts, C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 18 mm/h (less than 20), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8 to 1.2), femoral radiographs show generalised osteopenia with dense provisional zones of calcification

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence oral ascorbic acid replacement and arrange dietitian involvement
Commence intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures and orthopaedic review
Arrange urgent bone marrow aspiration and refer to paediatric oncology
Commence naproxen for suspected juvenile idiopathic arthritis and refer to rheumatology
Commence colecalciferol with calcium replacement and repeat the biochemistry

subtopic_detail: Persistent head tilt in an eight week old with a firm sternocleidomastoid swelling and full eye movements
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8-week-old boy whose mother says he has always held his head over to the right and only looks to his left when she feeds him. He was born at term by forceps delivery after a long second stage, and she has noticed the back of his head is becoming flat on the right.

He feeds and settles normally and is gaining weight along the 50th centile. On examination there is a firm painless swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid. He follows your face smoothly to both sides through a full range of eye movement, and the red reflex is present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted towards the right shoulder with the chin turned to the left, firm 1.5 cm swelling within the lower right sternocleidomastoid, passive rotation of the head to the right limited to about 45 degrees, passive left lateral flexion limited, right occipital flattening, full and equal eye movements with symmetrical red reflexes, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs, hips abduct fully with no clunk
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Request an ultrasound of the neck swelling before any other management
Refer to a paediatric physiotherapist for stretching and positioning
Request a cervical spine radiograph series to exclude a bony anomaly
Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist for assessment of ocular alignment
Refer for a moulding helmet to correct the flattening of the occiput

subtopic_detail: Persistent single joint swelling in a preschool girl with a positive antinuclear antibody and no eye symptoms
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose left knee has been swollen for ten weeks. Her mother says she is stiff and limping when she first gets up, and by lunchtime she is running about normally.

There has been no injury, no fever and no rash, and she has grown along the 75th centile throughout. Her eyes look normal to her parents and she has never complained of pain or blurring in them. Examination shows a warm knee with an effusion and a 10 degree loss of full extension, with no other joint involved.

data_table.Examination: Left knee warm with a moderate effusion, fixed flexion of 10 degrees, no erythema, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no rash, remaining joints and spine normal, eyes white with normal pupils on external inspection
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 121 g/L (110-140), white cell count 8.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), platelets 342 x10^9/L (150-450), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 24 mm/h (less than 15), antinuclear antibody positive at 1:320, blood culture negative

lead_in: Which additional step is most important to arrange now?

options.text: Arrange joint aspiration and start intravenous flucloxacillin empirically
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the knee under general anaesthesia
Arrange a bone marrow aspirate before any corticosteroid is prescribed
Arrange slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist within the month
Arrange serial antistreptolysin O titres and an echocardiogram this week

subtopic_detail: Preschool boy with late walking, bulky calves and a positive Gowers manoeuvre with preserved reflexes
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 4-year-old boy referred because he cannot keep up with other children. His mother says he first walked at 19 months, takes the stairs one foot at a time holding the rail, and gets up off the carpet by pushing on his own thighs with his hands.

He has about 50 words of speech and is otherwise well, with no regression of skills. His calves look bulky and feel firm. Deep tendon reflexes are present at the knees and ankles, tone is normal and there is no clonus, and his gait is waddling with no foot drop.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait, rises from the floor by climbing up his legs with his hands, hip girdle weakness with power 4 out of 5, shoulder girdle power 5 out of 5, calves firm and enlarged bilaterally, knee and ankle reflexes present and symmetrical, plantar responses flexor, no sensory level, spine straight with no hairy patch or dimple
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: Which investigation should be performed first?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with electromyography under sedation
Magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine with contrast
Serum creatine kinase measured before any other investigation
Referral to physiotherapy for gait retraining and review in six months
Open muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis arranged this month

subtopic_detail: Habitual snoring with witnessed pauses in a healthy five year old with large tonsils and normal growth
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old girl whose parents say she snores loudly every night and sleeps with her mouth open and her neck arched back. Twice a week her father has watched her stop breathing for several seconds before she gasps and starts again.

Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and afternoon irritability, and she still naps most days. She was born at term, has no asthma, no allergic rhinitis and no syndromic features, and she is growing along the 50th centile for height and weight. Her tonsils meet close to the midline and her nasal airway is narrow.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils enlarged to grade 3 bilaterally with no exudate, hyponasal voice, mouth breathing at rest, nasal mucosa pink with no polyps or allergic crease, tympanic membranes normal, chest clear with no chest wall deformity, cardiovascular examination normal, body mass index on the 55th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer to an otolaryngologist for consideration of adenotonsillectomy
Arrange overnight polysomnography before any referral is made
Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review her in three months
Provide sleep hygiene advice with a bedtime routine and review in a month
Refer to a paediatrician for assessment of attention and behaviour first

subtopic_detail: Fourteen months of waxing and waning blinking and throat clearing in a school aged boy with no functional impairment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy whose parents are worried about repeated hard blinking and a throat clearing noise that has been present on and off for 14 months. The movements come in runs for a few weeks, settle for a while, then return, and are worse when he is tired or excited before a football match.

He can hold them back for a minute or two when he concentrates, and then they come out in a burst. His teacher has not raised any concern, his marks are good and he has friends. He is not distressed by the movements himself, and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Examination: Frequent brief forceful eye blinking and intermittent throat clearing during the consultation, movements suppressible on request for about 90 seconds, no impairment of conscious state during the movements, cranial nerves normal, tone power and coordination normal, no chorea, gait normal, conjunctivae white with no discharge
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start risperidone at a low dose and review the response in six weeks
Start clonidine at night and titrate the dose over the next six weeks
Arrange an electroencephalogram to characterise the repeated movements
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and measure copper studies
Explain the natural history and arrange planned review in six months

subtopic_detail: Four months of bilateral evening leg pain in a well six year old who runs normally by day with a normal examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old girl who has been waking in the evening crying with pain in both calves and the fronts of both thighs, three or four nights a week for four months. Her mother rubs her legs and she settles within twenty minutes and sleeps through the rest of the night.

She is up and running at school the next morning with no limp and has not missed a day. There is no fever, no weight loss, no night sweats and no bruising, and she plays netball each weekend. Her aunt has juvenile arthritis and her mother is anxious about that. Examination of both legs is entirely normal.

data_table.Examination: Height and weight tracking along the 60th centile, no pallor, no bruising or petechiae, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly, no bone tenderness over the tibiae femora or spine, hips and knees with full painless range of movement, no joint swelling or warmth, normal gait and normal single leg hop on each side
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a full blood count with a blood film and measure lactate dehydrogenase
Explain the pattern, advise simple analgesia and review if features change
Arrange radiographs of both femora and both tibiae to exclude a bony lesion
Measure the serum 25 hydroxyvitamin D level and treat if it is below range
Refer to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of inflammatory joint pain

subtopic_detail: Painless scrotal swelling in a ten month old that transilluminates, has an upper border you can palpate above it, and does not change with crying
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10-month-old boy whose mother noticed at bath time that his left side of the scrotum looks bigger than the right. It has been there for at least two months, is the same size in the morning and the evening, and does not change when he cries or strains.

He feeds well, opens his bowels daily, has never vomited and is thriving on the 60th centile. He does not seem to mind when she washes the area. On examination the swelling is soft and non-tender, you can feel normal cord above it, and it lights up when you shine a torch behind it. Both testes are descended and the scrotal skin is normal.

data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender left scrotal swelling measuring about 3 cm, transilluminates brightly, upper border easily palpable with normal spermatic cord above it, no impulse on crying, no reducibility, both testes palpable within the scrotum, abdomen soft and non-distended, groins without swelling or tenderness
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric surgeon for herniotomy on the next available list
Arrange a scrotal ultrasound with Doppler before deciding on any referral
Arrange aspiration of the fluid in the clinic and send it for cell count analysis
Start a course of oral antibiotics and review the swelling again in one week
Reassure the parents and review him in the clinic after his second birthday

subtopic_detail: Two days of early morning vomiting and afternoon drowsiness in an afebrile child with a ventriculoperitoneal shunt in place since infancy
stem: A 6-year-old boy has vomited on waking for two mornings with headache. He was well between episodes yesterday but fell asleep this afternoon and is hard to rouse. He has a ventriculoperitoneal shunt inserted at four months.

data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck supple, pupils equal and reactive, reduced upgaze, shunt reservoir refills slowly

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Give intravenous ondansetron and observe in the short stay unit
Lumbar puncture for cell count and culture after blood cultures
Intranasal sumatriptan with outpatient neurology follow-up
Urgent non-contrast head computed tomogram and call neurosurgery
Abdominal ultrasound for a collection around the distal catheter

subtopic_detail: Alert four month old with profound axial hypotonia, absent reflexes, tongue fasciculations and paradoxical breathing who missed newborn screening
stem: A 4-month-old girl has never lifted her head and has stopped kicking her legs. She was born overseas and had no newborn screening test.

data_table.Examination: Alert and socially smiling, profound hypotonia with head lag, movement only at fingers and toes, reflexes absent, tongue fasciculations, paradoxical inspiratory chest movement
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 118 units per litre (less than 200), gas and glucose normal

lead_in: Which investigation will establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of brain and whole spine under anaesthesia
Muscle biopsy of quadriceps with enzyme histochemistry and microscopy
Targeted genetic testing of the survival motor neurone gene
Repeat newborn screening for metabolic and endocrine disorders
Repetitive nerve stimulation with acetylcholine receptor antibodies

subtopic_detail: Toddler with a harsh brassy cough and noisy breathing since infancy that worsens with crying and has not responded to eight weeks of inhaled therapy
stem: A 14-month-old boy has had noisy breathing since three months of age with a barking cough, loudest when he cries and absent in sleep. He has no eczema or family history of asthma. Salbutamol and eight weeks of inhaled corticosteroid changed nothing.

data_table.Examination: Monophonic expiratory wheeze over the trachea, chest clear when settled
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph normal, no right-sided arch

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to a respiratory service for flexible bronchoscopy
Increase inhaled corticosteroid and add a long-acting beta agonist
Arrange emergency rigid bronchoscopy for foreign body removal
Start two weeks of oral amoxicillin with clavulanate
Start a proton pump inhibitor with an oesophageal pH study

subtopic_detail: Head circumference crossing two centile lines between three and seven months with a full fontanelle in a developmentally normal infant
stem:
You are the general practitioner doing a 7 month check on a boy who was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother has no concerns and he sits with a straight back, transfers a block between his hands and babbles.

His head circumference was on the 50th centile at birth and the 50th at three months, and today it plots on the 97th. His length and weight remain on the 50th. His anterior fontanelle feels full when he is sitting quietly and not crying, and the skull sutures feel slightly separated at the coronal suture. His eyes move fully in all directions and he fixes and follows. Both parents have head circumferences on the 50th centile for adults.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 97th centile having tracked the 50th at birth and at three months, anterior fontanelle full but not tense at rest, slight separation of the coronal suture, scalp veins not distended, no setting sun sign with full upgaze, red reflexes present and symmetrical, tone and reflexes normal, sits unsupported and transfers objects, no organomegaly, no bruising
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure both parents' head circumferences and plot a repeat measurement monthly
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with sedation as the first study
Arrange skull radiographs to assess the sutures for premature fusion and ridging
Reassure the parents that development is normal and repeat the plot in three months
Arrange a cranial ultrasound through the fontanelle within the next few days

subtopic_detail: Six week old breastfed infant with a bulging fontanelle and bruising whose parents declined the birth injection, with prolonged clotting times and a normal platelet count
stem: A 6-week-old boy, fully breastfed, has been irritable and pale all day and had a one-minute focal seizure. His parents declined the injection offered after birth.

data_table.Examination: Pale, irritable, bulging fontanelle, oozing at the venepuncture site
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 388 x10^9/L, INR 6.4, APTT 92 seconds, fibrinogen 2.9 g/L, CRP 3 mg/L

lead_in: What is the single most important immediate intervention?

options.text: Platelet transfusion and urgent head computed tomography
Intravenous vitamin K and urgent head computed tomography
Intravenous cefotaxime and lumbar puncture once stable
Fresh frozen plasma alone and head computed tomography
Skeletal survey and referral to the child protection unit

subtopic_detail: Unilateral absent red reflex found at the six week check in an infant with no ocular discharge or watering
stem:
