You are the general practitioner performing the six week check on a boy born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy. His mother says that in photographs taken over the last fortnight the middle of his left eye looks cloudy and pale, and that he does not seem to look at her with that eye.

His eyes are not sticky and do not water. The newborn examination on day one recorded red reflexes present and symmetrical. He is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile, and there is no family history of childhood eye disease.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the left and present on the right, left pupil appears grey-white to the direct ophthalmoscope, no conjunctival injection or discharge, corneal diameters equal, eyes of equal size
data_table.Visual behaviour: Fixes and follows the examiner's face steadily when the left eye is covered, becomes distressed and turns away when the right eye is covered
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Repeat the red reflex examination at the four month health check
Refer to a community optometrist for refraction within three months
Arrange paediatric ophthalmology assessment within the next week
Request TORCH serology and review the infant when results return
Order a cranial ultrasound and review once the scan is reported

subtopic_detail: Angle of trunk rotation of eight degrees on forward bending in a thirteen year old girl eleven months after menarche
stem:
A 13-year-old girl is brought to your general practice because her mother noticed that one shoulder sits higher than the other and that one side of her back sticks up when she bends forward to pick things up. She has no back pain, no night pain and no change in bowel or bladder function.

Her menarche was eleven months ago. On examination she is well grown, her skin shows no birthmarks or patches of altered pigmentation, her foot arches are normal on standing and reflexes are symmetrical with downgoing plantar responses. On the Adams forward bend test there is a right thoracic prominence, and a scoliometer placed over it reads 8 degrees.

data_table.Examination: Right thoracic rib prominence on forward bending with a scoliometer angle of trunk rotation of 8 degrees, shoulder heights unequal by approximately 2 cm, waist creases asymmetric, no midline skin lesion over the spine, no cafe au lait macules, normal pes planus free foot arches, power and reflexes normal and symmetrical in both legs
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Reassure and review her in twelve months with a repeat examination
Arrange a standing whole spine radiograph and refer to a spine clinic
Refer for magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine before review
Refer to physiotherapy for a scoliosis specific exercise program
Fit a thoracolumbosacral brace and review her again in three months

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a raised alkaline phosphatase in an eighteen month old who is still breastfed and has had very little sun exposure
stem: An 18-month-old girl has increasingly bowed legs since walking at 14 months. She is still breastfed, has never had a vitamin supplement, and is almost always indoors.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum; widening of both distal radial metaphyses; frontal bossing
data_table.Investigations: Calcium 2.12 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); phosphate 0.82 mmol/L (1.10-1.90); alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (110-320); parathyroid hormone raised; 25 hydroxyvitamin D 14 nmol/L (>50); renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Oral calcium carbonate alone, with no vitamin supplement
Oral calcitriol 0.25 micrograms daily plus dietary calcium
Oral colecalciferol 400 units daily plus dietary calcium
No supplement, with repeat biochemistry and a bone survey
Oral colecalciferol 3000 units daily plus dietary calcium

subtopic_detail: Purulent conjunctivitis beginning on day nine of life with a negative gonococcal culture and a positive chlamydial nucleic acid test
stem:
You are the resident in the emergency department reviewing a 9-day-old boy whose mother says his eyes have been gluey and his eyelids puffy for three days, and that the discharge keeps coming back after she wipes it away. He was born at term at home, and his mother booked late in the pregnancy and had no antenatal screening swabs taken.

He is afebrile, feeding well and has gained weight since discharge. Both conjunctivae are injected with a copious yellow discharge and marked lid oedema, and the corneas are clear on fluorescein staining. A conjunctival swab shows no organisms on Gram stain and culture is negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, while nucleic acid amplification testing is positive for Chlamydia trachomatis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 68/42 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral lid oedema with copious mucopurulent discharge, conjunctival injection without follicles, clear corneas on fluorescein staining, chest clear on auscultation with no cough, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Conjunctival swab Gram stain shows polymorphs with no organisms seen, culture negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment plan?

options.text: Topical chloramphenicol ointment and review of the mother and her partner
Oral azithromycin for the infant and treatment of the mother and her partner
Intravenous ceftriaxone for the infant and treatment of mother and partner
Topical erythromycin ointment and treatment of the mother and her partner
Saline eye toilet alone and review of the mother and her partner in a week

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear in a four year old with a temperature of 38.7 degrees and a C reactive protein of 62
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 4-year-old boy who has refused to stand since waking this morning and cries when his mother lifts him. He had a mild runny nose a week ago that has since settled, and there has been no injury.

He looks unwell and flushed. He lies with the right hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, and he resists any passive movement through more than about 10 degrees in any direction. There is no rash, no joint swelling elsewhere and no bony tenderness over the tibia or femoral shaft.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed abducted and externally rotated with guarding through a 10 degree arc, no effusion palpable at the knee, no overlying erythema or warmth over the thigh, no rash, capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.4 x10^9/L (5.0 to 15.0), C reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 58 mm/h (less than 15), blood culture collected, hip radiograph shows no fracture and no femoral head abnormality

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Urgent orthopaedic referral for hip joint aspiration under anaesthesia
Oral ibuprofen and review in forty eight hours if he is not improving
Start intravenous flucloxacillin and review the response overnight
Arrange a hip radiograph and review once the film has been reported
Arrange bone scintigraphy and review once the scan has been reported

subtopic_detail: Soiling most days in a six year old with a palpable abdominal faecal mass who passed meconium on the first day of life
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose parents report that he is dirtying his underpants almost every day and that the smell has become a problem at school. They say he opens his bowels properly only once every week or so, and that when he does the stool is so large it blocks the toilet.

He passed his first bowel motion on the day he was born and grew normally through infancy. He is now withholding, standing on tiptoes and crossing his legs when he feels the urge. His abdomen is soft with a firm indentable mass palpable in the left iliac fossa and suprapubically. The perianal skin is normal, anal tone is normal on inspection with no fissure seen, and the lower limb neurological examination and back are normal.

data_table.Examination: Weight and height tracking the 50th centile, abdomen soft and non-tender with a firm indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa extending suprapubically, normally sited anus with normal perianal sensation, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normal power tone and reflexes in both legs
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: A phosphate enema daily until the impaction clears, then maintenance
A lactulose maintenance dose with a high fibre diet and toilet sitting
An escalating oral macrogol regimen followed by a maintenance dose
Referral for manual evacuation under anaesthesia, then maintenance
Referral for anorectal manometry before any laxative is commenced

subtopic_detail: Escherichia coli sepsis with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in a nine day old whose urine gives positive reducing substances with a negative glucose oxidase strip
stem: A 9-day-old girl with lethargy and poor feeding has grown Escherichia coli from blood culture. She fed well until her mother's milk came in, then vomited after most feeds. Newborn screening is pending.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, jaundiced to the abdomen, liver 3 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 268 micromol/L, conjugated 92 micromol/L, ALT 148 U/L, INR 1.9, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, urine reducing substances positive with a negative glucose oxidase strip

lead_in: What is the most appropriate feeding management?

options.text: Continue breastfeeding and start phototherapy
Stop lactose-containing feeds and give a soy formula
Continue breastfeeding and start ursodeoxycholic acid
Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula
Stop enteral feeds and give intravenous 10% dextrose

subtopic_detail: A femoral shaft fracture in a non ambulant five month old with blue sclerae and a father who broke bones easily as a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department to see a 5-month-old boy brought in because he cries whenever his nappy is changed. His parents say he rolled off a low couch onto a carpeted floor the previous afternoon and seemed briefly upset but then settled.

He has not yet rolled over deliberately, does not sit unsupported and is not crawling. His father says he broke his own arm twice as a child and that his teeth chipped easily. On examination the sclerae have a blue-grey tinge, the left thigh is swollen and he resists movement of that leg. The radiograph shows a transverse fracture of the left femoral shaft and the radiologist notes no other fractures on that film.

data_table.Examination: Swelling and tenderness of the left mid thigh with resistance to passive movement, blue-grey sclerae, no bruising over the trunk or limbs, no head or facial injury, anterior fontanelle soft, head circumference on the 50th centile, no joint hypermobility
data_table.Investigations: Left femoral radiograph shows a transverse mid shaft fracture with no periosteal reaction, full blood count within normal limits, corrected calcium phosphate and alkaline phosphatase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange a bone mineral density scan and review once it is reported
Refer to clinical genetics for collagen testing and review the result
Apply a hip spica and arrange orthopaedic review in the fracture clinic
Start bisphosphonate therapy and arrange paediatric endocrine follow up
Admit for a skeletal survey and make a child protection notification

subtopic_detail: Bradycardia with pinpoint pupils and preserved oxygenation in a two year old two hours after opening a grandparent's dosette box
stem:
You are the emergency registrar assessing a 2-year-old girl brought in two hours after her mother found her sitting beside her grandmother's opened dosette box with loose tablets on the floor. Nobody saw her swallow anything and the grandmother cannot say how many tablets were in the box.

The child was well earlier in the day and has had no fever, vomiting or diarrhoea. She is now drowsy but rouses to her name and pushes your hand away. Her pupils are 2 mm and sluggishly reactive. Her chest is clear, her breathing is unlaboured and her blood glucose is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 62 beats per minute, blood pressure 72/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13 rousing to voice, pupils 2 mm bilaterally and sluggishly reactive, chest clear with unlaboured breathing, capillary refill 3 seconds peripherally, skin warm and dry, bowel sounds present
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), electrocardiogram shows sinus bradycardia with a QRS of 82 ms and a QTc of 420 ms, venous blood gas and electrolytes within normal limits, paracetamol concentration below the level of detection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Give intravenous flumazenil and admit for cardiac monitoring overnight
Give activated charcoal and discharge after four hours of observation
Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate and admit for cardiac monitoring
Give intravenous naloxone and discharge after four hours of observation
Admit for cardiac monitoring, with atropine if the bradycardia is symptomatic

subtopic_detail: A flat red birthmark over the forehead and upper eyelid present since birth and unchanged in a six week old
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 6-week-old boy whose parents want advice about a birthmark. They say the red patch on the right side of his forehead and upper eyelid has been there since the day he was born, has not become raised or lumpy, and has not grown apart from keeping pace with his head.

He feeds well, has reached his weight gain milestones and has had no abnormal movements or episodes of staring. On examination there is a flat, sharply demarcated dark red patch occupying the right forehead and upper eyelid without crossing the midline, and it does not blanch fully on pressure. Neurological examination is normal for age and the red reflexes are present and symmetrical.

data_table.Examination: Flat sharply demarcated dark red patch over the right forehead and right upper eyelid respecting the midline, no surface elevation or nodularity, incomplete blanching on pressure, head circumference on the 50th centile, symmetrical tone and movement of all four limbs, red reflexes present and symmetrical
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging and ophthalmology review
Start oral propranolol and arrange dermatology review in four weeks
Reassure the parents and review the birthmark at the twelve month check
Arrange cranial ultrasound and review when the scan has been reported
Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment and review in the dermatology clinic

subtopic_detail: A migration percentage of thirty five per cent on a surveillance radiograph in a comfortable four year old with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy
stem: A 4-year-old boy with bilateral spastic cerebral palsy walks indoors with a frame. His parents report no change in comfort or function.

data_table.Examination: Hip abduction full, symmetrical and painless, equal leg lengths
data_table.Investigations: Pelvic radiograph migration percentage 35 per cent right, 22 per cent left; twelve months ago 24 per cent and 20 per cent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the radiograph in twelve months and continue the program
Start a night time hip abduction brace, repeating in six months
Refer to paediatric orthopaedics for assessment of the displacement
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of both hips before referral
Refer for botulinum toxin to the hip adductors and physiotherapy

subtopic_detail: An abdominal mass crossing the midline with periorbital bruising and limp in a three year old whose coagulation screen is normal
stem: A 3-year-old girl has six weeks of irritability, poor appetite and reluctance to walk. Her parents noticed dark shadowing around both eyes a fortnight ago. There has been no trauma or bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Pale; bilateral periorbital ecchymoses with left proptosis; firm irregular fixed left flank mass crossing the midline; femoral tenderness; blood pressure normal
data_table.Investigations: Hb 82 g/L; platelets 288 x10^9/L; INR 1.0 with normal APTT; urine dipstick negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Request a coagulation screen and refer to child protection
Measure urinary catecholamine metabolites and refer to oncology
Request a skeletal survey and refer to the child protection service
Measure serum alpha fetoprotein and refer urgently to oncology
Measure serum lactate dehydrogenase and review in two weeks

subtopic_detail: Testicular volume of 3 mL at fourteen years with a bone age delayed by two and a half years and an intact sense of smell
stem: A 14-year-old boy has not started puberty, with no headaches or visual symptoms and an intact sense of smell. His father did not shave until nearly 18.

data_table.Examination: Height 3rd centile, height velocity 4.5 cm/year, weight proportionate, testicular volume 3 mL, no pubic hair
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology, thyroid function and blood count normal; bone age 11 years 6 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for karyotype and review once the result is available
A three month course of low dose intramuscular testosterone
Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary and hypothalamus
Measure serum gonadotrophins and testosterone, review in six months
Reassure, with six monthly growth and pubertal staging review

subtopic_detail: A midline neck lump in a school aged boy that rides upward when he puts his tongue out
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general outpatient clinic seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother noticed a lump in the front of his neck about six weeks ago. It has not changed in size and he has no pain, no difficulty swallowing and no hoarseness.

He is thriving on the 60th centile for weight and height and has had no recent sore throat or febrile illness. On examination there is a smooth 2 cm swelling in the midline just above the thyroid cartilage. It is not tender and the overlying skin is normal. When you ask him to protrude his tongue, the lump moves upward; it does not move when he swallows a sip of water.

data_table.Examination: Smooth non-tender 2 cm midline swelling above the thyroid cartilage, rises on tongue protrusion, no movement on swallowing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, thyroid gland not separately palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his assessment?

options.text: Ultrasound of the neck with thyroid function tests
Fine needle aspiration of the lump in clinic today
Contrast computed tomography of the neck and chest
A ten day course of oral amoxicillin and review
Excision of the lump on the next elective list

subtopic_detail: A two month old who holds her head tilted to one side with a firm swelling within one neck muscle and full passive range achievable
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing an 8-week-old girl whose parents say she always holds her head tipped towards her right shoulder and prefers to look to the left. She was born at term by vacuum extraction after a prolonged second stage.

She feeds well and smiles responsively. On examination her head is tilted to the right with her chin rotated to the left. There is a firm painless fusiform swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. You can passively rotate her chin fully to the right and tilt her left ear to her left shoulder, although she resists the last few degrees. Her red reflexes are present and symmetrical and she fixes and follows across the midline in both directions.

data_table.Examination: Head tilted right with chin rotated left, firm fusiform 1.5 cm swelling within the right sternocleidomastoid, full passive cervical rotation and lateral flexion achievable with resistance at end range, occiput symmetrical with no flattening, red reflexes present bilaterally, fixes and follows across the midline, tone and reflexes normal in all four limbs

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Refer for cranial orthotic helmet fitting this month
Refer to physiotherapy for positioning and stretching
Arrange ultrasound of both sternocleidomastoid muscles
Refer to ophthalmology for assessment of eye movements
Arrange cervical spine radiographs before any treatment

subtopic_detail: A toddler who will not use one arm after being lifted by the hand, holding it slightly bent with the palm turned down
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 2-year-old girl brought in by her father an hour after she refused to use her left arm. He had been holding her hand as she stepped off a kerb, she stumbled, and he pulled her up by the hand to stop her falling. She cried briefly and has not used the arm since.

She is playing happily with her right hand and is not distressed at rest. She holds the left arm slightly flexed at the elbow with the forearm turned palm down and resists any attempt to turn the palm up. There is no swelling, deformity or bruising anywhere along the arm, and palpation of the clavicle, humerus, elbow, forearm and wrist produces no localised tenderness.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held in slight elbow flexion and forearm pronation, active supination refused, no swelling deformity or bruising, no focal bony tenderness over clavicle humerus elbow forearm or wrist, radial pulse present with normal capillary refill and warm hand

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange radiographs of the elbow before any manipulation
Apply a broad arm sling and review in the fracture clinic
Reduce it by supination and flexion of the affected elbow
Refer to orthopaedics for reduction under general anaesthesia
Arrange ultrasound of the elbow to look for an effusion

subtopic_detail: A four month old whose eye waters and crusts every morning since the first weeks of life with a clear white eye between episodes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4-month-old boy whose mother says his left eye has been watery since he was about two weeks old and that it is gummed shut with yellow crust most mornings. She wipes it clean and the eye looks normal for the rest of the day. He has had three courses of eye drops from different doctors with no lasting change.

He is thriving, immunised on schedule and otherwise well. On examination the left eye is watery with a tear film that overflows onto the cheek. The conjunctiva is white with no injection and the cornea is clear. Gentle pressure over the medial canthus produces a small bead of mucoid material at the inner corner. Red reflexes are present and symmetrical and the corneal diameters look equal.

data_table.Examination: Left eye with overflowing tear film and dried crust on the lashes, white non-injected conjunctiva, clear cornea, mucoid reflux from the medial canthus on pressure over the lacrimal sac, red reflexes present and symmetrical, corneal diameters equal with no photophobia or blepharospasm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer for probing of the tear duct under anaesthesia now
Prescribe chloramphenicol 0.5 per cent eye drops for a week
Refer urgently to ophthalmology for measurement of pressures
Advise lacrimal sac massage and review at twelve months
Send a conjunctival swab for chlamydia and gonorrhoea now

subtopic_detail: A small pit in front of the ear found at the newborn check in a baby who passed the hearing screen and has no other anomalies
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 3-day-old girl before discharge from the postnatal ward. The midwife has noted a tiny pit just in front of the right ear, which the parents had not seen. There is no discharge from it and no surrounding redness.

She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with an uncomplicated pregnancy, and the antenatal morphology scan at 20 weeks reported normal anatomy including the kidneys and urinary tract. She is feeding well and has passed urine and meconium. Examination is otherwise entirely normal, including facial symmetry, palate, neck, limbs and cardiovascular examination. Her automated auditory brainstem response newborn hearing screen was passed in both ears yesterday. There is no family history of deafness or kidney disease.

data_table.Examination: A 1 mm blind ending pit anterior to the right external ear with no discharge or erythema, normally formed and positioned pinnae bilaterally, facial features symmetrical, palate intact, no neck sinuses or branchial remnants, normal cardiovascular and abdominal examination
data_table.Investigations: Automated auditory brainstem response newborn hearing screen passed bilaterally, antenatal morphology scan at 20 weeks reported normal renal tract

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange renal ultrasound to look for structural anomalies
Refer for excision of the pit before her first birthday
Arrange genetic testing for branchio-oto-renal syndrome
Repeat the newborn hearing screen at three months of age
Reassure, advise on signs of infection, and review as needed

subtopic_detail: A soft bulge at the navel in a one year old that pushes back easily and enlarges when he cries
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 12-month-old boy at his immunisation visit. His mother asks about a soft bulge at his navel that has been present since the first weeks of life. It becomes larger when he cries or strains and flattens when he lies quietly. It has never been painful, red or hard, and he has never vomited with it.

He was born at term, is thriving on the 50th centile and is meeting his developmental milestones. On examination there is a 1.5 cm soft swelling at the umbilicus which reduces completely with gentle pressure. The fascial defect admits your fingertip and its edge is smooth and circular. The overlying skin is normal and the abdomen is soft and non-tender.

data_table.Examination: A 1.5 cm soft easily reducible umbilical swelling that enlarges on crying, fascial defect approximately 1 cm admitting a fingertip with a smooth circular edge, overlying skin normal, abdomen soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds, no groin swelling and both testes descended

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure and review, with referral if it persists past age four
Refer for elective repair before he starts kindergarten next year
Apply a compressive umbilical band to encourage early closure
Arrange abdominal ultrasound to measure the fascial defect size
Refer urgently to paediatric surgery for repair within four weeks

subtopic_detail: An intermittent groin bulge in a three month old born at thirty four weeks with both testes in the scrotum
stem: A 3-month-old boy born at 34 weeks, now 44 weeks corrected, has a right groin bulge of two weeks that appears when he cries. It has never been tender.

data_table.Examination: On crying, a smooth reducible swelling appears above and medial to the pubic tubercle, extending towards the scrotum; both testes in the scrotum

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Ultrasound of the groin to confirm the diagnosis first
Refer to paediatric surgery for repair on the next available list
Advise a reducing truss and review in the surgical clinic
Reassure and review at twelve months, as most close spontaneously
Refer to the emergency department for reduction under sedation

subtopic_detail: Witnessed pauses in breathing at home in a four week old with three days of coryza but only mild work of breathing in the department
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 4-week-old boy, born at 38 weeks, with three days of runny nose and cough. His mother reports he is taking about two thirds of his usual feeds. Twice last night and once this morning she saw him stop breathing for what she estimates was several seconds, going pale and floppy before starting again after she picked him up and rubbed his back.

In the department he is alert and settles in his mother's arms. He has mild subcostal recession with no nasal flaring or head bobbing, and you hear widespread fine crackles on auscultation. His nose is blocked with clear secretions. He has had no fever at home and his nappies remain wet. His vital signs are pulse 152 beats per minute, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent in air and temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Examination: Alert and consolable, mild subcostal recession without nasal flaring or head bobbing, widespread fine inspiratory crackles with no focal consolidation, blocked nose with clear secretions, anterior fontanelle normal, capillary refill under 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab sent for respiratory viral panel, no chest radiograph performed, no blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Discharge home with feeding advice and general practitioner review
Admit for a trial of high flow nasal cannula oxygen therapy now
Admit for continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and observation
Admit for nebulised salbutamol and reassessment after two hours
Observe for two hours in the department and then discharge home

subtopic_detail: A thriving three week old referred after newborn screening showed a raised trypsinogen with two variants found on the screening gene panel
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a respiratory clinic seeing a 3-week-old girl referred after newborn bloodspot screening. The laboratory reported an immunoreactive trypsinogen level above the screening cut off, and the reflex gene panel identified two variants in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator gene, one of which the laboratory has classified as being of uncertain clinical significance.

The parents are distressed and want to know whether their daughter has cystic fibrosis. She was born at term, passed meconium on day one and is breastfeeding well. Her weight has risen from 3.2 kg at birth to 3.6 kg today, tracking along the 50th centile. Examination is normal with a clear chest, no clubbing and a soft abdomen. Her stools are described by her mother as soft and yellow without any oily appearance.

data_table.Examination: Well grown and alert, chest clear on auscultation with no recession, abdomen soft with no organomegaly, no digital clubbing, hydration normal
data_table.Investigations: Newborn bloodspot immunoreactive trypsinogen above the screening cut off, reflex cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator panel reporting two variants with one classified as of uncertain significance, weight 3.6 kg tracking on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Start pancreatic enzyme replacement and airway clearance now
Repeat the immunoreactive trypsinogen level in four weeks' time
Arrange faecal elastase measurement to confirm the diagnosis
Arrange sweat chloride testing at an accredited paediatric centre
Reassure the parents, as the baby is thriving and asymptomatic

subtopic_detail: A six week old needing tube feeds for a weak suck with marked floppiness through the trunk but brisk knee reflexes and undescended testes
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-week-old boy who has needed nasogastric top up feeds since birth because he tires after a few sucks and milk spills from his mouth. His mother recalls that he moved much less in the womb than her older child did.

He was born at 39 weeks in good condition. On examination he is alert and makes eye contact, but he slips through your hands on vertical suspension and drapes over your forearm on ventral suspension. His cry is weak. His deep tendon reflexes are present and brisk at the knees and ankles, his tongue shows no fasciculation and there is no ptosis or facial weakness. Both testes are impalpable and the scrotum is underdeveloped. His creatine kinase is 96 U/L (less than 200).

data_table.Examination: Alert with normal social response, marked axial hypotonia with head lag and draping on ventral suspension, weak cry, limb power reduced but antigravity movement present, deep tendon reflexes present and brisk at knees and ankles, no tongue fasciculation, no ptosis or ophthalmoplegia, both testes impalpable with a hypoplastic scrotum
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 96 U/L (less than 200), sodium 139 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), thyroid stimulating hormone and free thyroxine within normal limits, cranial ultrasound reported as normal

lead_in: Which investigation is most likely to establish the diagnosis?

options.text: SMN1 gene deletion testing for spinal muscular atrophy
Muscle biopsy to look for a congenital myopathy or dystrophy
Repeat creatine kinase with nerve conduction and electromyography
Maternal and infant acetylcholine receptor antibody measurement
DNA methylation analysis of the chromosome 15 imprinted region

subtopic_detail: Breast tissue in a fourteen year old boy whose height is above the ninety seventh centile with small firm testes and difficulty at school
stem: A 14-year-old boy has had breast tissue for a year and is distressed by it. He needs extra help at school and takes no medication.

data_table.Examination: 3 cm of firm glandular tissue under each areola, height above the 97th centile, pubic hair Tanner stage 4, testes firm and about 3 mL with no mass
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid and liver function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Measure gonadotrophins and testosterone, and request a karyotype
Reassure him that this will resolve within eighteen months
Request testicular ultrasound for an oestrogen secreting tumour
Repeat thyroid and liver function tests with a prolactin level
Refer for surgical reduction of the breast tissue this year

subtopic_detail: Tummy aches and loose motions with weight crossing centiles in a nine year old whose parents removed all wheat six weeks before the blood test was taken
stem: A 9-year-old girl has eight months of abdominal pain and loose motions, with weight falling from the 50th to the 15th centile and height steady on the 40th. Her parents removed all wheat six weeks before these tests.

data_table.Examination: Slim; abdomen soft and non-tender; no mouth ulcers or perianal abnormality
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase IgA negative with normal total IgA; ferritin 14 micrograms/L; calprotectin normal; HLA DQ2 positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the negative serology and look for other causes
Reintroduce gluten daily for six weeks, then repeat the testing
Refer for duodenal biopsy now while she still avoids gluten
Diagnose coeliac disease from the positive HLA DQ2 result
Repeat the tissue transglutaminase in three months on this diet

subtopic_detail: A flat red facial birthmark occupying the forehead and upper eyelid in a well six week old infant
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-week-old boy referred by his general practitioner because of a birthmark that has been present since birth. His mother says it has not grown or thickened, but it deepens in colour when he cries.

He is breastfeeding well and his weight is tracking along the 50th centile. He has had no seizures or unusual movements, and he smiles responsively at his mother.

data_table.Examination: Flat pink to red patch covering the right forehead, the right upper eyelid and the skin over the right cheekbone, sharply demarcated at the midline, partially blanching with pressure, with no thickening, nodularity or ulceration; red reflexes present and symmetrical, corneal diameters appear equal, fixes and follows past the midline, anterior fontanelle soft, tone and limb movements symmetrical, head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Refer him for pulsed dye laser therapy and review the appearance of the skin at twelve months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and refer him for an ophthalmology assessment
Reassure the parents that the patch will fade over months and review him at his next immunisation visit
Commence oral propranolol after a baseline electrocardiogram and paediatric cardiology review
Arrange cranial ultrasound through the anterior fontanelle now and repeat the scan at six months of age

subtopic_detail: Recurrent bilateral evening leg pain in a thriving six year old with a normal examination and normal daytime function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose mother is worried about leg pains. For about four months he has woken crying two or three evenings a week, pointing to both calves and the fronts of both thighs, and settles after twenty minutes of rubbing and cuddles.

He is fully himself the next morning, walks to school and plays soccer on Saturdays without complaint. His weight and height are tracking along the 50th centile and he has had no fevers, weight loss or rashes.

data_table.Examination: Gait normal with normal heel toe pattern and normal running, no limp, no joint swelling, warmth or effusion, full and painless range of movement at hips, knees and ankles, no bony tenderness on direct palpation of the tibiae or femora, no muscle wasting, spine straight with normal forward flexion, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the benign pattern to the family, advise massage and simple analgesia, and review if the pattern changes
Order a full blood count with blood film and inflammatory markers, and review him when the results return
Request plain radiographs of both tibiae and femora, and arrange orthopaedic review of the films with the family
Refer him to a paediatric rheumatologist for assessment of possible juvenile idiopathic arthritis and its treatment
Check serum vitamin D and calcium levels, and commence a colecalciferol supplement while awaiting the results

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear after a witnessed twisting fall in a toddler whose initial radiographs are reported as normal
stem:
You are the emergency department resident assessing an 18-month-old girl who will not walk. Yesterday afternoon her father watched her catch her foot at the bottom of a slide at the park and twist as she came off it, and she cried immediately and has not borne weight since.

She crawls, plays and feeds normally and settles with paracetamol. Her father is with her and gives a consistent account, and her growth and developmental milestones are age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Refuses to stand on the right leg but moves it spontaneously when lying, tenderness on palpation over the lower third of the right tibia, no deformity, no swelling, no bruising anywhere on the body, hips and knees with full painless range of movement, no warmth over any joint, skin and frenulum intact
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral radiographs of the right tibia and fibula reported as showing no fracture, C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Arrange an urgent technetium bone scan today and admit her under the orthopaedic team pending the result
Discharge her with simple analgesia and advise her father to return only if she is still not walking in one week
Immobilise the leg in a below knee cast, provide analgesia, and review her with repeat radiographs in ten days
Request an ultrasound of both hips looking for an effusion and aspirate the joint if any fluid is demonstrated
Admit her for a skeletal survey and fundoscopy, and notify the state child protection service before discharge

subtopic_detail: Vulval soreness with intermittent non bloody discharge in a five year old girl with normal external genital examination
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 5-year-old girl brought by her mother with six weeks of vulval soreness and itch. Her mother has noticed a pale yellow mark on the gusset of her underpants most days and has been washing her in a bubble bath each night to help.

She started swimming lessons two months ago and often stays in her wet bathers afterwards. She passes urine without pain or urgency, her bowels open daily without straining, and she is her usual cheerful self at school.

data_table.Examination: Diffuse erythema of the vulval skin and the skin between the labia majora and the thighs, no vesicles, ulcers, fissures or excoriation, no bruising, hymen appears normal with no bleeding, scant non offensive discharge at the introitus, perianal skin intact and not excoriated, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days after sending a vulval swab for bacterial culture and sensitivities
Prescribe topical clotrimazole cream twice daily for two weeks and review her symptoms at the end of that course
Give a single dose of mebendazole now and repeat it in two weeks, treating all members of the household together
Advise stopping bubble bath and soap, wearing loose cotton underwear, and applying a barrier ointment, then review
Refer her for examination under anaesthesia and vaginoscopy to exclude a retained foreign body in the vagina

subtopic_detail: Eight months of sound repetition with visible facial tension in a three year old whose language is otherwise typical
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old boy whose parents are worried about his speech. For about eight months he has repeated the first sound of words, and in the last two months they have noticed his eyes screw up and his jaw tighten as he pushes a word out.

He has begun to say things such as it is too hard and to give up on sentences. He uses four to five word sentences, follows two step instructions, plays imaginatively with his older sister and passed his newborn hearing screen. His father stuttered as a child and did not receive treatment until he was ten.

data_table.Examination: Repetition of initial sounds on about one in five words with two audible blocks during the consultation, visible tension around the eyes and jaw during blocks, normal articulation between dysfluencies, vocabulary and sentence structure appropriate for age, responds to conversational speech at normal volume from across the room, oromotor examination normal with symmetrical palatal elevation and normal tongue movement

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Reassure the parents that most preschool dysfluency resolves and arrange to review his speech in twelve months
Advise the parents to ask him to slow down, take a breath and repeat the word each time he becomes stuck
Refer him to a paediatrician for a multidisciplinary autism assessment before considering any speech intervention
Arrange formal audiology assessment and defer any decision about speech therapy until the hearing result is known
Refer him now to a speech pathologist for assessment and a parent delivered early stuttering treatment program

subtopic_detail: Widespread umbilicated papules with one inflamed crusted lesion in a well six year old with normal skin elsewhere
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6-year-old boy whose parents want his spots removed. They have spread over four months from his left flank to his trunk and arms, and the school swimming teacher has told the family he should stay out of the pool until they are gone.

One lesion on his forearm became red and crusted last week and is now smaller than it was. He is otherwise well, plays normally and takes no regular medicines.

data_table.Examination: Approximately thirty dome shaped pearly papules two to four millimetres across with central umbilication, scattered over the left flank, trunk and both forearms, one lesion on the right forearm red and crusted with surrounding erythema of three millimetres and no fluctuance, skin between lesions normal without eczema, no regional lymphadenopathy, no lesions on the eyelids or genitals

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Explain the natural course, advise covering lesions for contact sport, and confirm he may continue swimming lessons
Refer him for cryotherapy to each lesion, with repeat treatments every three weeks until the lesions have cleared
Arrange curettage of the lesions under general anaesthesia, with topical anaesthetic applied before the procedure
Prescribe oral cefalexin for five days to treat the inflamed forearm lesion and the surrounding area of erythema
Prescribe topical imiquimod cream three nights per week and review the response to treatment after twelve weeks

subtopic_detail: Repetitive vomiting with pallor and lethargy two hours after a first exposure to rice cereal in a six month old
stem: A 6-month-old boy vomited repeatedly beginning two hours after his first ever feed of rice cereal, and by the eighth vomit had gone grey and floppy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 178 /min, BP 68/40 mmHg, T 36.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale and hypotonic, capillary refill four seconds, no urticaria, chest clear with no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.28, lactate 3.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 micrograms in the lateral thigh
Blood cultures and intravenous ceftriaxone, then a fluid bolus
Intravenous sodium chloride 20 mL/kg and intravenous ondansetron
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg and observation for four hours
Skin prick testing to rice and cow milk protein today

subtopic_detail: Episodes of back arching and head turning during and after feeds in a thriving four month old who stays alert
stem: A four-month-old girl is referred with possible seizures. She arches her back, turns her head to one side and stiffens for up to a minute, during or shortly after a feed, up to six times daily and never in sleep. She watches her mother and settles when held upright.

data_table.Examination: Alert and socially responsive; tone, power and reflexes normal
data_table.Growth: Weight on the 25th centile; small posset after most feeds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent electroencephalogram with neurology review once reported
Upright positioning after feeds with smaller volumes, review in two weeks
Oral levetiracetam at a weight based starting dose, with review
Magnetic resonance imaging of brain and spine under anaesthesia
Upper gastrointestinal contrast study to document and quantify reflux

subtopic_detail: Progressive pallor after a viral illness in a well two year old with isolated anaemia and a low reticulocyte count
stem: A two-year-old boy has looked pale for a fortnight. Four weeks ago he had a week of fever and coryza. He still runs about and eats normally.

data_table.Examination: Pale, alert and playing, no organomegaly or lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 64 g/L, MCV 78 fL, reticulocytes 8 x10^9/L (20 to 100), normal white cells and platelets, film normal with no blasts, ferritin 46 micrograms/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the count tomorrow
Oral iron and less cow milk, review in four weeks
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
Intravenous immunoglobulin, then haematology review
Repeat the blood count and reticulocytes in one week

subtopic_detail: Six months of lightheadedness and fatigue on standing in a fifteen year old with a sustained rise in heart rate and no fall in blood pressure
stem: A 15-year-old girl has six months of lightheadedness and palpitations within a minute of standing. She has never fainted and has no family history of sudden cardiac death.

data_table.Examination: Ten-minute active stand: HR 118 /min, BP 116/74 mmHg; no murmur
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 42 micrograms/L, TSH normal, ECG normal with QTc 410 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for tilt table testing before any treatment advice
Commence oral fludrocortisone and check electrolytes in two weeks
Commence a low-dose beta blocker and review in four weeks
Start increased fluid and salt intake with graded exercise
Arrange echocardiography and 24-hour Holter monitoring

subtopic_detail: Timing of the first retinal examination in an extremely preterm infant stable on low flow oxygen at two weeks of age
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar reviewing a boy born at 27 weeks gestation weighing 890 g who is now 14 days old. He needed surfactant and three days of mechanical ventilation and is now on nasal high flow in 25 per cent oxygen, tolerating expressed breast milk feeds and gaining weight.

His mother asks when his eyes will be checked, having read that premature babies can go blind. The unit's ophthalmologist attends weekly and the nursing staff ask you to write the screening plan in the notes.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits for corrected gestational age
data_table.Examination: Active with good tone for corrected gestation, anterior fontanelle soft, chest clear on nasal high flow, abdomen soft with tolerated enteral feeds, red reflexes present bilaterally on bedside examination
data_table.Investigations: Cranial ultrasound at day 7 with no intraventricular haemorrhage, haemoglobin 142 g/L (140 to 220 for age), C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: When should his first retinal examination be arranged?

options.text: At 31 weeks postmenstrual age, which for this infant falls at four weeks after birth
Within the next 48 hours, since he required mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen
At 36 weeks postmenstrual age, when the retinal vasculature has reached the temporal periphery
At discharge from the neonatal unit, with community ophthalmology follow up thereafter
At three months of corrected age in the outpatient clinic, unless the red reflexes become abnormal

subtopic_detail: Lethargy with 13 per cent weight loss and a raised sodium on day five of exclusive breastfeeding
stem: A five-day-old girl, born at 39 weeks weighing 3400 g, is sleepy and hard to wake for feeds. She is exclusively breastfed and her mother has cracked nipples. She weighs 2960 g.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, sunken fontanelle, doughy skin, jaundiced
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 158 mmol/L, bilirubin 268 micromol/L against a treatment threshold of 340, CRP less than 5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bolus of 5 per cent glucose, then maintenance fluid
Lactation support with formula top ups at home tomorrow
Admit for intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride
Admit for intensive phototherapy and intravenous fluid
Septic screen with lumbar puncture and antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Recurrent bone pain at multiple sites with sterile biopsy cultures and no response to prolonged antibiotics in an eleven year old
stem: An 11-year-old girl had left clavicular pain and swelling nine months ago. Open biopsy was sterile; she completed six weeks of flucloxacillin and the pain returned once treatment stopped. She now has three weeks of right thigh pain, worst at night.

data_table.Investigations: CRP 11 mg/L, blood count and lactate dehydrogenase normal; lucent right femoral metaphyseal lesion with sclerotic margins

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Recommence intravenous antibiotics for another six weeks
Arrange whole body magnetic resonance imaging and rheumatology referral
Perform a bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics
Request a technetium bone scan to map skeletal involvement
Commence oral prednisolone daily for the next four weeks

subtopic_detail: Both feet turning inwards when running in a four year old who sits between his heels with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy whose parents are worried that both feet turn inwards when he runs and that he trips more than other children at kindergarten. They have been told by a relative that he needs special boots.

He walked at thirteen months, has no pain, and keeps up with his friends at the playground. His parents say he always sits on the floor between his heels with his knees together.

data_table.Examination: Both patellae point inwards on walking, hip internal rotation 80 degrees with external rotation 15 degrees bilaterally in the prone position, thigh foot angle neutral on both sides, lateral borders of both feet straight with no forefoot deviation, tone power and reflexes normal in both legs with downgoing plantar responses, symmetrical leg lengths, no joint swelling
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him to an orthopaedic surgeon to be assessed for a derotation osteotomy of both femurs before he starts school next year
Reassure the parents that this is physiological femoral anteversion and review only if it persists beyond the age of eight
Prescribe a night time derotation brace to be worn until the rotational profile of both of his legs has normalised
Refer him for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot that is causing his gait
Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine to look for a neurological cause of his in-toeing and his tripping

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of pale greasy stools and weight loss in a preschooler after a childcare outbreak of loose motions
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother reports three weeks of loose, pale, foul smelling motions that float, with a lot of wind and a swollen tummy. She has lost 0.8 kg over that time.

Four other children at her childcare centre have had similar prolonged loose motions in the past month. There has been no blood in the stool, no fever and no vomiting. She has eaten bread and cereal daily since she was seven months old without any previous bowel trouble, and her growth had tracked the 50th centile until this illness.

data_table.Examination: Mildly distended soft abdomen, no organomegaly, no mouth ulcers, no perianal disease, no rash, no clubbing, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 38 g/L (35 to 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a faecal specimen for protozoal nucleic acid amplification testing before starting any antimicrobial treatment
Start oral metronidazole empirically for three days and review her symptoms and weight in the clinic in two weeks
Request coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A level and arrange gastroenterology review for possible biopsy
Advise a two week trial of a strictly lactose free diet and review whether the stool frequency and bloating improve
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to look for a structural cause of her distension and her three weeks of loose stools

subtopic_detail: Screaming and thrashing an hour and a half after falling asleep in a preschooler who has no memory of it next day
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old girl whose parents describe frightening episodes three or four nights a week. About ninety minutes after she falls asleep she sits up screaming, pushes them away and thrashes about with her eyes wide open, appearing terrified and not recognising them.

Each episode lasts around five minutes and she then settles back to sleep. In the morning she is cheerful and remembers nothing about it. Her father had similar episodes as a boy. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness.

data_table.Examination: Growth along the 50th centile, development age appropriate with fluent sentences, tonsils not enlarged on inspection, no dysmorphic features, neurological examination normal with normal tone power and reflexes, no skin stigmata of a neurocutaneous syndrome
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her parents, advise safety measures in the bedroom and explain that the episodes settle without treatment
Arrange an overnight sleep electroencephalogram to look for frontal lobe seizures arising out of sleep
Commence low dose clonazepam at bedtime and review the frequency of the episodes in the clinic after four weeks
Refer her for polysomnography and adenotonsillectomy assessment on the basis that sleep disordered breathing is triggering the episodes
Refer her to a child psychologist on the basis that these episodes represent anxiety dreams requiring trauma-focused assessment

subtopic_detail: Flattening at the back of the head in a five month old with the ear on the flattened side sitting forward of the other
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-month-old girl whose parents are distressed about the shape of her head. They say the back right side looks squashed and that it has become more obvious over the past two months, and they have read that a helmet may be needed.

She was born at term, rolls both ways, has good head control and has no feeding difficulty. She sleeps on her back and spends much of the day in a rocker.

data_table.Examination: Flattening of the right occiput with the right ear displaced anteriorly relative to the left and mild fullness of the right forehead, giving a parallelogram outline when viewed from above, no ridging palpable over any suture, no mastoid bulge behind either ear, anterior fontanelle soft and open, head circumference tracking the 50th centile, full passive neck rotation to both sides

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise counter positioning with supervised tummy time and cot repositioning, and review her head shape in two months
Refer her urgently to the craniofacial service on the basis that a fused lambdoid suture is the likeliest explanation
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction to assess all of the cranial sutures
Refer her now for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted, because the deformity has been progressing over recent months
Refer her to physiotherapy for treatment of an underlying tightness of the neck muscles driving the positional preference

subtopic_detail: Blotchy pink rash appearing on the trunk of a well eleven month old on the day a three day high fever settled
stem: An eleven-month-old boy has a pink blotchy rash that appeared this morning on his trunk and has spread to his neck. He had a temperature to 39.5 degrees C for three days, which broke overnight. He is now playing happily.

data_table.Examination: Blanching pink maculopapular rash on trunk and neck, sparing the face; afebrile, no conjunctival injection or coryza, no lymphadenopathy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain a self-limiting viral exanthem and give return advice
Notify public health and send measles serology
Admit for blood cultures and intravenous antibiotics
Request a full blood count and film to exclude malignancy
Start oral amoxicillin and review the rash in two days

subtopic_detail: Refusal to use one arm in a toddler after being lifted by the hand, with no swelling and no bony tenderness
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 2-year-old girl brought in by her father twenty minutes after he lifted her by the hand up a kerb as she stumbled. He and her older brother both saw it happen. She cried immediately and has not used the left arm since.

She is now settled on her father's lap, playing with a toy in her right hand, and holds the left arm slightly bent at the elbow with the palm turned down against her body. She has no other injuries and there are no concerns about her care at home.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling, deformity or bruising anywhere on the limb, no tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist, mild discomfort on attempted supination at the elbow, hand warm and pink with a normal radial pulse, moves fingers normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a reduction manoeuvre at the elbow and observe her for return of normal use of the arm before discharge
Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm first and arrange reduction only once a fracture has been formally excluded
Apply a broad arm sling for comfort and arrange review in the fracture clinic within forty eight hours for reassessment
Refer her to the orthopaedic registrar for assessment of the elbow and definitive management of the arm she is not using
Undertake a skeletal survey and make a child protection notification before any attempt is made to treat the affected arm

subtopic_detail: Drooling and refusal to drink in a toddler forty five minutes after swallowing strongly alkaline dishwasher powder
stem: A 2-year-old boy was found beside an open dishwasher with powder around his mouth 45 minutes ago; the container confirms a strongly alkaline detergent. He vomited once and has since drooled continuously and refused water.

data_table.Examination: Continuous drooling with pooled saliva, erythema of the tongue and palate with a white buccal plaque, no stridor or hoarseness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Nil by mouth with intravenous fluids and endoscopy at 12 to 24 hours
Give a single dose of activated charcoal and observe
Encourage milk or water to dilute the alkali and observe
Give diluted lemon juice to neutralise the alkali now
Commence high-dose oral corticosteroids to prevent stricture

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent discharge from both eyes with marked lid swelling on the third day of life after an unbooked pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the postnatal ward to see a baby girl on her third day of life. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning there is thick yellow discharge that reaccumulates within minutes of being wiped away.

Her mother arrived in labour without any antenatal care and no antenatal screening bloods or swabs were taken. The baby is feeding, has a normal temperature and has passed urine and meconium normally.

data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral eyelid oedema requiring gentle retraction to open the lids, profuse purulent discharge reaccumulating immediately, intense conjunctival injection and chemosis, corneas appear clear on the limited view obtained, no vesicles on the lids or scalp, anterior fontanelle soft, tone normal, no rash
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing, give parenteral ceftriaxone and start hourly saline eye irrigation
Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly to both eyes
Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and commence a two week course of oral erythromycin for the baby
Take conjunctival swabs for culture and nucleic acid testing and observe with regular saline cleaning and review the eyes tomorrow
Take conjunctival swabs for viral testing and commence intravenous aciclovir with topical antiviral therapy to both affected eyes

subtopic_detail: Displaced elbow fracture in a school aged child whose hand stays warm and pink with no palpable radial pulse
stem: A 6-year-old boy fell onto an outstretched hand an hour ago. Radiographs show a completely displaced extension type supracondylar humeral fracture.

data_table.Examination: Deformity above the elbow, hand warm and pink, radial pulse impalpable and undetectable on Doppler, cannot make the circle sign with thumb and index finger, sensation intact

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Immediate theatre for closed reduction and percutaneous wire fixation
Above elbow backslab and fracture clinic review within forty eight hours
Urgent computed tomography angiogram of the limb before any reduction
Vascular surgery referral for brachial artery exploration before manipulation
Closed reduction under sedation in the emergency department with a backslab

subtopic_detail: Six months of pain around the navel in a thriving nine year old with normal screening bloods whose parents want a scan
stem: A 9-year-old girl has six months of periumbilical pain on school mornings, easing at weekends and in holidays, never waking her at night. Her parents have asked for a scan.

data_table.Examination: Growth on the 50th centile, mild periumbilical tenderness only
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and CRP normal, negative coeliac serology with normal IgA, faecal calprotectin 22 micrograms/g

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to complete the assessment
Diagnose functional abdominal pain and agree a graded school return
Refer for endoscopy with duodenal biopsies to exclude inflammation
Trial a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review
Advise strict wheat and lactose exclusion for six weeks

subtopic_detail: Eight weeks of daily rattly cough in a thriving preschooler with a clear chest and a normal chest radiograph
stem: A four-year-old boy has eight weeks of daily wet, rattly cough, present through the day. Two courses of oral salbutamol and four weeks of an inhaled corticosteroid made no difference. There was no choking episode beforehand.

data_table.Examination: Wet cough audible in the room, chest clear, no clubbing, growth on the 75th centile
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph normal, sweat chloride 18 mmol/L, immunoglobulins normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Two to four weeks of amoxicillin with clavulanate
Increase the inhaled corticosteroid and add a beta agonist
High resolution computed tomography of the chest
Flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage
Reassure as post viral cough, review in eight weeks

subtopic_detail: Toddler treated as gastroenteritis who has an enlarged liver and a gallop and deteriorates after an initial fluid bolus
stem: A three-year-old girl has two days of vomiting without diarrhoea, treated as gastroenteritis this morning. She arrived mottled, and after a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus her breathing has worsened. Paediatric intensive care is four hours away.

data_table.Examination: Liver 4 cm below costal margin, gallop rhythm, new bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph cardiomegaly; ECG low voltage QRS

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Further 20 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus over ten minutes
Withhold fluid, urgent echocardiography, retrieval for inotropes
Blood cultures, ceftriaxone and fluid to 60 mL/kg total
Immunoglobulin now, then transfer to the paediatric ward
Rapid sequence intubation, then continued volume resuscitation

subtopic_detail: Bruising over the cheek with a torn upper lip frenulum in a four month old who cannot yet roll
stem: A 4-month-old boy has a facial bruise. His parents say he rolled off the change table onto carpet, but the parent-held record shows he has not yet rolled.

data_table.Examination: Bruise on the left cheek and the left ear helix, torn upper lip frenulum, no other marks
data_table.Investigations: INR 1.0, APTT 31 seconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for skeletal survey, neuroimaging and fundoscopy, and notify child protection
Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey and discharge him home today
Order a skeletal survey and clotting profile, reassuring if normal
Photograph the bruises and repeat the coagulation screen next week
Accept the history, give head injury advice and arrange a home visit

subtopic_detail: Toe walking with calf hypertrophy and a creatine kinase of 12400 in a four year old boy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4-year-old boy whose parents are worried that he walks on his toes and cannot keep up with his older cousins. He falls more than other children at kindergarten and his teacher has noticed he pushes on his thighs to get up from sitting on the floor.

He walked at eighteen months and says short sentences that his family understand. His calves look bulky compared with his thighs. You arranged blood tests at the last visit and the results are now available.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait with toe walking, bulky firm calves, proximal weakness with a positive Gowers manoeuvre, reflexes present at the knees and reduced at the ankles, no fasciculation and no sensory deficit
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 12400 units per litre (60-305), alanine aminotransferase 180 units per litre (10-40), aspartate aminotransferase 210 units per litre (10-45), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an orthopaedic surgeon for serial casting of the ankles to correct the toe walking and to improve his gait pattern
Refer him for an open muscle biopsy of the quadriceps for dystrophin immunostaining before any other investigation is undertaken
Repeat the liver enzymes and arrange a liver ultrasound, since the raised transaminases suggest an underlying hepatic disorder in this child
Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant of gait in preschool children and repeat the creatine kinase measurement in six months
Refer to a paediatric neurology service for genetic testing of the dystrophin gene with genetic counselling for the family

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and poor weight gain at five weeks with sodium 122 and potassium 7.1
stem: A 5-week-old boy has four days of forceful milky vomiting after feeds and is hungry again straight afterwards. He is drowsy but rousable with reduced skin turgor.

data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, delayed capillary refill; deeply pigmented scrotum and areolae
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L; K 7.1 mmol/L; chloride 112 mmol/L; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L; glucose 2.4 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Steroid profile, then intravenous hydrocortisone with saline and dextrose
Cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin after cultures, with a fluid bolus
Fluid bolus and correction of the alkalosis before theatre
Insulin and dextrose with nebulised salbutamol for the potassium
Steroid profile, then oral fludrocortisone and salt once feeds stay down

subtopic_detail: Systolic murmur with weak femoral pulses at the six week check in a thriving infant
stem: A baby girl is seen for her six week check. She feeds well and has gained 900 g since birth.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/54 mmHg right arm, SpO2 98% right hand, 96% right foot
data_table.Examination: Soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal edge radiating to the back, brachial pulses normal, femoral pulses not palpable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral furosemide with paediatric cardiology review within the week
Reassure that this is an innocent murmur, reviewing at immunisation
Same day paediatric assessment with four limb blood pressures and echocardiography
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph today, reviewing her when back
Routine paediatric cardiology referral, returning sooner if feeding worsens

subtopic_detail: Cyanotic episodes triggered by crying with rapid recovery and a normal electrocardiogram at fifteen months
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 15-month-old girl who has had six frightening episodes over three months. Each begins when she is upset, after a fall or when a toy is taken away.

Her mother describes a long silent cry, then the lips turning blue, then a few seconds of limpness before she comes round and wants a cuddle. She is back to normal within a minute and has never been sleepy afterwards. She is fully immunised, her development is normal and an electrocardiogram arranged by the general practitioner was reported as normal with a normal corrected QT interval.

data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, pale conjunctivae, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiac examination with no murmur, normal tone and power with age-appropriate gait, developmental milestones appropriate
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with normal corrected QT interval

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to look for an epileptiform focus that could explain the recurrent episodes of limpness and colour change
Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram with video recording and review her in the neurology clinic when the report is available
Arrange an echocardiogram to exclude a structural cardiac cause for the cyanosis and the transient loss of postural tone during the episodes
Send a full blood count with ferritin, since correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency of these episodes in a substantial proportion of children
Send a venous blood gas with lactate and an ammonia level during a well period to screen for an underlying metabolic disorder causing the events

subtopic_detail: Breech presentation at term as the only risk factor for hip dysplasia in a newborn with a normal examination
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward reviewing a 2-day-old girl before discharge. She was born at thirty nine weeks by caesarean section for a persistent breech presentation and has fed well since birth.

There is no family history of hip problems and the pregnancy was otherwise unremarkable with normal liquor volume. Her mother asks whether anything needs to be arranged for the hips because a friend's baby was put in a harness.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical thigh creases, full and equal abduction of both hips, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing, legs of equal length on Galeazzi testing, spine and feet normal, neurological examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for her hips?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic radiograph now to assess the acetabular index and refer to the orthopaedic clinic if the femoral head appears displaced
Refer her for fitting of a Pavlik harness now on the basis of the breech presentation and review her in the orthopaedic clinic in six weeks
Reassure her mother that the normal newborn examination excludes the condition and arrange no imaging beyond the routine child health checks
Arrange a hip ultrasound at around six weeks of age and continue routine clinical examination of the hips at each scheduled review
Arrange a hip ultrasound before discharge from the postnatal ward and refer to orthopaedics if any measurement falls outside the normal range

subtopic_detail: Unimmunised ten month old exposed to measles two days ago in a hospital waiting room
stem: A ten-month-old boy sat in an emergency department waiting room two days ago at the same time as a person later confirmed to have measles. His parents have declined all immunisations. He is well today.

data_table.Examination: Alert and playful; no rash, conjunctivitis or Koplik spots

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Normal human immunoglobulin today, with his first vaccine brought forward
Measles mumps and rubella vaccine today, extra to the two doses due at twelve months
No action now, with isolation advice and review if fever develops
Measles serology today, vaccinating only if immunoglobulin G is negative
Defer vaccination to twelve months as scheduled, with oral vitamin A

subtopic_detail: Secondary prevention after a first episode of acute rheumatic fever in a remote community child
stem: A nine-year-old boy in a remote Northern Territory community has a confirmed first episode of acute rheumatic fever. His streptococcal infection has been treated and his arthritis has settled. His mother asks about home.

data_table.Examination: Soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla; joints settled
data_table.Investigations: ESR 62 mm/h; CRP 28 mg/L; ECG first degree atrioventricular block; mild mitral regurgitation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Twice daily oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for five years with dose aids
Annual echocardiography and dental review, treating sore throats promptly
Continue naproxen and add a low dose corticosteroid to protect the valve
Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin, with registration
Ten days of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin, reviewing if symptoms recur

subtopic_detail: Microcytic anaemia in a toddler drinking one and a half litres of cow milk each day
stem: A 2-year-old girl looks pale but is otherwise well, with no bruising or blood in her stool. She drinks about 1.5 L of cow milk daily and eats little meat or vegetables.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no organomegaly or petechiae
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L (110-140), MCV 62 fL, RDW 19%, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, CRP normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce milk to 500 mL daily, start oral iron and recheck in four weeks
Send coeliac serology and defer iron until results return
Refer to haematology for haemoglobin electrophoresis first
Admit for packed red cell transfusion then start oral iron
Advise more red meat and vegetables alone, recheck in three months

subtopic_detail: Fever twelve days after chemotherapy with a neutrophil count of 0.3 in a well looking child
stem: A 6-year-old girl with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a central venous line, twelve days past her last chemotherapy block, has a fever of 38.5 degrees C. She looks well with no localising symptoms.

data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.3 x10^9/L, platelets 62 x10^9/L, CRP 42 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take blood cultures and await the C-reactive protein result
Give oral amoxicillin with clavulanate and review tomorrow in the day unit
Give paracetamol and observe for four hours before deciding
