Arrange a chest radiograph and urine culture, then treat any focus found
Take blood cultures from the line and peripherally, then give antibiotics

subtopic_detail: Glucose surveillance at two hours of age in a large for gestational age infant of a diabetic mother
stem: A boy born two hours ago at 39 weeks weighs 4.35 kg. His mother had insulin-treated gestational diabetes. He breastfed within the first half hour and no glucose has been measured.

data_table.Examination: Pink, warm and asleep in the cot, plethoric, no jitteriness, strong suck

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of his glucose?

options.text: Measure the glucose before the next feed and support frequent feeding
Measure the glucose only if he becomes jittery or feeds poorly
Measure the glucose now and transfer for intravenous dextrose if low
Give a formula top up after each breastfeed and measure daily
Give buccal dextrose gel now and measure the glucose at six hours

subtopic_detail: Jitteriness and poor feeding on day three in the baby of a mother on methadone maintenance
stem: A three-day-old girl born at 38 weeks is unsettled between feeds. Her mother is on a stable methadone program. The midwives report a high pitched cry, difficulty settling after feeds and three loose stools today. She is breastfeeding with some difficulty attaching.

data_table.Examination: Tremulous when disturbed, settles when swaddled, increased limb tone, excoriation over the nose, afebrile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral morphine now and wean it over the following week
Replace breastfeeding with formula and observe for 48 hours
Give naloxone to clarify whether the symptoms are opioid related
Full septic screen with intravenous antibiotics pending cultures
Withdrawal scoring with supportive care, medicating above threshold

subtopic_detail: Six cafe au lait macules with axillary freckling in a seven year old with a normal examination
stem: A 7-year-old boy has had increasing brown skin patches over two years. He is well and progressing normally at school, with no headaches or visual complaints. His father has similar patches.

data_table.Examination: Six flat light brown macules over 5 mm on the trunk and limbs, axillary freckling, no cutaneous nodules, no scoliosis, normal neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Genetic testing of the responsible gene before any surveillance
Annual ophthalmology, blood pressure and spine review, plus genetics
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits today
Skin biopsy of one pigmented lesion to confirm the diagnosis
Reassure that these are inherited birthmarks and review as needed

subtopic_detail: One white pupil and one red pupil across several recent phone photographs in a thriving nine month old
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 9-month-old girl in a general clinic. Her mother has brought her phone and shows you six photographs taken over the past two months, in which one pupil looks white while the other glows orange red.

The baby was born at term, feeds well and is tracking along the fiftieth centile for weight and length. She fixes on faces, follows a rolling ball across the room and reaches accurately for a small toy with either hand. There is no family history of childhood eye disease and no squint noticed by either parent.

data_table.Examination: Red reflex absent on the right and present on the left, no proptosis, no orbital swelling, corneal light reflex symmetrical, cover test reveals no shift on either side, anterior segments clear to penlight examination
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange urgent referral to a paediatric ophthalmologist for examination under anaesthesia within one week
Reassure the mother that asymmetric camera flash is common and review the child at her twelve month health check
Request an outpatient orbital ultrasound and review the result at a routine clinic appointment in six weeks
Refer to a community optometrist for refraction and occlusion therapy to prevent amblyopia in the affected eye
Arrange a screening magnetic resonance scan of the brain and orbits before making any ophthalmology referral

subtopic_detail: Profuse purulent eye discharge with marked lid swelling on day three of life after an unscreened pregnancy
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a baby boy who is seventy hours old. The midwife reports that both eyes began weeping yesterday evening and that this morning she could barely part the lids to clean them.

He was born at term by normal vaginal delivery to a 19-year-old woman who booked late and declined the routine first trimester sexual health screen. He has fed hungrily throughout and has had six wet nappies in the past day. He is afebrile and handles normally when undressed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 142 beats per minute, blood pressure 64/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Marked bilateral lid oedema with thick yellow discharge reaccumulating within a minute of cleaning, conjunctival injection with chemosis, corneas clear to penlight, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash and no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Eye swab taken for Gram stain, bacterial culture and nucleic acid amplification testing, results pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence topical chloramphenicol drops two hourly and review the baby on the postnatal ward the following morning
Admit for intravenous ceftriaxone and frequent saline eye irrigation, with maternal and partner contact tracing
Start oral azithromycin for fourteen days and arrange community midwife review of the eyes every second day
Observe with hourly saline cleaning alone and start antibiotics only once the swab results have become available
Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and start intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin

subtopic_detail: Painful restriction of eye movement with reduced colour vision emerging during treatment of a sinus infection
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 7-year-old boy who has had a blocked nose and facial pain for eight days and was started on oral amoxicillin by his general practitioner three days ago. His mother brings him back because the swelling around his left eye has worsened since this morning and he now cries when he looks up.

He is alert, drinking and has had no vomiting. He has no history of trauma, insect bite or preceding skin lesion, and his immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Tense left periorbital swelling with erythema extending to the brow, globe displaced forwards and laterally, pain and limitation on upgaze and abduction, red desaturation on comparing a red object between the two eyes, visual acuity 6/6 right and 6/12 left
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 17.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 96 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Change to oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for ten days and arrange a clinic review in forty eight hours
Arrange contrast computed tomography of the orbits and sinuses and start intravenous antibiotics with eye review
Apply warm compresses with topical chloramphenicol ointment and review in the short stay unit in six hours
Perform a lumbar puncture to exclude meningitis before committing the child to any intravenous antibiotic therapy
Refer directly for urgent surgical drainage of the orbit without obtaining any cross sectional imaging beforehand

subtopic_detail: Pallor and irritability in a toddler taking nine hundred millilitres of cow milk daily with a normal ferritin during a viral illness
stem: An 18-month-old boy has become pale and less active over two months. He drinks about 900 mL of cow milk daily and eats little else. A viral illness three days ago has settled.

data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, soft flow murmur, no organomegaly or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Hb 88 g/L, MCV 64 fL, RDW 18.4% (11.5-14.5), ferritin 48 micrograms/L (15-200), CRP 22 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral iron 3 mg/kg daily and limit cow milk to 500 mL
Order haemoglobin electrophoresis before treatment
Arrange an urgent bone marrow aspirate and film review
Reassure that the ferritin is normal and repeat after recovery
Refer for an intravenous iron infusion first line

subtopic_detail: Witnessed breathing pauses and morning headache in a four year old with large tonsils and poor weight gain
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 4-year-old girl whose parents describe loud snoring on most nights since she was two. Her father has recorded a video on his phone in which she stops breathing for around twelve seconds, then gasps and rolls over.

She wakes unrefreshed, complains of headache on several mornings a week and falls asleep in the car on short trips. Her kindergarten teacher has raised concerns about inattention and oppositional behaviour in the afternoons. Her weight has drifted from the fiftieth to the tenth centile over eighteen months while her height has tracked steadily.

data_table.Examination: Mouth breathing at rest with hyponasal speech, tonsils meeting in the midline, no cervical lymphadenopathy, normal tympanic membranes, no adenoidal facies, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal, body mass index on the tenth centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of adenotonsillectomy as the definitive treatment
Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray for six weeks and review the symptoms at the end of that treatment period
Arrange a trial of continuous positive airway pressure delivered overnight through a paediatric nasal interface
Refer for developmental assessment of attention difficulties before pursuing any investigation of the sleep symptoms
Request overnight oximetry at home and treat only if the trace shows at least three clusters of desaturation below ninety

subtopic_detail: Bedwetting most nights in a seven year old who is dry by day and has never had a dry spell lasting six months
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old boy whose parents want help with bedwetting. He wets five or six nights a week and has never been reliably dry overnight for longer than a fortnight. He is dry during the day, does not rush to the toilet, passes urine four to five times a day and opens his bowels daily without straining.

He has started avoiding school camps and a friend's sleepover, which is what prompted the visit. His parents have already tried lifting him at eleven each night and restricting drinks after dinner without benefit. There is no snoring and no daytime somnolence.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable bladder or faecal loading, normal external genitalia, normal lower limb tone power and reflexes, no sacral dimple or hair tuft, spine straight, growth along the fiftieth centile
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose protein leucocytes and nitrites, bladder diary shows age-appropriate voided volumes with no urgency episodes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oral oxybutynin at night and titrate the dose upwards over four weeks according to the response
Continue nightly lifting and fluid restriction after dinner, and reassure the family that this resolves with age
Arrange a bedwetting alarm with structured family support and review the response after four to six weeks
Prescribe oral desmopressin nightly as an ongoing treatment and continue it until he becomes reliably dry
Refer for renal tract ultrasound and urodynamic studies before committing the family to any specific treatment

subtopic_detail: Sudden painful clustered erosions of uniform size on eczematous skin with fever after contact with a relative with a cold sore
stem: A 2-year-old girl with eczema has a facial rash that changed over 24 hours. She is in pain and has stopped drinking. Her grandmother had a lip blister three days ago.

data_table.Examination: Clustered erosions of uniform size, no honey coloured crusting, eyelids involved to the lash line, fluorescein negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase to a potent topical corticosteroid with wet dressings
Oral cefalexin for seven days with review by the general practitioner
Admit for intravenous aciclovir with ophthalmology review
Topical aciclovir cream five times daily with clinic review tomorrow
Analgesia and oral rehydration while awaiting the viral swab result

subtopic_detail: Timing of a live attenuated vaccine after completing two months of high dose prednisolone for nephrotic syndrome
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a nephrology clinic reviewing a 3-year-old boy who has just completed an eight week course of prednisolone at 2 mg/kg daily for his first episode of nephrotic syndrome. He is now in remission and off all treatment as of four days ago.

His mother asks about his overdue measles mumps and rubella and varicella vaccinations, which were deferred when he became unwell. His 2-year-old sister is fully immunised and there are no household contacts who are immunosuppressed or pregnant. He has had no blood product or immunoglobulin exposure.

data_table.Examination: Weight tracking on the fiftieth centile, no periorbital or peripheral oedema, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, chest clear, abdomen soft with no ascites
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio within normal limits, serum albumin 38 g/L (35-50), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about these two vaccines?

options.text: Give both vaccines today, since he is in remission and has been off corticosteroid therapy for several days
Give the measles mumps and rubella vaccine today and defer the varicella vaccine for a further twelve months
Withhold both vaccines permanently and rely on maintaining household and childcare contact immunity instead
Defer both live vaccines until at least one month after the last corticosteroid dose, then give them together
Check measles and varicella serology first and vaccinate only if the antibody titres return below protective levels

subtopic_detail: Disc battery seen below the diaphragm on radiograph in an asymptomatic four year old who swallowed it two hours earlier
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 4-year-old girl who was found with an opened remote control two hours ago, and her father is certain that the twenty millimetre disc battery it contained is missing. She has had no drooling, no vomiting, no chest or abdominal pain, and she drank a cup of juice in the waiting room without difficulty.

She has no previous gastrointestinal surgery and no known swallowing problem. A single radiograph of the neck chest and abdomen has been performed.

data_table.Examination: Handling the situation calmly, no drooling, chest clear with no stridor, abdomen soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph shows a twenty millimetre disc shaped radio opaque foreign body with a double ring halo sign lying in the gastric antrum, with no free gas beneath either hemidiaphragm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange emergency endoscopic removal within two hours regardless of the position shown on the radiograph
Give a dose of oral honey now and discharge her with advice to return only if she develops abdominal pain
Admit for observation with four hourly abdominal examination and a repeat radiograph before any discharge home
Discharge with written return advice and arrange a repeat radiograph in ten to fourteen days to confirm passage
Prescribe a stimulant laxative and a high fibre diet to accelerate transit, with review by the local doctor next week

subtopic_detail: Two witnessed breathing pauses at home in a seven week old with mild work of breathing and oxygen saturation of 94 per cent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 7-week-old boy, born at thirty five weeks gestation, on day three of a coryzal illness. His parents describe two episodes at home in which he went quiet, stopped breathing for what they estimate was fifteen seconds and looked dusky around the mouth, each ending when they picked him up and rubbed his back.

He has taken about two thirds of his usual feed volume over the past twelve hours. In the department he is alert between examinations and has had no further episode in the ninety minutes since arrival. His older sister has a cold.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 148 beats per minute, blood pressure 74/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 52 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 37.1 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Mild subcostal recession with no tracheal tug or head bob, widespread fine inspiratory crackles with scattered expiratory wheeze, anterior fontanelle soft, capillary refill two seconds, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal swab positive for respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with written advice, as his oxygen saturation and work of breathing are both reassuring
Discharge home after a four hour period of observation in the department with continuous saturation monitoring
Commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen at two litres per kilogram per minute and admit to the ward for monitoring
Perform a full septic screen with lumbar puncture and start intravenous antibiotics pending the culture results
Admit for inpatient cardiorespiratory monitoring and feeding support, without supplemental oxygen at present

subtopic_detail: Worsening stridor and high fever twelve hours after dexamethasone and nebulised adrenaline produced no sustained improvement
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 3-year-old boy who was brought in last night with a barking cough and stridor, given oral dexamethasone and two doses of nebulised adrenaline, and admitted to the short stay unit when his stridor kept returning.

This morning he looks worse. He is sitting forward, is not interested in his mother's phone and has a weak cough that no longer sounds barking. He is fully immunised. Over the past six hours his temperature has climbed and he has become increasingly reluctant to swallow his own secretions, though he is not drooling.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 168 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 38 breaths per minute, SpO2 93 per cent in room air, temperature 39.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Biphasic stridor at rest with marked tracheal tug and intercostal recession, toxic appearance, no rash, chest sounds symmetrical with poor air entry throughout
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 148 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a second dose of oral dexamethasone at 0.6 mg/kg and repeat nebulised adrenaline every twenty minutes
Request an urgent lateral neck radiograph to look for a thumbprint sign before making any airway decision
Activate the difficult airway team for inspection in theatre and start intravenous flucloxacillin with ceftriaxone
Start high flow humidified oxygen and observe for a further two hours before escalating care any further
Give intramuscular adrenaline for presumed anaphylaxis and commence intravenous hydrocortisone and antihistamine

subtopic_detail: Quiet chest with a normalising respiratory rate and a rising carbon dioxide after an hour of continuous salbutamol
stem:
You are the emergency registrar managing a 9-year-old girl who arrived an hour ago with a severe asthma exacerbation. She has had continuous nebulised salbutamol, nebulised ipratropium and oral prednisolone since arrival.

The nurse calls you because the family think she looks calmer. She is no longer speaking in single words because she is not speaking at all, and she is slumped against her mother rather than sitting upright as she was on arrival. Her mother mentions that she was admitted to intensive care with asthma two winters ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158 beats per minute, blood pressure 104/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 91 per cent on eight litres per minute of oxygen, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Minimal audible wheeze with markedly reduced air entry throughout both lung fields, poor respiratory effort with reducing accessory muscle use, drowsy but rousable to voice
data_table.Investigations: Venous blood gas shows pH 7.21 (7.32-7.42), carbon dioxide 68 mmHg (41-51), bicarbonate 24 mmol/L (22-32), lactate 3.1 mmol/L (less than 2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Continue the current nebulised therapy and repeat the blood gas in thirty minutes to confirm the trend
Reduce the oxygen to maintain saturations between 92 and 94 per cent to avoid suppressing respiratory drive
Arrange an urgent chest radiograph to exclude pneumothorax before escalating to any further pharmacotherapy
Give intravenous magnesium sulfate and call the intensive care team for urgent review at the bedside
Change the prednisolone to intravenous hydrocortisone and add a further dose of nebulised ipratropium bromide

subtopic_detail: Doughy skin with preserved blood pressure and a sodium of 163 in an infant whose formula has been scooped incorrectly
stem: A five-month-old boy has four days of vomiting and loose stools. His formula has been made up with an unfamiliar scoop. He weighs 6.4 kg, down from 7.0 kg at four months.

data_table.Examination: Sunken fontanelle, dry mucous membranes, doughy abdominal skin, capillary refill two seconds
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 163 mmol/L, venous pH 7.31, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate fluid management?

options.text: Repeated rapid 20 mL/kg sodium chloride boluses
0.9 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 48 hours
0.45 per cent sodium chloride with glucose over 12 hours
Nasogastric oral rehydration solution at maintenance rate
3 per cent sodium chloride before any rehydration

subtopic_detail: Persisting jaundice at three weeks in a breastfed infant with pale stools and a conjugated fraction of 68 micromol/L
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-week-old girl brought in because she still looks yellow. She is exclusively breastfed, feeding eight times a day, and her mother is confident about attachment.

Her weight has regained birth weight and is now 200 g above it. Her mother has brought a photograph of this morning's nappy, which shows a putty coloured stool, and mentions that his nappies have looked darker than her older child's did at this age. She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, received vitamin K at birth and passed meconium on day one.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced to the abdomen, alert and vigorous, liver edge palpable 2 cm below the costal margin with a firm texture, spleen not palpable, no bruising or petechiae, anterior fontanelle soft
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 212 micromol/L, conjugated fraction 68 micromol/L, alanine aminotransferase 96 U/L (less than 40), gamma glutamyl transferase 384 U/L (less than 50), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.1 (0.9-1.2), full blood count within normal limits, direct antiglobulin test negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer urgently to a paediatric liver service the same day for investigation of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
Reassure the mother that this is breast milk jaundice and recheck the bilirubin level in a further two weeks
Commence intensive phototherapy and repeat the total serum bilirubin level in six hours to assess the response
Advise a 24 hour trial of formula feeding and repeat the bilirubin to see whether the level falls appreciably
Arrange a urine sample for culture and treat for urinary tract infection while awaiting the laboratory result

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear with a C reactive protein of 62 after apparent improvement on ibuprofen for a presumed irritable hip
stem: A four-year-old boy diagnosed with an irritable hip three days ago improved at first on ibuprofen. Since yesterday he refuses to stand. His mother recorded temperatures of 38.2 and 38.5 degrees C at home.

data_table.Examination: Right hip held flexed and externally rotated, guarding on passive internal rotation
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 62 mg/L, ESR 48 mm/h, ultrasound shows a 9 mm right hip effusion, pelvic radiograph normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue ibuprofen, orthopaedic review in one week
Urgent image guided aspiration before antibiotics
Intravenous flucloxacillin, reviewing response tomorrow
Magnetic resonance of both hips before aspiration
Oral prednisolone, repeat inflammatory markers in 48 hours

subtopic_detail: Headache with a pulse of 62 and a rising blood pressure six hours into treatment as the biochemistry improves
stem: An eleven-year-old girl is six hours into treatment for new onset diabetic ketoacidosis. Her glucose has fallen from 34 to 14 mmol/L. She now has a headache, has vomited, and is irritable and slow to answer.

data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 13, no focal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH improved from 7.02 to 7.28; corrected sodium 139 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the insulin infusion rate and continue fluids
Give a 10 mL/kg sodium chloride bolus now
Give hypertonic saline and reduce the fluid rate
Arrange an urgent computed tomography of the brain
Add intravenous glucose to the current regimen

subtopic_detail: next investigation for a six week old with a raised conjugated bilirubin fraction after an ultrasound that failed to visualise the gallbladder
stem: A six-week-old breastfed girl is still jaundiced. She feeds well and is gaining weight on the tenth centile. Her nappies stain orange and her stools are putty coloured.

data_table.Examination: Firm liver edge 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L with conjugated fraction 68, ALT 128 U/L, GGT 410 U/L
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound after four hours fasting: gallbladder not visualised

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Transfer to a paediatric liver unit for cholangiography
Repeat the ultrasound after a six hour fast before referral
Iminodiacetic acid scan after phenobarbital pre-treatment
Reassure as breast milk jaundice, review in two weeks
Ursodeoxycholic acid and fat soluble vitamins, weekly review

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with referred knee pain and an externally rotated leg whose frontal hip radiograph was reported as normal
stem: A 13-year-old boy has six weeks of dull left knee ache. A knee radiograph was normal and ibuprofen has not helped. He has limped for a fortnight. His body mass index is on the 97th centile.

data_table.Examination: Knee examination normal; left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 on the right, with obligatory external rotation on flexion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Screening bloods for juvenile arthritis, then review
Frog leg lateral hip views, non-weight-bearing meanwhile
Magnetic resonance of the left hip, weight bearing allowed
Ultrasound of the left hip and inflammatory markers
Physiotherapy for patellofemoral rehabilitation, review in six weeks

subtopic_detail: choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia first noticed at seven months when the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 7-month-old girl for her routine check. Her mother has noticed that the creases on the back of the thighs do not match and that one leg seems shorter when she changes the nappy.

The pregnancy was complicated by breech presentation from 34 weeks, and she was born by elective caesarean at term. She has an older sister who wore a harness as a baby. On examination, with the hips and knees flexed and the feet together on the couch, the left knee sits visibly lower than the right. Abduction of the left hip is limited to 45 degrees compared with 75 degrees on the right. You feel no clunk on either side. Her tone, reflexes and spine are normal and she is meeting her developmental milestones.

data_table.Examination: Asymmetrical thigh creases, left knee lower than right on Galeazzi testing, left hip abduction 45 degrees versus 75 degrees on the right, no clunk elicited
data_table.Background: Breech from 34 weeks, first degree relative treated in a harness, normal neurological examination

lead_in: Which imaging would you request?

options.text: No imaging, because the absence of a palpable clunk makes significant dysplasia unlikely here
A limited computed tomography of the pelvis, because it defines acetabular version most precisely
A frontal pelvic radiograph, because the femoral head ossifies by around four to six months
A static and dynamic hip ultrasound, because it avoids ionising radiation in a young infant
A magnetic resonance scan of both hips, because it images cartilage and bone simultaneously

subtopic_detail: ophthalmology surveillance interval for a young girl with persistent knee swelling and a positive antinuclear antibody who has no eye symptoms
stem: A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for four months, with an hour of morning stiffness and then normal activity. She has had no fever or rash.

data_table.Examination: Right knee effusion with 10 degree fixed flexion, small right ankle effusion, eyes white
data_table.Investigations: Inflammatory markers normal, antinuclear antibody positive, rheumatoid factor negative

lead_in: What eye care would you arrange?

options.text: Visual acuity at each visit, referring only if acuity falls
Slit lamp examination now, repeated only if the arthritis remains active
Dilated fundoscopy at each visit, referring if red reflex is lost
Slit lamp examination now and then three monthly thereafter
Slit lamp examination now and then twelve monthly thereafter

subtopic_detail: timing of a delayed live viral vaccine in a child who has just finished a prolonged high dose oral corticosteroid course
stem: A 2-year-old boy has finished an eight-week course of oral prednisolone 2 mg/kg daily for nephrotic syndrome, his last dose four days ago. His parents want the measles, mumps and rubella and varicella vaccines deferred at his 18-month visit. He takes no other immunosuppressant.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oedema, growth on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for protein for three weeks

lead_in: When should the live vaccines be given?

options.text: Now, since the course has finished and he is in remission
After three months, giving both vaccines together
After one month, giving the vaccines four weeks apart
Never, as nephrotic syndrome is a contraindication
After one month, giving both vaccines together

subtopic_detail: an adolescent with sudden scrotal pain whose ultrasound is reported as showing preserved arterial flow
stem: A 13-year-old boy woke at 7 am with sudden severe left scrotal pain and vomited twice. Too embarrassed to tell anyone until this evening, he now reports less pain.

data_table.Examination: Left hemiscrotum swollen, left testis high riding and transverse, absent cremasteric reflex, no relief on elevation
data_table.Imaging: Scrotal ultrasound: swollen testis, oedematous epididymis, arterial flow present

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Immediate scrotal exploration with bilateral orchidopexy
Oral antibiotics for epididymo-orchitis with urology review in 48 hours
Observe overnight with analgesia and repeat the ultrasound tomorrow
Attempt manual detorsion and discharge him if the pain settles
Request a radionuclide scrotal perfusion scan to resolve the discrepancy

subtopic_detail: purulent eye discharge appearing on the third day of life in a baby whose mother declined antenatal screening
stem: A term baby boy is 60 hours old. Both eyelids became markedly swollen this morning with thick yellow discharge that reaccumulates within minutes of wiping. His mother declined antenatal screening and had an untreated vaginal discharge in the third trimester.

data_table.Examination: Tense bilateral lid oedema, chemosis, copious purulent discharge, cornea clear
data_table.Investigations: Gram stain shows intracellular Gram negative diplococci; nucleic acid testing pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Await nucleic acid testing before starting any antimicrobial
Admit for intravenous third generation cephalosporin and irrigation
Oral erythromycin for fourteen days with saline irrigation
Topical chloramphenicol drops with saline irrigation only
Reassure that this is chemical irritation and irrigate

subtopic_detail: secondary prophylaxis decision after a first episode of migratory polyarthritis with a raised streptococcal titre in a high incidence remote community
stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy in a remote Northern Territory community has three weeks of migratory large joint pain, each joint hot and swollen for a few days. He had an untreated sore throat five weeks ago.

data_table.Examination: New soft apical pansystolic murmur radiating to the axilla
data_table.Investigations: ESR 78 mm/h (<15); CRP 62 mg/L (<5); antistreptolysin O 620 IU/mL raised
data_table.Cardiac: ECG PR 0.20 seconds; mild mitral regurgitation

lead_in: What matters most in his ongoing care?

options.text: Oral corticosteroid for the carditis with echocardiography afterwards
Annual echocardiographic surveillance, antibiotics only for sore throats
Four weekly intramuscular benzathine benzylpenicillin for ten years
Ten days of oral phenoxymethylpenicillin with no further prophylaxis
High dose aspirin until the inflammatory markers normalise, then review

subtopic_detail: displaced elbow fracture in a child with an absent radial pulse but a hand that remains warm and well perfused
stem: A 6-year-old girl fell onto an outstretched hand 90 minutes ago. Radiographs show a completely displaced supracondylar humeral fracture with posterolateral displacement. Her pain is increasing despite repeated analgesia.

data_table.Examination: Anterior skin puckering, radial pulse impalpable and absent on Doppler, hand warm and pink with capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Neurological: Finger and thumb movement intact, sensation normal in all three nerve distributions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Backslab in 90 degrees of flexion with hourly neurovascular observation
Computed tomography angiography of the arm before theatre
Closed reduction under sedation then discharge if perfused
Urgent operative reduction and fixation, reassessing perfusion afterwards
Immediate vascular exploration of the brachial artery before reduction

subtopic_detail: persistent unilateral wheeze weeks after a choking episode in a toddler whose chest radiograph on inspiration is reported as normal
stem: A 2-year-old boy has been treated for presumed asthma for five weeks with salbutamol and two weeks of prednisolone, without improvement. His symptoms began the afternoon he was eating mixed nuts.

data_table.Examination: Monophonic wheeze localised to the right chest with reduced right basal air entry
data_table.Background: No personal or family history of atopy; normal growth
data_table.Imaging: Inspiratory chest radiograph: no consolidation or collapse

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Expiratory or lateral decubitus chest radiographs before deciding
Inhaled corticosteroid by spacer with clinical review in four weeks
Flexible bronchoscopy under sedation in the clinic to inspect the airway
Chest physiotherapy with postural drainage and oral antibiotics
Rigid bronchoscopy under general anaesthesia for inspection and retrieval

subtopic_detail: encephalopathy on the fourth day of life with a respiratory alkalosis and a very high ammonia after an uncomplicated term birth
stem: A term boy fed well for two days and was discharged. He returned on day four sleepy, having vomited three times and stopped feeding. He is poorly responsive with reduced tone and lip smacking.

data_table.Blood gas: pH 7.51; pCO2 26 mmHg; bicarbonate 20 mmol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L
data_table.Investigations: Ammonia 620 micromol/L (<100); glucose 3.6 mmol/L; ketones negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Stop protein, high rate intravenous dextrose with lipid, arrange dialysis
Cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin for sepsis, continuing breastfeeding
Load phenobarbital and observe with two hourly ammonia levels
A 10 per cent dextrose bolus, rechecking glucose and ammonia hourly
Sodium bicarbonate and fluid restriction pending newborn screening

subtopic_detail: deciding when persistent bilateral middle ear effusion with documented hearing loss crosses from watchful waiting to surgical referral
stem: A 4-year-old boy turns the television up loudly and does not answer when spoken to from another room. Strangers find his speech hard to understand, as his kindergarten teacher has noticed.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes dull and retracted with a fluid level
data_table.Audiology: Flat tympanograms bilaterally at three visits over four months; pure tone average 32 dB better ear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to ear nose and throat for bilateral ventilation tubes
Intranasal mometasone 50 micrograms once daily for three months
Repeat audiometry and tympanometry after a further three months
Refer to ear nose and throat for adenoidectomy without tubes
Amoxicillin 15 mg/kg orally three times daily for ten days

subtopic_detail: choosing the confirmatory test after a markedly raised creatine kinase in a boy with late walking and calf hypertrophy
stem: A 4-year-old boy did not walk until 19 months and cannot keep up with other children. Transaminases were raised on a screen for recurrent abdominal pain.

data_table.Examination: Bulky firm calves, proximal weakness with a positive Gowers manoeuvre, reflexes present
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 14 200 U/L (60 to 305), alanine aminotransferase 186 U/L, gamma glutamyl transferase normal

lead_in: Which investigation would confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Nerve conduction studies with needle electromyography of the legs
Genetic testing for deletions and sequence variants in the DMD gene
Liver ultrasound with a metabolic screen for glycogen storage disease
Open muscle biopsy of the vastus lateralis for dystrophin immunostaining
Magnetic resonance imaging of both thighs to map muscle involvement

subtopic_detail: first line treatment of asymptomatic low blood glucose in an at risk term newborn who is feeding and rooming in with mother
stem: A term boy weighing 4320 g is 3 hours old. His mother had diet controlled gestational diabetes. He has fed well at the breast and is rooming in.

data_table.Examination: Alert and rooting, normal tone and cry, no jitteriness, well perfused
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 1.9 mmol/L before the second feed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Offer a further breastfeed and repeat the glucose pre-feed
Hourly bottle formula top ups, repeating the glucose in 3 hours
40 per cent dextrose gel buccally with a feed, recheck at 30 minutes
Transfer to the nursery for intravenous 10 per cent glucose
A 2 mL/kg intravenous bolus of 10 per cent glucose, then admit

subtopic_detail: applying gestational age and birth weight thresholds to decide which preterm infant enters the retinal screening program and when
stem:
You are the neonatal registrar planning the week's screening list on a tertiary nursery. Four infants are under your care and the ophthalmology service visits every Thursday.

The infant you are asked about was born at 29 weeks and 2 days gestation weighing 1180 g and is now 25 days old, corrected to 32 weeks and 6 days. He needed continuous positive airway pressure for 11 days and two days of supplemental oxygen at 30 per cent, and is now in air and fully enterally fed. He has had no retinal examination since birth. His cranial ultrasound was normal and he has had no culture proven sepsis. The consultant asks you to confirm the timing of his first eye examination before the list is finalised.

data_table.Examination: Settled in an open cot in air, weight now 1560 g, no dysmorphic features
data_table.Birth details: 29 weeks and 2 days gestation, birth weight 1180 g, currently 32 weeks and 6 days corrected
data_table.Respiratory course: Continuous positive airway pressure for 11 days, supplemental oxygen to a maximum of 30 per cent for 2 days, now in air

lead_in: When should his first retinal examination be performed?

options.text: At 36 weeks corrected age once he is established in an open cot in air
At discharge from the nursery or at term corrected age, whichever comes first
Only if he requires further supplemental oxygen or develops culture proven sepsis
At 4 weeks after birth or 31 weeks corrected age, whichever comes later
At 6 weeks after birth regardless of the corrected gestational age reached

subtopic_detail: selecting the assessment pathway for a child labelled penicillin allergic after a delayed rash during a course of amoxicillin
stem: A 5-year-old girl carries a penicillin allergy label from age 2, when a flat pink non-itchy rash appeared over her trunk and limbs on day 6 of a 10-day amoxicillin course and faded over four days untreated. There was no swelling, breathing difficulty, blistering or mucosal involvement. She has since tolerated cefalexin twice.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach to her allergy label?

options.text: Skin prick and intradermal testing to penicillin determinants before challenge
Measure serum specific immunoglobulin E to penicilloyl determinants
Retain the label and continue prescribing non-penicillin agents when needed
Graded oral desensitisation with incremental amoxicillin doses over one day
Direct oral amoxicillin challenge under observation without skin testing

subtopic_detail: sequencing treatment against imaging after an abnormal newborn screening thyroid stimulating hormone result
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar telephoned by the newborn screening laboratory about a 9-day-old girl born at term. The screening card taken on day 3 showed a thyroid stimulating hormone above the action threshold and a venous confirmatory sample drawn yesterday shows thyroid stimulating hormone 84 mIU/L (1.7 to 9.1) with a free thyroxine of 7.2 pmol/L (10 to 26).

She is feeding every three hours, has regained her birth weight, and opened her bowels this morning. On examination she has a small anterior fontanelle, no goitre, no umbilical hernia and normal tone. The parents are in the department now and are asking what happens next. Your hospital can perform a thyroid ultrasound today but the nuclear medicine department cannot offer a radionuclide uptake scan until next Tuesday, which is six days away.

data_table.Examination: No goitre, no umbilical hernia, normal tone and activity, anterior fontanelle small, weight back to birth weight at day 9
data_table.Investigations: Venous thyroid stimulating hormone 84 mIU/L (1.7 to 9.1), free thyroxine 7.2 pmol/L (10 to 26)
data_table.Logistics: Thyroid ultrasound available today, radionuclide uptake scan not available for 6 days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start oral thyroxine today and arrange imaging without letting it delay treatment
Wait for the radionuclide uptake scan next Tuesday and start thyroxine once the aetiology is known
Repeat the thyroid function tests in two weeks and treat only if the results remain abnormal
Measure maternal thyroid antibodies and withhold treatment pending the antibody result
Start oral iodine supplementation and review the thyroid function tests in one week

subtopic_detail: managing falling urine output and a falling haemoglobin in the week after bloody diarrhoea in a preschool child
stem: A 3-year-old girl returns seven days after bloody diarrhoea that settled four days ago. She has had one wet nappy since yesterday and her face is puffy in the mornings.

data_table.Examination: Pale, periorbital puffiness, ankle oedema, BP 112/74 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L, platelets 42 x10^9/L, creatinine 138 micromol/L (20 to 45), red cell fragments, DAT negative, stool culture Shiga toxin positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management approach?

options.text: Loperamide with generous oral rehydration to restore urine output
Supportive fluid and electrolyte management with nephrology involvement
Intravenous ceftriaxone to clear the organism and shorten illness
High dose methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisolone
Urgent platelet transfusion to correct the thrombocytopenia

subtopic_detail: responding to knee pain with a restricted hip in an overweight adolescent whose knee imaging is normal
stem: A 12-year-old boy has six weeks of left knee pain and now limps at school. He recalls no injury. His body mass index is above the 97th centile.

data_table.Examination: Left knee full painless range; left hip guarded on log roll with obligatory external rotation on flexion
data_table.Investigations: Afebrile; C-reactive protein and white cell count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bone scan of the pelvis and lower limbs for a stress injury
Magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee for a meniscal injury
Non weight bearing with urgent pelvic frog lateral radiographs
Ibuprofen with a graded quadriceps program, review in six weeks
Ultrasound guided hip aspiration for microscopy and culture

subtopic_detail: recognising that a child presenting with vomiting and lethargy has a cardiac rather than gastrointestinal cause before giving fluid
stem: A 6-year-old boy has three days of vomiting and lethargy after a febrile household illness. He has had no diarrhoea and became breathless walking. A 20 mL/kg saline bolus is drawn up for presumed gastroenteritis.

data_table.Examination: Mottled, capillary refill 4 seconds, liver 4 cm below costal margin, bibasal crackles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Start nasogastric rehydration at 25 mL/kg over four hours
Give intravenous ondansetron and observe him for two hours
Take blood cultures, give ceftriaxone and fluid to 60 mL/kg
Hold the bolus and obtain electrocardiogram, troponin and chest film
Give the 20 mL/kg saline bolus and reassess his perfusion

subtopic_detail: interpreting jaundice persisting beyond two weeks in a breastfed infant whose nappies show pale stools
stem: A 3-week-old girl is still jaundiced. She is exclusively breastfed, feeds well and has gained weight steadily. Her stools have become pale and creamy over the past week and her urine stains the nappy dark.

data_table.Examination: Jaundiced to the thighs, alert, liver 2 cm below the costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 168 micromol/L with conjugated 74, ALT 96 U/L, GGT 412 U/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Phototherapy, with the bilirubin rechecked in twelve hours
A 48 hour trial of formula, then repeat the bilirubin
Repeat antiglobulin test, reticulocytes and blood film
Reassure and review the bilirubin in two weeks
Urgent referral to a paediatric liver service

subtopic_detail: arranging surveillance for asymptomatic eye disease in a young child with a persistently swollen knee and a positive antinuclear antibody
stem: A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen left knee for four months with 30 minutes of morning stiffness. She has had no fever, rash or eye symptoms.

data_table.Examination: Warm left knee with a small effusion and 10 degree fixed flexion, other joints normal, eyes white
data_table.Investigations: Inflammatory markers normal, rheumatoid factor negative, antinuclear antibody 1 in 320 positive

lead_in: Besides treating the joint, what surveillance would you arrange?

options.text: Three monthly slit lamp examination by an ophthalmologist
Three monthly visual acuity testing, referring if acuity falls
Ophthalmology review only if she develops eye pain or redness
Annual dilated fundoscopy in the general paediatric clinic
Three monthly antinuclear antibody titres, referring if rising

subtopic_detail: distinguishing a fused suture from a positional head shape in an infant with progressive skull asymmetry
stem: A 5-month-old boy has a head shape his parents say is worsening despite four months of alternating his sleeping position and daily tummy time. His development is age appropriate.

data_table.Examination: Skull long front to back and narrow side to side, firm midline ridge, small anterior fontanelle, full neck rotation
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue repositioning and tummy time, review in three months
Refer to a craniofacial service and image the sutures
Physiotherapy for neck tightness contributing to the asymmetry
Arrange a moulding helmet and review after eight weeks
Measure thyroid function and vitamin D before referral

subtopic_detail: choosing between a surgical and an endocrine cause of vomiting in a second week infant when the electrolytes contradict the expected pattern
stem: A 12-day-old boy has vomited forcefully after feeds for four days and is hungry straight afterwards. He is lethargic, mottled and poorly perfused. There is no abdominal mass after a test feed.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, mottled, capillary refill 4 s; normal male genitalia, testes descended
data_table.Investigations: Na 119 mmol/L; K 7.4 mmol/L; glucose 2.1 mmol/L; pH 7.19; bicarbonate 12 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Hypertonic saline 3 per cent 4 mL/kg before any other treatment
Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous fludrocortisone and dextrose
Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous hydrocortisone and potassium treatment
Saline 20 mL/kg and surgical referral for pyloromyotomy
Saline 20 mL/kg with intravenous cefotaxime after blood cultures

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation from low-flow nasal prongs
stem: A 5-month-old girl with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis was started on nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min two hours ago for saturations of 88%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 /min, RR 62 /min, SpO2 91% on 1 L/min nasal prongs
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal and intercostal recession, nasal flaring, no grunting

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in respiratory support?

options.text: Increase low-flow nasal prong oxygen to 2 L/min and reassess
Start high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min, FiO2 0.4
Start mask continuous positive airway pressure at 6 cmH2O
Give nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg and reassess at 20 minutes
Add four-hourly nebulised 3 per cent hypertonic saline

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dose selection in moderate croup at emergency department presentation
stem: A 2-year-old boy has a barking cough and noisy breathing that began this evening, after two days of coryza and low-grade fever. He has no asthma and has never been intubated.

data_table.Vital signs: RR 34 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, T 37.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor at rest that settles when he is calm, suprasternal recession, no drooling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg as a single dose
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose
Nebulised adrenaline with oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing functional constipation from organic disease requiring investigation in a toddler
stem: A 20-month-old boy passes one hard pellet-like stool every four to five days, and has done for six months, with visible straining. There has been no soiling. He passed meconium within 12 hours of birth.

data_table.Growth: Weight and height on the 25th centile, stable
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen, no mass; anus normally sited; normal lower limb neurology and spine
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and coeliac serology normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Anorectal manometry and rectal suction biopsy
Oral macrogol disimpaction then titrated maintenance
Abdominal radiograph and thyroid function tests
Cow milk protein exclusion diet for four weeks
Daily sodium citrate enema for one week

subtopic_detail: Recognition and treatment of incomplete Kawasaki disease in a young infant with prolonged fever
stem: A 9-month-old girl has seven days of fever with irritability and poor feeding. Her parents report red eyes and cracked lips.

data_table.Examination: T 39.4 degrees C, non-purulent conjunctivitis, cracked lips, strawberry tongue, 2 cm cervical node, no rash
data_table.Investigations: CRP 148 mg/L, platelets 620 x10^9/L, Hb 96 g/L, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 78 U/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone with blood cultures repeated at 48 hours
Intravenous immunoglobulin with high-dose aspirin, admit to cardiology
High-dose oral prednisolone for two weeks with low-dose aspirin
Intravenous infliximab with low-dose aspirin and cardiology review
Intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin pending cultures

subtopic_detail: Cyanosis with normal pulse oximetry saturation and normal arterial oxygen tension in a neonate
stem: A 4-week-old boy has had intermittent perioral cyanosis for two days. He started home-prepared vegetable puree this week, from a garden irrigated with well water. Central cyanosis persists on 15 L/min oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, RR 46 /min, SpO2 87% on 15 L/min, T 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.36, PaO2 240 mmHg, PaCO2 34 mmHg, chocolate-brown blood; echocardiogram structurally normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime and amoxicillin with a fluid bolus
Prostaglandin E1 infusion and urgent cardiology transfer
Intravenous methylene blue and stop the vegetable puree
Exchange transfusion via an umbilical venous catheter
Intravenous ascorbic acid with continued high-flow oxygen

subtopic_detail: Choice of induction therapy in newly diagnosed paediatric Crohn disease with terminal ileal and colonic involvement
stem: A 14-year-old boy has two months of abdominal pain and non-bloody diarrhoea four to six times daily. Perianal examination is normal.

data_table.Growth: Weight fallen from the 50th to the 10th centile, height velocity reduced
data_table.Investigations: Terminal ileal cobblestoning, patchy colitis, non-caseating granulomas; no stricture, fistula or perianal disease on MR enterography

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction therapy?

options.text: Intravenous infliximab at weeks zero, two and six with weekly methotrexate
Oral prednisolone tapered over eight weeks with azathioprine maintenance
Exclusive enteral nutrition with polymeric formula for six to eight weeks
Intravenous methylprednisolone for five days, then oral prednisolone
Oral mesalazine in divided doses with colonoscopy review at twelve weeks

subtopic_detail: Tachypnoea and poor feeding at seven weeks
stem: A 7-week-old boy has had 10 days of cough, poor feeding and sweating during bottles. He was born at term and has gained 80 g since his 4 week check.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 176, RR 70, SpO2 95 percent in room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Fine crackles, subcostal recession, liver 4 cm below the costal margin, harsh pansystolic murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Chest radiograph with transthoracic echocardiography
Nasopharyngeal aspirate for respiratory viral testing
Full blood count with blood cultures and urine culture
Sweat chloride test with a faecal elastase level
Twenty four hour oesophageal pH and impedance study

subtopic_detail: Paediatric DKA fluid rate with cerebral oedema risk balance
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9-year-old boy with new-onset type 1 diabetes. He presented with 2 weeks of polyuria and polydipsia and a 4 kg weight loss. He has been vomiting for 12 hours and is drowsy but rousable. His mother reports no headache and no visual complaints before arrival.

Weight today is 28 kg. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.14, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22 to 32), glucose 26 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.4), sodium 132 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), and beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 100 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 3 seconds and mucous membranes are dry. GCS is 14.

data_table.Weight and vitals: 28 kg; HR 130; BP 96/58; RR 34 Kussmaul; SpO2 100 percent; T 36.9
data_table.VBG: pH 7.14; HCO3 8 mmol/L (22 to 32); glucose 26 mmol/L; Na 132 mmol/L; K 4.8 mmol/L; beta-hydroxybutyrate 5.6 mmol/L
data_table.Neurology: GCS 14; drowsy but rousable; no headache or visual complaints

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intravenous fluid regimen?

options.text: 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 15 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance over 24 hours
Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h before starting any intravenous fluid replacement
10 mL/kg 0.9 percent sodium chloride bolus over 30 minutes, then deficit plus maintenance evenly over 48 hours
Give oral rehydration solution with subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin for 4 hours before intravenous access
5 mL/kg 0.45 percent sodium chloride bolus over 60 minutes with an 8.4 percent sodium bicarbonate infusion

subtopic_detail: Preventing fever after meningococcal B vaccination in a young infant
stem: You are seeing a healthy 6-week-old boy for his scheduled immunisations, which include the meningococcal B vaccine. His mother is anxious because his older sister had a high fever after that vaccine.

data_table.Growth: Born at term, thriving, weight on the 50th centile
data_table.Examination: Afebrile and well; chest and abdomen normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg with the vaccine, then six-hourly twice
Give ibuprofen 10 mg/kg with the vaccine, then six-hourly twice
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg only if a fever develops after the vaccine
Give prednisolone 1 mg/kg on the morning of the vaccination only
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg the evening before the vaccination only

subtopic_detail: Simple febrile seizure workup and disposition
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18-month-old girl in the emergency department 90 minutes after a generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 3 minutes at home. She has been coryzal for 2 days and reached a temperature of 39.2 degrees Celsius shortly before the seizure. She returned to her baseline within 20 minutes and has since been playing with a toy at triage. Her immunisations are up to date and there is no family history of epilepsy.

On examination she is alert and interactive with clear rhinorrhoea, red pharynx without exudate, and no rash. Neurological examination including tone, gait, and cranial nerves is normal. Vital signs: pulse 130/min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 28/min, SpO2 99 percent in room air, temperature 38.4 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is under 2 seconds.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 130; BP 98/62; RR 28; SpO2 99 percent; T 38.4
data_table.Seizure: Generalised tonic-clonic, 3 minutes, single, resolved 90 minutes ago
data_table.Examination: Alert, interactive; normal neurology; coryzal features; no rash
data_table.Background: Immunisations up to date; no family history of epilepsy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Arrange lumbar puncture and empirical intravenous ceftriaxone before considering discharge
Order an urgent outpatient EEG within 1 week to exclude an underlying epilepsy syndrome
Commence daily oral sodium valproate 20 mg/kg/day as long-term seizure prophylaxis
Prescribe rectal diazepam for the family to give at the onset of any future febrile illness
Give antipyretic advice, reassure the family, and discharge with GP review

subtopic_detail: Incomplete Kawasaki disease supplemental criteria and IVIG threshold
stem: A 2-year-old boy is on day 6 of fever above 39 degrees C, fractious and inconsolable. His parents describe a truncal rash that resolved on day 3.

data_table.Examination: Non-purulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, cracked lips, palmar erythema, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, platelets 480 x10^9/L, CRP 92 mg/L, ESR 68 mm/h, albumin 28 g/L, ALT 74 U/L, sterile pyuria

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone alone as first-line therapy
Blood and urine culture and chest radiograph, deferring therapy 24 hours
Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone with immunoglobulin deferred
Echocardiography with intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin now
Observation with paracetamol and repeat markers on day 10

subtopic_detail: Late preterm hypoglycaemia intervention threshold and glucose gel first-line
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the postnatal ward reviewing a 36 plus 4 week baby girl born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3 hours ago. Birthweight is 2450 g. Her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin during pregnancy. The baby is skin-to-skin, has latched but only briefly, and looks pink and settled. The midwife has performed the routine pre-feed heel-prick glucose per the trust pathway.

On examination she is alert, well perfused, and euvolaemic. There is no jitteriness, tone is normal, and the cry is strong. Vital signs: pulse 148/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The pre-feed heel-prick blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L (above 2.6). Umbilical cord pH was 7.32 with base excess minus 2.

data_table.Baby: 36+4 weeks; 2450 g; 3 hours old; skin-to-skin; alert and pink; no jitteriness
data_table.Risk factor: Mother with type 2 diabetes on metformin during pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a single formula top-up feed of 15 mL/kg and defer repeat glucose testing until the next routine 3 hour check
Give buccal 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg, feed at the breast, and repeat the blood glucose in 30 minutes
Transfer to the neonatal unit for an intravenous 10 percent glucose infusion at 4 mg/kg/min
Reassure the mother, encourage continued skin-to-skin, and repeat the glucose after the next feed in 3 hours
Administer intramuscular glucagon 0.2 mg/kg and continue routine breastfeeding on the postnatal ward

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease and prostaglandin E1
stem: A 3-day-old term boy went grey during feeds. He was discharged well on day 1 and the 20 week morphology scan was normal.

data_table.Saturations: Pre-ductal 96 per cent; post-ductal 82 per cent
data_table.Blood pressure: 62/38 mmHg right arm; 44/26 mmHg right leg
data_table.Examination: Pale and cool with reduced femoral pulses; soft systolic murmur

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial drug?

options.text: Prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 ng/kg/min with urgent cardiology transfer
Adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min for cardiogenic shock
Intravenous furosemide 1 mg/kg with oral captopril to reduce afterload
A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with ceftriaxone for suspected sepsis
100 per cent oxygen by facemask with continued ward observation

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia salt-losing crisis in a neonate
stem: A 12-day-old term boy has vomited for three days and lost 12 percent of his birthweight, with no diarrhoea or fever. Newborn screening results are pending.

data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds, hyperpigmented but normal male genitalia
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L, K 6.8 mmol/L, glucose 2.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: A 20 mL/kg saline bolus with intravenous ceftriaxone
Oral fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily with oral rehydration
A 10 mL/kg saline bolus, dextrose and hydrocortisone 25 mg
Intravenous calcium gluconate and salbutamol for the hyperkalaemia
Hypertonic saline 3 percent 3 mL/kg to raise sodium 8 mmol/L hourly

subtopic_detail: Croup severity assessment and dexamethasone dosing
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a metropolitan emergency department. A 2-year-old boy is brought in by his mother at 2 am with a 1 day history of a barking cough and a hoarse voice.

On arrival he is alert and consolable in his mother's arms. He has a barking cough but no stridor when calm. Stridor becomes audible when he cries during examination. There is mild suprasternal recession only when upset, no tracheal tug at rest, and air entry is equal with no wheeze. He has taken a small amount of oral fluid in the last hour.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degrees C. His immunisations are up to date.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 100/60 mmHg; RR 32/min; SpO2 98% RA; T 37.6 C
data_table.Examination: Alert; barking cough; hoarse voice; stridor only when crying; mild suprasternal recession when upset; air entry equal; no wheeze
data_table.History: 1 day symptoms; immunisations up to date; taking small oral fluids

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and discharge home once settled and tolerating fluids
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose, and observe for 30 minutes before discharge
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days, and review with the general practitioner in the morning
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single dose, and nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 immediately
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose, and admit for overnight observation of the airway

subtopic_detail: Rehydration route in paediatric gastroenteritis
stem: An 18-month-old boy weighing 12 kg has 24 hours of profuse watery diarrhoea and vomiting. A supervised trial of oral rehydration solution by syringe in triage failed after two vomits.

data_table.Examination: Rousable and interactive, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 2 sec, warm peripheries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in rehydration?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 20 mL/kg over 15 minutes
Nasogastric oral rehydration solution 20 mL/kg over the first hour
Oral ondansetron 4 mg wafer and continued syringe feeds
Intravenous 5% dextrose with 0.45% sodium chloride at 46 mL/hour
Admit and offer oral rehydration solution ad libitum at the bedside

subtopic_detail: Serious bacterial infection workup in neonates
stem: A 25-day-old girl born at term has six hours of poor feeding and felt hot to her mother two hours ago. Her older brother has a runny nose.

data_table.Examination: Alert, fontanelle soft and flat, no rash
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 8 mg/L, urine dipstick negative; nasopharyngeal aspirate pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for observation, starting antibiotics only if she deteriorates
Await the nasopharyngeal aspirate before doing a lumbar puncture
Lumbar puncture, blood and urine cultures, then cefotaxime and benzylpenicillin
Give intramuscular ceftriaxone and discharge for review tomorrow
Take a catheter urine specimen and observe her for four hours

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation and admission decision
stem: A 3-month-old boy born at 38 weeks has four days of coryza and two days of wet cough, with one apnoea during a feed this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168/min, RR 62/min, SpO2 88 per cent in air, 92 per cent on 2 L/min prongs after 20 minutes
data_table.Examination: Recession and tracheal tug persisting on prongs
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate: respiratory syncytial virus

lead_in: What is the most appropriate respiratory support?

options.text: Continue 2 L/min nasal prongs and reassess in two hours
Back to back nebulised salbutamol, then reassess
Nebulised 3 per cent sodium chloride, then reassess
High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min, target SpO2 90
Intubate and ventilate now for the reported apnoea

subtopic_detail: Recognition and reporting of suspected non-accidental injury
stem: A 5-month-old boy has reduced right arm movement noticed at a nappy change. No fall is reported. An older half-sibling is in out of home care.

data_table.Examination: Bruising right upper arm, three circular bruises left cheek, healing linear mark left thigh; weight fallen to the 3rd centile
data_table.Investigations: Right humerus radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Refer to the community child health nurse for a home visit
Immobilise the arm and discharge with the mother's partner
Order a skeletal survey and coagulation screen, then discharge
Consult orthopaedics and defer safeguarding until the plan is set
Admit for a child protection workup and notify child protection

subtopic_detail: Prolonged neonatal jaundice with pale stools
stem: A 4-week-old exclusively breastfed girl remains jaundiced since discharge. Her stools have been pale for 10 days and her urine dark. She is alert, feeding well and back to birth weight.

data_table.Examination: Icteric to the mid abdomen, abdomen soft, liver not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Total bilirubin 148 micromol/L, direct bilirubin 62 micromol/L (<20), ALT 78 U/L, thyroid function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure that this is breast milk jaundice and review in two weeks
Arrange urgent same-day admission for hepatology assessment
Commence phototherapy and repeat the bilirubin in 24 hours
Give intramuscular vitamin K and repeat coagulation studies
Trial formula feeding for 48 hours and repeat the bilirubin

subtopic_detail: Post UTI imaging decision at 20 months per RCH
stem: A 20-month-old girl is reviewed six weeks after her first febrile urinary tract infection, treated orally for Escherichia coli. She was well throughout and defervesced within 24 hours. Her antenatal morphology scan was normal and there is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux.

data_table.Examination: Well grown, normal examination; repeat urine culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No imaging, with prompt culture and treatment of any future febrile illness
Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal scan at six months for cortical scarring
Micturating cystourethrogram to grade reflux and guide prophylaxis
Renal tract ultrasound this week to exclude obstruction and dilatation
Continuous low-dose trimethoprim prophylaxis with imaging if UTI recurs

subtopic_detail: First line oxygen delivery in moderate bronchiolitis per RCH
stem: A 7-month-old boy born at term has three days of coryza and 24 hours of cough, tachypnoea and feeds at half his usual intake.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 158 /min, RR 62 /min, SpO2 89% in room air
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild subcostal recession, widespread wheeze and crackles

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen delivery?

options.text: High flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min, target saturations 94 to 98 percent
Nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min, target saturations at least 90 percent
Hudson mask oxygen 6 L/min, target saturations 94 to 98 percent
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg before any supplemental oxygen is given
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with three hours observation

subtopic_detail: Dexamethasone dosing in mild to moderate croup per RCH
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 2-year-old boy brought in overnight with a 1 day history of coryza, hoarse voice, and a barking cough. He is settled on his mother's lap and has stridor only when upset. There is no drooling and he has been drinking sips of oral fluid.

He has no chronic respiratory disease, no cardiac disease, and no history of intubation. Immunisations are up to date. Older siblings have had similar symptoms this week.

Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 34/min, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 37.9 degrees C. Weight today is measured at 13 kg. He has mild suprasternal recession at rest and a barking cough on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128/min; BP 96/58 mmHg; RR 34/min; SpO2 97% RA; T 37.9 C
data_table.Examination: Settled on lap; mild suprasternal recession at rest; barking cough; stridor only when upset
data_table.Investigations: None indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid regimen?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily for 3 days as an outpatient course of steroids with a review by the general practitioner in 48 hours
Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge
Intramuscular dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg as a single stat dose in the department and reassess symptoms after 2 hours before discharge

subtopic_detail: First line adrenaline dosing in anaphylaxis in a 4 year old per ASCIA
stem: A 4-year-old girl with known peanut allergy developed generalised urticaria, facial swelling, wheeze and a hoarse cry ten minutes after eating a peanut butter sandwich. Her autoinjector was left at home.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 148 /min, BP 88/54 mmHg, SpO2 93% in room air
data_table.Examination: Audible stridor with diffuse wheeze
data_table.Growth: Weight 16 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first adrenaline dose?

options.text: Adrenaline 100 microgram intravenously by slow bolus with cardiac monitoring
Adrenaline 160 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 300 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
Adrenaline 150 microgram intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 with high flow oxygen

subtopic_detail: Full septic workup in an unwell 6 week old with normal inflammatory markers
stem: A 6-week-old boy has 8 hours of poor feeding, one bilious vomit and reduced tone. He was born at term and had been gaining weight well.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188/min; BP 62/38 mmHg; RR 62/min; T 36.2 C
data_table.Examination: Poorly rousable; mottled; delayed central capillary refill
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.28, lactate 4.9 mmol/L; WCC 6.2 x10^9/L; CRP 8 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Oral paracetamol and ward admission, with cultures reviewed overnight
Adrenaline infusion first, then cultures, cefotaxime and a fluid bolus
A 20 mL/kg bolus first, then cultures, then benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
Withhold antibiotics because the inflammatory markers are normal
Access, cultures, cefotaxime, then 20 mL/kg saline over 5 minutes

subtopic_detail: Choice of rehydration route in moderate paediatric gastroenteritis per RCH
stem: An 18-month-old girl has 3 days of vomiting and watery diarrhoea. She has vomited back most of an hour of syringe-fed oral rehydration solution and now refuses it.

data_table.Examination: HR 148/min; interactive; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Na 137 mmol/L; HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate rehydration plan?

options.text: Nasogastric rehydration solution at 25 mL/kg per hour for 4 hours
Intravenous saline with glucose at maintenance plus 50 percent
Continue oral rehydration by syringe, reassessing in 4 hours
A single oral dose of ondansetron, then retrial of syringe feeding
Intravenous saline 20 mL/kg over 30 minutes, then reassessment

subtopic_detail: Severe croup management with concurrent adrenaline and dexamethasone
stem: A 20-month-old boy weighing 12 kg has two days of coryza and a barking cough and now has stridor at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 /min, RR 48 /min, SpO2 93% in air, T 38.4 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Agitated when disturbed, stridor at rest, intercostal and suprasternal recession, tiring between cries

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 0.5 mg/kg of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg
Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1 in 1000 plus oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg
Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg alone with two hours of observation
Rapid sequence intubation now under paediatric anaesthetic support
Heliox by loose fitting mask plus intravenous dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg

subtopic_detail: Complex early neonatal jaundice with disconfirming DAT and normal groups
stem: A term female neonate is jaundiced to the abdomen at 30 hours of age. She is exclusively breastfed and has lost 3 percent of her birthweight. Both parents are of northern European heritage; her maternal grandfather had a splenectomy in his thirties.

data_table.Examination: Alert, no cephalohaematoma or bruising
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 285 micromol/L (conjugated 10); Hb 152 g/L; reticulocytes 8 percent; film frequent spherocytes; DAT negative; maternal O positive, neonatal A positive; G6PD pending

lead_in: What is the most likely aetiology of this baby's jaundice?

options.text: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn
Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency
Hereditary spherocytosis causing haemolysis
Physiological jaundice with poor milk intake
Delayed jaundice from cephalohaematoma resorption

subtopic_detail: Initial treatment of steroid sensitive nephrotic syndrome in a preschool child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 4-year-old boy whose parents noticed his eyes were puffy in the mornings for the past week, and that his tummy now looks swollen. He is otherwise well, eating and playing normally.

He has had no fever, rash or joint swelling, and his urine has been pale rather than dark or tea coloured. He was born at term with no antenatal renal abnormality and has no family history of kidney disease. On examination he has periorbital oedema, mild ascites and pitting oedema to mid shin. His blood pressure is on the 50th centile for age and height. His urine microscopy shows no red cell casts.
