data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 92/58, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein creatinine ratio 640 mg/mmol; urine microscopy no red cell casts; complement C3 and C4 within normal limits
data_table.Blood tests: Serum albumin 17 g/L (35-50); creatinine 32 micromol/L (25-55); total cholesterol 9.2 mmol/L (below 4.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Percutaneous renal biopsy before any treatment to establish the underlying histological diagnosis
Oral prednisolone daily for four to six weeks followed by an alternate day tapering course
Intravenous albumin infusion followed by intravenous furosemide to mobilise the accumulated oedema
Oral furosemide with strict fluid restriction and daily weights until the oedema has resolved
Oral enalapril to reduce proteinuria with monitoring of renal function and serum potassium

subtopic_detail: Renal surveillance schedule after Henoch Schonlein purpura
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old girl in the short stay unit. Over four days she has developed a rash over her buttocks and the backs of her legs that her mother describes as raised purple spots that do not fade when pressed, along with sore swollen ankles and intermittent tummy pain.

She is afebrile and looks well between episodes of pain. Her platelet count and coagulation screen are within normal limits, which excludes a bleeding disorder as the cause of the rash. Her abdomen is soft with no mass, guarding or rectal bleeding. Her blood pressure is on the 60th centile for age and height and her creatinine is within normal limits. Her urinalysis today shows blood 2+ and protein 1+.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 98/60, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura over buttocks and extensor surfaces of both legs; bilateral ankle swelling; abdomen soft, no mass
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis blood 2+ and protein 1+; urine protein creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol; platelets, coagulation screen and creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow up plan?

options.text: No specific renal follow up is required, since the rash and joint symptoms resolve spontaneously
Renal biopsy arranged within the next fortnight to grade the severity of the glomerular involvement
Oral prednisolone for four weeks to prevent progression of the renal involvement over time
Weekly blood pressure and urinalysis for the first month, then at decreasing intervals to twelve months
Renal tract ultrasound now and repeated at six months to assess for structural renal damage

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia from excessive cow milk intake in a toddler
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18-month-old boy whose mother is worried he looks pale and has become fussy and less interested in playing over two months. He walks and has around ten words.

He drinks about 1200 mL of cow milk daily from a bottle and eats very little solid food, refusing meat entirely. He has no diarrhoea, no blood in his nappies and normal growth along the 50th centile for weight and height. He was born at term and has no family history of anaemia or bleeding disorders. His coeliac serology, taken with total immunoglobulin A, is negative and his stool testing shows no occult blood. His blood film shows hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 92/56, RR 26, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Investigations: Blood film: hypochromic microcytic red cells with anisocytosis; coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A negative; faecal occult blood negative
data_table.Blood tests: Haemoglobin 84 g/L (105-135); mean cell volume 62 fL (73-85); ferritin 6 micrograms/L (15-150); C reactive protein within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Transfuse packed red cells and recheck the full blood count before discharge from the day unit
Intravenous iron infusion arranged at the paediatric day unit within the next two weeks
Oral iron supplementation with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and iron rich solids introduced
Dietary advice alone with cow milk reduced below 500 mL daily and repeat blood testing in three months
Haemoglobin electrophoresis before any treatment to exclude an underlying thalassaemia trait

subtopic_detail: Imaging choice for suspected developmental dysplasia of the hip at six weeks
stem:
You are the general practitioner performing a six week check on a baby girl. She was born at 38 weeks by caesarean section for breech presentation at term and her mother's sister was treated in a harness as an infant.

The baby is feeding well and gaining weight along the 50th centile. On examination the Ortolani and Barlow tests are both negative today, but abduction of the left hip in flexion is limited to 55 degrees compared with 80 degrees on the right, and there is an extra skin crease on the left thigh. Leg lengths appear equal with the knees flexed and the feet together. Her neonatal hip examination in the postnatal ward was documented as normal and her tone and reflexes are normal today.

data_table.Examination: Ortolani and Barlow negative; left hip abduction in flexion 55 degrees versus 80 degrees on the right; asymmetric left thigh skin crease; Galeazzi test negative
data_table.Investigations: Neonatal hip examination documented as normal in the postnatal ward

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Plain anteroposterior radiograph of the pelvis arranged today with orthopaedic review of the films
Repeat clinical examination at the six month immunisation visit with no imaging in the interim
Commence a Pavlik harness now and arrange orthopaedic review within the following two weeks
Magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under sedation to define the position of the femoral heads
Ultrasound of both hips arranged now with orthopaedic referral if the acetabular indices are abnormal

subtopic_detail: Preventer initiation threshold in childhood asthma
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 7-year-old boy who has attended three times this year for wheeze. He has a written asthma action plan and uses salbutamol through a spacer.

Over the last three months he has needed salbutamol three times most weeks for chest tightness during football training, and wakes coughing about twice a month. He has had no oral corticosteroid course and no emergency presentation this year. His inhaler technique with the spacer was checked by the practice nurse today and was correct, and his mother confirms he has no exposure to tobacco smoke at home. He has eczema and allergic rhinitis, both well controlled. His spirometry today shows a forced expiratory volume in one second of 88 per cent predicted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 100/62, RR 20, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Chest clear on auscultation today; no accessory muscle use; growth along the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Spirometry: forced expiratory volume in one second 88 per cent predicted; inhaler technique with spacer verified as correct

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence a low dose inhaled corticosteroid preventer through the spacer and review in four weeks
Commence oral montelukast at night as the preventer of choice given his coexisting allergic rhinitis
Commence a combination inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta agonist inhaler through the spacer
Increase salbutamol to a regular four times daily schedule through the spacer and review in one month
Commence a five day course of oral prednisolone and continue reliever therapy as currently prescribed

subtopic_detail: Antibiotic threshold in acute otitis media for an Aboriginal child
stem:
You are the general practitioner at a regional clinic seeing a 3-year-old Aboriginal boy brought in by his grandmother. He has been pulling at his right ear, sleeping poorly and off his food for two days, and she says he has been grizzly and hot.

He has had two previous ear infections in the past year. On otoscopy the right tympanic membrane is bulging, opaque and red with loss of the light reflex, and there is no perforation and no discharge in the canal. The left drum is normal. He is alert, drinking well and has no neck stiffness, mastoid tenderness or facial weakness. He has had all scheduled immunisations including pneumococcal conjugate vaccine. He has no drug allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 96/58, RR 24, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 38.3
data_table.Examination: Right tympanic membrane bulging, opaque and erythematous with absent light reflex; no perforation or discharge; left drum normal; no mastoid tenderness

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Regular paracetamol with review in 48 hours and antibiotics only if he has not improved
Topical ciprofloxacin ear drops with analgesia and review by the practice nurse in three days
Immediate oral amoxicillin with regular analgesia and clinical review to confirm resolution
Immediate oral amoxicillin with clavulanate given his two previous episodes in the past year
Urgent same day referral to the ear nose and throat service for consideration of tympanostomy tubes

subtopic_detail: Choosing between enema reduction and laparotomy in intussusception
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a tertiary emergency department reviewing an 8-month-old boy. His mother says that since yesterday he starts crying suddenly, draws his legs up, then settles and goes floppy between episodes, and he has vomited six times with the vomit now looking green.

Over the last two hours he has become harder to rouse and his nappies have been dry. On examination his abdomen is distended and he cries and tenses when you palpate anywhere, with guarding in all quadrants that persists between spasms. His capillary refill is four seconds centrally. Ultrasound performed 20 minutes ago shows a target lesion in the right upper quadrant with free fluid and absent colour Doppler flow within the intussuscipiens. Radiology and theatre are both immediately available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 186, BP 68/38, RR 48, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.6
data_table.Examination: Abdominal distension with generalised guarding persisting between spasms; capillary refill 4 seconds; reduced responsiveness
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound: target lesion right upper quadrant, free fluid, absent colour Doppler flow within the intussuscipiens; venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Air enema reduction in the radiology department with a surgical team standing by in theatre
Fluid resuscitation and antibiotics with immediate transfer to theatre for operative reduction
Hydrostatic contrast enema reduction under fluoroscopic guidance after a fluid bolus is completed
Nasogastric decompression with intravenous fluids and repeat ultrasound in four to six hours
Computed tomography of the abdomen with contrast to define the lead point before any intervention

subtopic_detail: Acute scrotal pain with coexisting urinary symptoms in an adolescent
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 14-year-old boy who developed severe left scrotal pain five hours ago while sitting in class. He vomited twice on the way to hospital and has not been able to walk comfortably.

He reports stinging when passing urine over the last three days and his urine dipstick today shows leucocytes and nitrites. On examination the left testis sits higher than the right and lies transversely, the cremasteric reflex is absent on the left and present on the right, and elevating the testis does not relieve his pain. There is no scrotal erythema or fixed swelling and he is afebrile. Ultrasound is available but the sonographer is 45 minutes away from the hospital.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 122/70, RR 18, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Left testis high riding and transverse; cremasteric reflex absent on the left, present on the right; Prehn sign negative; no scrotal erythema
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick leucocytes and nitrites positive; urine culture sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral trimethoprim with analgesia and outpatient urology review once the urine culture returns
Urgent scrotal ultrasound with Doppler and surgical referral only if arterial flow is reduced
Manual detorsion at the bedside with analgesia and discharge home if the pain settles completely
Immediate urological referral for scrotal exploration with fixation of both testes if confirmed
Intravenous antibiotics with admission for observation and reassessment by the surgical team overnight

subtopic_detail: Late presentation of a duct dependent systemic circulation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the emergency department for a 6-day-old term baby girl. Her mother says she has gone off her feeds since yesterday, is breathing fast, and looked grey and mottled this morning.

She was born at 39 weeks by normal vaginal delivery with no antenatal concerns and was discharged at 36 hours of age. On examination she is pale and mottled with cool legs. Her right brachial pulse is easily palpable but both femoral pulses are impalpable. Pre-ductal saturation in the right hand is 96 per cent and post-ductal saturation in the right foot is 88 per cent. Her chest is clear on auscultation and her liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. Her venous blood gas shows pH 7.18 with a lactate of 7.4 mmol/L and her blood glucose is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 178, BP 62/34 right arm, RR 66, SpO2 96% right hand and 88% right foot, temperature 36.2
data_table.Examination: Pale and mottled with cool legs; right brachial pulse present, both femoral pulses impalpable; liver 3 cm below costal margin
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.18 (7.32-7.42); lactate 7.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.0); blood glucose 4.2 mmol/L (2.6-6.0); chest radiograph cardiomegaly with pulmonary plethora

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous 0.9 per cent sodium chloride 20 mL/kg bolus with intravenous benzylpenicillin and gentamicin
Intubation with hyperventilation and high flow oxygen to correct the metabolic acidosis rapidly
Intravenous adrenaline infusion titrated to restore blood pressure and peripheral perfusion
Urgent echocardiography to define the anatomy before commencing any cardiovascular treatment
Intravenous prostaglandin E1 infusion with antibiotics and preparation for intubation and transfer

subtopic_detail: Femoral fracture in a pre-ambulant infant with a normal bone profile
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department seeing a 3-month-old boy brought in because he cries whenever his left leg is moved and his mother's partner noticed his thigh looked swollen this morning.

The history given is that he rolled from a lounge onto a carpeted floor yesterday afternoon, a distance of about 40 cm. He is not yet rolling or crawling according to his developmental history taken separately. Radiography shows a mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur. His sclerae are white, he has no joint hypermobility, his growth is along the 50th centile and there is no family history of fractures or hearing loss. His corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D are all within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 148, BP 78/46, RR 40, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Swollen left thigh with pain on movement; white sclerae; no joint hypermobility; no bruising elsewhere on exposed skin
data_table.Investigations: Radiograph: mid shaft spiral fracture of the left femur; corrected calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, parathyroid hormone and 25 hydroxyvitamin D within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit, notify child protection services and arrange a skeletal survey with paediatric review
Apply a hip spica cast and discharge with orthopaedic outpatient and general practitioner follow up
Arrange an outpatient skeletal survey next week with a scheduled paediatric clinic appointment
Send genetic testing for osteogenesis imperfecta and defer notification until those results return
Discharge with analgesia and safety netting advice, with review by the child health nurse this week

subtopic_detail: Oxygen and feeding thresholds in bronchiolitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-month-old boy admitted overnight on day three of a coryzal illness. He was born at term and has no cardiac or respiratory background.

His mother says he is taking about half his usual bottle volume and had four wet nappies in the past 24 hours instead of his usual seven. He is alert between feeds and settles when held. On examination he has moderate subcostal recession, a respiratory rate of 58 and widespread fine crackles with expiratory wheeze. He has had no apnoeic episodes witnessed by nursing staff or by his mother, and his oxygen saturation has been recorded between 91 and 93 per cent over the past four hours.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 152, BP 84/52, RR 58, SpO2 92% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Moderate subcostal recession, no tracheal tug, widespread fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, capillary refill 2 seconds, moist mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate positive for respiratory syncytial virus; no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence high flow nasal cannula oxygen at 2 L/kg/min and continue oral feeding
Commence low flow nasal prong oxygen at 1 L/min and continue oral feeding as tolerated
Commence a trial of nebulised salbutamol and reassess his work of breathing afterwards
Commence nasogastric feeding at a reduced volume and continue observation on room air
Commence intravenous maintenance fluid at full rate and withhold all oral intake

subtopic_detail: First line investigation of global developmental delay
stem:
You are the paediatrics registrar seeing a 26-month-old boy referred by his child health nurse because he is not yet walking independently and says only four words. He sat unsupported at eleven months and crawled at sixteen months.

He was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy with no perinatal concerns, and his newborn hearing screen and formal audiology testing were both normal. His parents are not related, there is no family history of developmental problems, and his growth is tracking along the 25th centile for length and weight. Examination shows mild generalised hypotonia with normal facial features and an otherwise normal neurological examination.

data_table.Examination: Head circumference on the 50th centile, mild generalised hypotonia, no dysmorphism, no hepatosplenomegaly, no neurocutaneous stigmata
data_table.Investigations: Formal audiology normal; full blood count, thyroid function and creatine kinase within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line investigation?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain under general anaesthesia
Serum lead level with urine metabolic screening for organic acid disorders
Chromosomal microarray with fragile X testing and early intervention referral
Standard karyotype with testing for the common trisomies by rapid assay
Repeat developmental assessment in six months before requesting any investigation

subtopic_detail: White pupillary reflex in a toddler
stem:
You are the paediatrics registrar seeing a 14-month-old girl whose mother has brought in three photographs taken over the past two months. In each one the left pupil appears white while the right shows the usual red reflex.

The child is well, feeding normally and meeting her milestones, and there is no family history of eye disease. On examination the red reflex is present on the right and absent on the left, with a white reflex seen instead. There is no proptosis or conjunctival injection, and cover testing shows no squint.

data_table.Examination: Absent red reflex on the left with a white pupillary reflex, right red reflex normal, no proptosis, no squint, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange routine community optometry review within the next four to six weeks
Reassure the mother that a white reflex in photographs is usually a camera artefact
Arrange computed tomography of the orbits to characterise the abnormality first
Prescribe topical antibiotic drops and review the eye again in one week
Refer for same day paediatric ophthalmology assessment with dilated fundus examination

subtopic_detail: Rickets with a normal parathyroid response
stem:
You are the paediatrics registrar seeing a 3-year-old boy referred with bowing of both legs that his parents first noticed when he began walking and which has become more obvious over the past year. He has no bone pain and no fractures.

He eats a varied diet including dairy, plays outdoors daily and has never been on restricted feeds. His height has fallen from the 25th to the 3rd centile while his weight tracks on the 25th. His father had bowed legs as a child and multiple dental abscesses, and radiographs of the boy's knees show cupping and fraying of the metaphyses.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened wrists, no craniotabes, no rachitic rosary, no proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.20-2.65); phosphate 0.72 mmol/L (1.20-1.80); alkaline phosphatase 690 U/L (100-320); parathyroid hormone within normal limits; 25-hydroxyvitamin D 74 nmol/L (more than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Refer to paediatric endocrinology and measure urinary phosphate handling
Start high dose oral vitamin D for twelve weeks and repeat the bone profile
Start oral calcium supplementation and review the bone profile in eight weeks
Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of guided growth surgery for the bowing
Reassure the parents that this is physiological bowing and review him in six months

subtopic_detail: Acute haematogenous osteomyelitis versus septic arthritis in a school aged child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department. A 7-year-old boy has been limping for four days and since yesterday will not put any weight on his left leg. His mother says he has been hot and off his food, and that he has not had any fall or twisting injury.

He holds the leg still but allows you to move the knee through a full range without resisting, and there is no swelling or warmth over the joint line. There is sharply localised tenderness over the bone just above the knee. A plain radiograph of the femur and knee is reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 98/60, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.7
data_table.Examination: Point tenderness over the distal femoral metaphysis, full passive knee range with no effusion, no rash
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 14.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5); two sets of blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Aspirate the left knee under sedation and send fluid for urgent culture
Start oral cefalexin and review in the outpatient clinic in 48 hours
Start intravenous flucloxacillin and arrange magnetic resonance imaging
Repeat the plain radiograph in seven days and withhold antibiotics now
Arrange a technetium bone scan before starting antimicrobial therapy

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing an innocent murmur from pathology at a routine child health check
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4-year-old boy for his routine health check. His mother mentions that he seemed puffed at a swimming lesson last month, although he keeps up with his older sister in the backyard and has never gone blue or floppy.

He was born at term and his growth has tracked along the 50th centile for height and weight. You hear a soft systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge with a musical vibratory quality. It becomes much quieter when he stands, the second heart sound splits normally with respiration, and femoral pulses are equal and easily felt. There is no thrill and no radiation to the back or neck.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Grade 2 of 6 vibratory systolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge, quieter on standing, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Growth parameters on the 50th centile, no previous cardiac investigations

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the murmur at the next health check
Refer for transthoracic echocardiography before any further review
Arrange an electrocardiogram and chest radiograph at the local hospital
Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for review within one week
Commence antibiotic prophylaxis before any future dental procedures

subtopic_detail: Imaging versus structured observation after minor head injury in a toddler
stem:
You are the emergency department resident assessing an 18-month-old girl who rolled off a kitchen bench while her father was changing her, falling about 1.5 metres onto tiles two hours ago. She cried immediately, was never floppy or unresponsive, and her father says she is behaving completely normally now and has taken a full bottle without vomiting.

She is alert, tracks you around the cubicle and reaches for her toy. There is a boggy swelling over the right parietal region about 4 cm across. The anterior fontanelle is closed, the pupils are equal and reactive, and she moves all four limbs symmetrically.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128, blood pressure 94/56, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Glasgow coma scale 15, boggy right parietal haematoma 4 cm, no palpable step, no bruising behind the ears
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform an immediate computed tomography scan of her brain
Discharge now with written head injury advice for the parents
Arrange a skull radiograph to exclude an underlying linear fracture
Admit her for magnetic resonance imaging of the brain in the morning
Observe with hourly neurological observations for at least four hours

subtopic_detail: First hour management of a suspected snake bite in a rural child
stem:
You are the sole doctor at a small rural Victorian hospital. A 9-year-old boy is brought in 40 minutes after he felt a sharp scratch on his ankle while walking through long dry grass and saw a snake move away. His father applied a broad elasticised bandage firmly from the foot upwards over the whole leg and splinted it before driving him in.

The boy is alert and talking, says his leg feels tight but not painful, and has not vomited. There is no bleeding from the bandage edge and no swelling of the visible toes. The bandage is intact and correctly applied. Your hospital stocks antivenom and has a laboratory on site.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96, blood pressure 108/64, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 100 per cent on room air, temperature 36.5
data_table.Examination: Pressure immobilisation bandage and splint in place over the left leg, no ptosis, no tender lymph nodes, power and speech normal
data_table.Investigations: No blood tests performed yet

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Remove the bandage now and observe closely for local swelling
Leave the bandage in place and take coagulation studies and creatine kinase
Give one vial of polyvalent antivenom before any blood tests are taken
Swab the bite site for a venom detection kit and await that result
Give intramuscular adrenaline and transfer to the nearest tertiary hospital

subtopic_detail: Retractile versus true undescended testis and the timing of referral
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 8-month-old boy brought in by his father for a routine check. He was born at term and has grown along the 50th centile.

On a warm couch with relaxed legs, the right hemiscrotum is empty and flat. You can feel the right testis in the inguinal canal and can coax it down as far as the upper scrotum, but it springs back up as soon as you let go and will not sit in the scrotum. The left testis is normally sited and of equal size. The penis is normally formed with a terminal meatus, and the same right sided finding was documented at his 3 month check.

data_table.Examination: Right testis palpable in the inguinal canal, does not remain in the scrotum on release, left testis normally descended, no hernia
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that this is a retractile testis and review him at age two years
Request an inguinal and scrotal ultrasound to locate the right testis
Arrange a chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation test before any referral
Refer to paediatric surgery now for operative correction before 12 months
Review him again in the general practice clinic at 18 months of age

subtopic_detail: Persistent otitis media with effusion causing speech delay
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 year 6-month-old boy whose parents say he turns the television up until the neighbours complain and often does not answer when called from another room. His childcare educator has raised that he uses only about thirty words and that strangers cannot understand him.

He has had frequent colds but has never had a painful discharging ear or a fever with ear pain. His parents first raised the hearing concern with you four months ago and the same findings were documented then. Otoscopy today shows dull retracted tympanic membranes bilaterally with a visible air fluid level and no erythema or bulging. Tympanometry gives a flat trace in both ears.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral dull retracted tympanic membranes with air fluid levels, no discharge, no cervical lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Type B flat tympanogram bilaterally, growth and developmental milestones otherwise age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for formal audiology and ear nose and throat assessment now
Prescribe a two week course of oral amoxicillin and then review him
Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review in three months
Advise autoinflation with a nasal balloon and review him in six months
Reassure that this resolves spontaneously and review him at age four

subtopic_detail: Adrenaline autoinjector device banding after a first food reaction in infancy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing an 11-month-old girl two days after her first taste of scrambled egg. Her mother says that within ten minutes her lips puffed up, red itchy welts spread over her whole body, she vomited three times and went pale and floppy in her highchair for a minute or so before perking up after a dose of the antihistamine they had at home.

She has mild eczema controlled with a moisturiser and has tolerated dairy, wheat and peanut without any reaction. She is thriving and today is completely well with a normal examination. Her weight is 9.2 kg.

data_table.Examination: Weight 9.2 kg on the 50th centile, chest clear, skin shows mild flexural eczema only
data_table.Investigations: No allergy testing performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management to arrange today?

options.text: Prescribe a 300 microgram adrenaline autoinjector and refer to allergy
Arrange skin prick testing first and defer any device prescription
Prescribe a 150 microgram adrenaline autoinjector and refer to allergy
Advise strict egg avoidance with an oral antihistamine kept for reactions
Arrange a supervised hospital egg challenge within the next two weeks

subtopic_detail: Disimpaction regimen for functional constipation with overflow soiling
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in an outpatient clinic seeing a 4-year-old boy. His parents report that for six months he has opened his bowels only every four or five days, passing hard pellets that hurt him, and that he hides behind the couch and crosses his legs when he needs to go. For the last month he has been leaving loose smears in his underpants several times a day, which his parents describe as diarrhoea and find very distressing.

He passed meconium on day one, has grown along the 50th centile and has a normal diet with adequate fluids. His abdomen is soft with a palpable indentable mass in the left iliac fossa. The spine, gluteal cleft, anal position and lower limb reflexes are all normal.

data_table.Examination: Palpable indentable faecal mass in the left iliac fossa, normal perianal appearance, normal lower limb neurology
data_table.Investigations: Growth on the 50th centile, no investigations performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Advise increased dietary fibre and fluids with review in one month
Arrange an abdominal radiograph to confirm the degree of faecal loading
Give a phosphate enema now and start maintenance therapy from tomorrow
Refer for anorectal manometry and a rectal suction biopsy of the bowel
Start an escalating oral macrogol regimen over up to seven days

subtopic_detail: Excessive weight loss in an exclusively breastfed term newborn on day five
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal domiciliary round seeing a 5-day-old term girl born by normal vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Her birth weight was 3540 g and she weighs 3180 g today. Her mother is a first time parent who says the baby feeds about eight times in twenty four hours and comes off the breast quickly, and that her nipples are cracked and sore at the start of each feed.

The baby has had four heavy wet nappies and two yellow stools in the last day. She is alert between feeds, has moist mucous membranes and a soft fontanelle, and has no dysmorphic features. You watch a full feed and see a shallow latch with the baby taking only the nipple and clicking as she sucks. A serum bilirubin taken this morning sits well below the phototherapy threshold for her age.

data_table.Examination: Weight 3180 g representing a 10.2 per cent loss from birth weight, alert, moist mucous membranes, soft fontanelle
data_table.Investigations: Serum bilirubin well below the age specific phototherapy threshold, newborn screening sample already collected

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit her for nasogastric feeding and intravenous fluid rehydration
Arrange lactation review with expressed milk top ups and reweigh daily
Reassure that this is expected and reweigh her at the six week check
Change to exclusive infant formula feeding and stop breastfeeding now
Check serum bilirubin and start phototherapy while feeding continues

subtopic_detail: Short stature with falling growth velocity despite a delayed bone age
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy referred because he is the shortest in his class and is being teased about it. His height is on the 3rd centile and his weight on the 10th. Serial school measurements show he was on the 25th centile at age 9 and has crossed downward since, with a height velocity of 3 cm per year over the last two years.

His father says he himself did not shave until he was seventeen and grew after school finished. The boy eats well and reports no abdominal pain or altered bowels, and he plays soccer without limitation. His testicular volume is 3 mL bilaterally with no pubic hair, and a bone age radiograph is reported as delayed by two and a half years. His examination is otherwise normal with no dysmorphic features and a normal visual field to confrontation.

data_table.Examination: Height on the 3rd centile, weight on the 10th centile, mid parental height on the 50th centile, testicular volume 3 mL bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: Bone age delayed by two and a half years, height velocity 3 cm per year, no blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure the family and reassess the height velocity in twelve months
Refer for growth hormone stimulation testing at the endocrine clinic
Request a karyotype and pituitary magnetic resonance imaging scan now
Request coeliac serology, thyroid function and biochemical screening
Start testosterone priming to induce puberty and reassess in six months

subtopic_detail: Confirming central precocious puberty in a girl with accelerated growth
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6 year 8-month-old girl whose mother noticed breast development about eight months ago that has steadily progressed. The school nurse has commented that she has shot up and now stands taller than every child in her class.

Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 91st centile over eighteen months. She has Tanner stage 3 breast development and Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, with no clitoromegaly, no acne and no rapid deepening of her voice. Her mother reports no headache, no vomiting and no change in vision, and there are no cafe au lait patches on her skin. A bone age radiograph is advanced by two years.

data_table.Examination: Tanner stage 3 breast, Tanner stage 2 pubic hair, no virilisation, normal visual fields to confrontation, no skin pigmentation
data_table.Investigations: Height crossed from the 50th to the 91st centile in eighteen months, bone age advanced by two years

lead_in: Which investigation will best establish the underlying mechanism?

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary
Measure dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate and 17 hydroxyprogesterone levels
Arrange a pelvic ultrasound to measure ovarian and uterine volumes
Repeat the bone age radiograph in six months before any further testing
Perform a gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation test now

subtopic_detail: Raised intracranial pressure presenting as headache previously labelled migraine
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 6-year-old boy brought in by his mother, who is frustrated that nothing has helped. For six weeks he has woken at about five in the morning with a headache and has vomited soon after, then felt well enough for school by mid morning. He was diagnosed with migraine four weeks ago and started on regular preventive medication with no change.

Over the past week he has been seeing double when he looks to the left, and his mother says he has become wobbly and grabs the furniture when he turns around. He is afebrile with no neck stiffness and no rash. Fundoscopy shows blurred disc margins with loss of venous pulsation in both eyes, and his gait is wide based with a tendency to fall to the right.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78, blood pressure 112/72, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Bilateral blurred disc margins, left abducens palsy, wide based ataxic gait, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: No imaging or blood tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure now
Start regular propranolol for migraine and review in four weeks
Arrange urgent neuroimaging before any lumbar puncture is done
Refer to ophthalmology for formal visual field assessment first
Give intravenous dexamethasone and review the headache tomorrow

subtopic_detail: Parapneumonic effusion complicating community acquired pneumonia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl who was diagnosed with pneumonia five days ago and started on oral amoxicillin by her general practitioner. Her mother says the fevers have not settled at all, she is breathing faster than before and she now refuses to lie flat.

She is drinking about half her usual amount and has had three wet nappies today. On examination there is reduced chest expansion on the right with stony dullness to percussion and absent breath sounds over the lower half of that side. A chest radiograph shows homogeneous opacification of the lower right hemithorax with blunting of the costophrenic angle and a meniscus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 152, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 46, SpO2 92 per cent on room air, temperature 39.4
data_table.Examination: Reduced right chest expansion, stony dullness at the right base, absent breath sounds over the lower right hemithorax, mild subcostal recession
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 22.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 210 mg/L (less than 5); chest radiograph shows a right pleural effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start intravenous antibiotics and arrange a chest ultrasound scan
Arrange computed tomography of the chest with intravenous contrast
Insert an intercostal catheter in the emergency department immediately
Continue oral amoxicillin and repeat the chest radiograph in 48 hours
Perform a diagnostic pleural tap and send the fluid for cytology only

subtopic_detail: Inattention driven by sleep disordered breathing rather than attention deficit
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old boy whose mother brings a letter from his teacher describing him as fidgety, unable to finish tasks and drifting off during reading. She has read about attention difficulties and asks you to start medication before the next school term.

At home he snores loudly most nights, sleeps with his mouth open and his mother has watched him stop breathing and then gasp several times. He wakes unrefreshed and complains of a headache before breakfast two or three mornings a week. His concentration difficulties were first raised eight months ago when he started grade two and were not present in his preschool reports. His tonsils are large and nearly touching in the midline, and his growth has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils grade 3 with near midline contact, adenoidal facies with mouth breathing, no cardiac murmur
data_table.Investigations: Weight has fallen from the 50th to the 25th centile over twelve months, no sleep study or rating scales completed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start immediate release methylphenidate and review him in four weeks
Complete Conners rating scales and start atomoxetine if these are positive
Refer for cognitive assessment to exclude a specific learning disorder
Refer for ear nose and throat review of sleep disordered breathing
Advise a trial of dietary elimination and review him in three months

subtopic_detail: Atypical curve features in an adolescent presenting with scoliosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner assessing a 12-year-old girl whose mother noticed that one shoulder blade sticks out when she leans forward to wash her hair. She reports occasional back discomfort that sometimes wakes her at night.

On the forward bend test there is a rib hump on the left side of the thoracic spine. Her feet have high arches with clawed toes that her mother says have always looked that way. Abdominal reflexes are present in all four quadrants on the left but absent on the right. She has reached menarche and her lower limb power, tone and sensation are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Left sided thoracic rib hump on forward bending, bilateral pes cavus with clawing, absent right sided abdominal reflexes, symmetrical limb power
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a standing whole spine radiograph and review in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine urgently
Refer for a thoracolumbosacral orthosis to be fitted for her now
Reassure and repeat the forward bend test at the next school check
Refer to physiotherapy for a scoliosis specific exercise program

subtopic_detail: Appendicitis masquerading as gastroenteritis in a preschool child
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy with three days of tummy ache. His father says the pain started around the belly button, and that since yesterday he has vomited five times and passed several loose stools, so the family assumed he had caught the gastro going around childcare.

He has not eaten since yesterday and has had one wet nappy today. He lies very still on the trolley and walks bent forward with small steps when asked to move. His abdomen is rigid in the right lower quadrant with involuntary guarding and he cries when the trolley is knocked. No other child at his centre has been unwell.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 34, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Involuntary guarding and rigidity in the right lower quadrant, pain on percussion, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 19.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 168 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Start oral rehydration solution and reassess the abdomen in four hours
Arrange an abdominal ultrasound before making any surgical referral
Start intravenous fluids and refer urgently to the surgical team
Send stool for culture and start oral metronidazole empirically today
Arrange computed tomography of the abdomen with oral contrast today

subtopic_detail: Facial nerve palsy complicating acute otitis media versus idiopathic Bell palsy in a child
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on call. A 5-year-old girl is brought in by her father because the right side of her face has been drooping since he woke her this morning. She has had a sore right ear for four days and has been hot and off her food.

She cannot wrinkle her forehead or close her right eye, and the right corner of her mouth does not move when she cries. The right tympanic membrane is bulging, red and immobile on pneumatic otoscopy. There are no vesicles in the ear canal or on the pinna, and the remaining cranial nerve and limb examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: Complete right upper and lower facial weakness, bulging immobile right tympanic membrane, no mastoid tenderness or postauricular swelling
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.8 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); C-reactive protein 62 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone for five days together with lubricating eye drops
Oral amoxicillin for five days with review by her general practitioner in 48 hours
Admit for intravenous antibiotics with urgent ear nose and throat review for myringotomy
Oral aciclovir and prednisolone with an urgent outpatient audiology appointment
Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before starting any treatment

subtopic_detail: Persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion and the threshold for ventilation tube referral
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 4-year-old boy whose parents have been coming back about his hearing since the autumn. They say he turns the television up, does not answer when called from another room, and that his kindergarten teacher has raised that other children are hard to understand him.

You first documented dull immobile drums with visible fluid levels at a visit four months ago and again eight weeks ago, and today both drums look the same. He has had no ear pain, discharge or fever in that time. A formal audiogram today shows a bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB with flat tympanograms.

data_table.Examination: Both tympanic membranes dull and retracted with an air fluid level, no perforation or discharge, normal facial movements
data_table.Investigations: Pure tone audiometry bilateral conductive loss averaging 35 dB; type B flat tympanogram bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for consideration of ventilation tubes
Prescribe a two week course of oral amoxicillin and reassess the drums afterwards
Start an intranasal corticosteroid spray and review the audiogram in three months
Reassure the parents and review again in three months with a repeat audiogram
Arrange a computed tomography scan of the temporal bones before any referral

subtopic_detail: Rapidly worsening atopic eczema with punched out erosions and the decision to treat as viral superinfection
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the emergency department. A 2-year-old girl with moderate atopic eczema has become much worse over 36 hours. Her mother says the rash on her face and neck now looks like small round sores that all seem the same size, that they are weeping clear fluid, and that her daughter screams when anything touches them.

She has been febrile at home and has refused to drink since last night. Her eczema is usually controlled with a moderate potency topical corticosteroid and she started that again two days ago without improvement. The lesions extend onto the right upper eyelid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 158, blood pressure 92/54, respiratory rate 30, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 38.9
data_table.Examination: Clustered uniform 2 to 3 mm shallow erosions with haemorrhagic crusting over face and neck, lesions on the right upper eyelid, no purulent discharge or honey coloured crust
data_table.Investigations: Viral swab of a deroofed lesion sent for polymerase chain reaction; white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase to a potent topical corticosteroid and arrange dermatology review this week
Start oral cefalexin and continue the current topical corticosteroid at home
Apply wet dressings with bleach baths and review in the ambulatory clinic tomorrow
Give a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin and admit for observation overnight
Admit for intravenous aciclovir with same day ophthalmology review of the eye

subtopic_detail: First line treatment choice in primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis at school age
stem:
You are the paediatric outpatient registrar seeing a 7-year-old boy referred for bedwetting. His mother says he has never had a run of dry nights, that it happens most nights, and that he sleeps so heavily he does not wake when it happens. He is dry during the day with no urgency, wetting or straining, and he opens his bowels to a soft stool daily.

He is otherwise well, is growing along the 50th centile and is doing well at school. His mother has already reduced evening drinks and started lifting him at 11 pm without any change. He is upset about missing a school camp in six months.

data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with no palpable faecal loading, normal external genitalia, normal lower limb neurology and normal lumbosacral spine
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative for glucose, protein, blood, nitrites and leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe oxybutynin at night and review his bladder diary in eight weeks
Start an enuresis alarm with review of the record after four to six weeks
Prescribe oral desmopressin nightly and review his response after four weeks
Begin a macrogol disimpaction regimen and reassess the wetting in six weeks
Arrange a renal tract ultrasound and refer to a paediatric urology clinic

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing positional head shape deformity from premature suture fusion in an infant
stem:
You are the general practice registrar at a 5 month immunisation visit. The mother says the back of her son's head has looked flattened on one side since about six weeks of age and that it has not changed since she started giving him more time on his tummy.

Looking down on the vertex from above, the right occiput is flattened, the right ear sits forward of the left, and the right forehead is more prominent than the left. The anterior fontanelle is soft and open and the sutures feel mobile with no palpable ridge. He turns his head fully to both sides against gentle resistance and his head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening with ipsilateral anterior displacement of the ear and forehead, open mobile sutures, full passive and active neck rotation both ways
data_table.Investigations: Head circumference on the 50th centile at 6 weeks, 3 months and today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction
Refer urgently to a craniofacial surgical unit for consideration of vault surgery
Fit a custom moulding helmet now and review the head shape again in three months
Continue repositioning and tummy time and review the head shape in three months
Refer to physiotherapy for stretches to the right sternocleidomastoid muscle this week

subtopic_detail: Radiographic discrimination of an ingested disc battery from a coin and the resulting urgency
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 2-year-old boy was found next to an opened remote control about 90 minutes ago and his father thinks he swallowed something from it. He gagged once, cried briefly and has been drinking water since without difficulty.

He is alert with no drooling, stridor or respiratory distress. An anteroposterior chest radiograph shows a 20 mm rounded radiodense object at the level of the thoracic inlet with a narrow rim of lower density around its circumference, and the lateral film shows a step off in its profile.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 94/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Handling secretions normally, chest clear on auscultation, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Anteroposterior and lateral chest radiographs as described; no free air under the diaphragm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange immediate endoscopic removal in theatre and give honey while awaiting transfer
Repeat the radiograph in six hours and remove endoscopically only if it has not passed
Discharge with advice to check the stools and return if he develops any new symptoms
Give oral activated charcoal and admit for observation with hourly nursing review
Induce vomiting with a gastric irritant and repeat the radiograph after the attempt

subtopic_detail: Observation period and disposition after a brief unwitnessed submersion in a well child
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a district hospital. A 3-year-old girl was pulled from a backyard pool about four hours ago after her grandmother noticed her missing for less than a minute. She was face down but came up coughing immediately and cried at once. No rescue breaths or compressions were given.

She coughed intermittently for about ten minutes in the car and has been playing in the waiting room since. Her chest is clear and she has maintained normal saturations on room air throughout four hours of continuous monitoring in the department. Her parents want to know whether she needs to stay in overnight in case her lungs fill up later.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 96/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Alert and playful, chest clear with equal air entry, no cough on exertion, no accessory muscle use
data_table.Investigations: Continuous pulse oximetry over four hours with no desaturation; no chest radiograph performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Obtain a chest radiograph and admit if any interstitial change is seen on the film
Admit overnight for continuous oximetry because deterioration can occur up to 24 hours later
Discharge home with written advice and address pool fencing before she leaves
Start prophylactic amoxicillin clavulanate and review in the short stay unit tomorrow
Give a single dose of oral dexamethasone and observe for a further four hours

subtopic_detail: First aid and antivenom decision after a spider bite where pressure immobilisation is contraindicated
stem:
You are the emergency registrar in a Sydney hospital at 9 pm. A 6-year-old boy was bitten on the back of the right calf 40 minutes ago while pulling a bike out from under a garden bench. His mother killed the spider and has brought it in; it is small, dark and shiny with a red stripe on the upper abdomen.

He is distressed and says the pain has spread up his thigh and is getting worse, and he is sweating heavily over the bitten leg. No first aid was applied. There is a small red mark on the calf with local sweating around it, and his abdomen is soft with no guarding.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 118/74, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1
data_table.Examination: Punctum on the right calf with localised piloerection and sweating, pain radiating to the groin, normal conscious state, no fasciculation or muscle spasm
data_table.Investigations: Point-of-care testing not indicated; no coagulation studies performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Apply a pressure immobilisation bandage to the whole leg and splint it, then observe
Give intravenous antivenom immediately and admit to the high dependency unit overnight
Apply an ice pack and give oral analgesia, then reassess the pain in 30 minutes
Take blood for coagulation studies and creatine kinase before giving any analgesia
Infiltrate the bite site with local anaesthetic and discharge once the pain has settled

subtopic_detail: Sleep study before adenotonsillectomy when the airway phenotype is atypical for tonsillar hypertrophy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic. A 4-year-old boy with trisomy 21 is referred because he snores every night, and his mother describes pauses in his breathing that end with a gasp, and says he sleeps with his neck extended and is exhausted during the day.

He has a repaired atrioventricular septal defect with normal ventricular function on echocardiography six months ago. His tonsils are small and sit well within the tonsillar pillars, and his body mass index is on the 95th centile. He has a small midface, a relatively large tongue and mild generalised hypotonia. The referring letter asks whether he should simply have his tonsils and adenoids removed.

data_table.Examination: Tonsils graded 1 of 4 bilaterally, midface hypoplasia, relative macroglossia, generalised hypotonia, no chest wall deformity
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram six months ago with repaired defect and normal ventricular function; overnight oximetry not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial an intranasal corticosteroid for six weeks and reassess the snoring afterwards
Arrange a laboratory polysomnogram before deciding on any surgical intervention
Refer for adenotonsillectomy on the strength of the witnessed apnoeas and daytime sleepiness
Start continuous positive airway pressure at home and review his symptoms in three months
Repeat the echocardiogram to look for pulmonary hypertension before any further assessment

subtopic_detail: Adolescent hip pathology presenting as referred knee pain with a normal knee examination
stem:
You are the emergency registrar. A 12-year-old boy has had a dull ache in the front of his left thigh and knee for six weeks, worse after football, with no injury. He has been seen twice for the same complaint and given a knee brace and simple analgesia without improvement. He walked in today but says the leg feels like it is giving way.

His knee has full painless range with no effusion, no joint line tenderness and negative ligament testing. When you flex the left hip the leg rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation of that hip is limited to 5 degrees with pain at the extreme. His weight is above the 97th centile. He is afebrile and has had no weight loss or night pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84, blood pressure 122/70, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Normal knee examination, obligate external rotation of the left hip on passive flexion, internal rotation limited to 5 degrees, no groin swelling or erythema
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 7.1 x10^9/L (4.5-13.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an outpatient knee magnetic resonance scan and continue the brace meanwhile
Aspirate the left hip under ultrasound guidance after taking blood cultures
Prescribe regular ibuprofen with physiotherapy for the hip and review in four weeks
Make him non weight bearing and obtain frog lateral pelvic views with orthopaedic referral
Request a technetium bone scan of both lower limbs to localise the source of the pain

subtopic_detail: Persistent head lice after repeated insecticide use and the significance of live versus hatched eggs
stem:
You are the general practice registrar. A mother brings her 6-year-old daughter in frustrated because the school has sent her home twice. She has used a pyrethrin containing lotion three times over five weeks, each time as a single application, and says she still finds moving insects in the hair two days after each treatment.

The mother has not treated anyone else in the house. On wet combing you recover four live lice and numerous eggs, of which the ones close to the scalp are brown and full and those more than two centimetres out along the shaft are pale and empty. The scalp skin is intact with no pustules, crusting or tender nodes.

data_table.Examination: Four live adult lice recovered on wet combing, viable eggs within 1 cm of the scalp, empty egg cases distally, no excoriation or secondary infection
data_table.Investigations: No investigations indicated

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe oral ivermectin for the child and treat the household contacts at the same time
Advise hot washing of all bedding and clothing and repeat the same lotion in seven days
Reassure that the remaining eggs are not viable and that no further treatment is needed
Prescribe oral trimethoprim sulfamethoxazole for ten days and recheck the scalp afterwards
Switch to a dimeticone preparation applied twice seven days apart with weekly wet combing

subtopic_detail: Referral urgency for a newly constant convergent squint in a preschool child
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 3-year-old girl whose grandmother says her left eye has started turning in towards her nose. It was only occasional when she was tired six months ago but is now there all the time, and she has begun tilting her head and closing that eye in bright light.

On cover testing the left eye moves outwards to take up fixation when the right is covered. The corneal light reflex sits lateral to the centre of the left pupil. Red reflexes are present, equal and normal in both eyes, and eye movements are full in all directions with no proptosis. Her parents have been told by a friend that squints get better on their own by school age.

data_table.Examination: Constant left convergent deviation, cover test shows outward refixation movement of the left eye, symmetrical normal red reflexes, full extraocular movements
data_table.Investigations: No investigations performed in the practice

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and orbits before any referral
Refer to a paediatric ophthalmologist now for refraction and amblyopia assessment
Reassure the family that most squints of this type resolve and review her before school
Start patching of the right eye for two hours daily and reassess in three months
Refer to an optometrist for glasses and review the alignment again in six months

subtopic_detail: Infant with fixed head turning preference and the associated screening obligation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a community clinic. A 10-week-old boy is brought in because he always looks to the right and his mother cannot get him to feed comfortably on one side. She noticed a firm lump in the side of his neck at about four weeks that has not changed since.

He was born at term by breech extraction at caesarean section and was the first baby. There is a firm non-tender 2 cm swelling within the left sternocleidomastoid. His head rests tilted towards the left shoulder with the chin turned to the right, and passive rotation of the chin to the left stops at 45 degrees. The lump does not transilluminate, the overlying skin is normal and he is thriving on the 75th centile.

data_table.Examination: Firm 2 cm intramuscular swelling in the left sternocleidomastoid, left head tilt with right chin rotation, passive left rotation limited to 45 degrees, symmetrical Moro and normal tone in all four limbs
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed to date

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange fine needle aspiration of the neck swelling and refer to paediatric surgery
Refer for physiotherapy and reassess the range of neck rotation again in three months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine to exclude a bony anomaly
Refer for physiotherapy and arrange a hip ultrasound to screen for dysplasia
Reassure the mother that the head position will correct itself once he starts to sit

subtopic_detail: Chronic wet cough in a preschool child unresponsive to escalating asthma preventer therapy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the respiratory clinic. A 3-year-old girl has coughed every day for nine weeks. Her mother says it is a rattly cough that sounds like it is bringing something up, that it is worse first thing in the morning, and that it does not wake her at night.

She was started on an inhaled corticosteroid six weeks ago and the dose has since been doubled with no change. She has never wheezed, has never needed a reliever for breathlessness, and has never choked on food or a toy. She was born at term, is fully immunised, is growing along the 50th centile and has normal stools. Her chest is clear today with no wheeze, crackles or clubbing, and a chest radiograph taken last week was reported as normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Wet sounding cough on request, chest clear with no wheeze or crackles, no digital clubbing, normal growth centiles
data_table.Investigations: Chest radiograph reported as normal; sweat test not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prescribe amoxicillin clavulanate for two weeks and review the cough at the end of it
Double the inhaled corticosteroid again and add a leukotriene receptor antagonist
Arrange flexible bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage before any further treatment
Start a proton pump inhibitor for eight weeks and review the response to treatment
Request a sweat chloride test and a high resolution chest tomography scan this week

subtopic_detail: Recurrent cyanotic episodes after a provoking cry and the investigations that actually change management
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar. An 18-month-old boy has had six episodes over three months in which he cries hard after a fall or a frustration, stops breathing in expiration, turns blue around the lips, goes limp and loses consciousness for about ten seconds. He then has a few jerks of all four limbs, wakes quickly and is back to normal within a minute.

Every episode has followed a bout of crying. His mother says he still drinks about a litre of cow milk a day and eats very little meat or vegetables. He is developmentally appropriate with a normal neurological examination and normal growth. His parents are frightened and want to know whether he is having fits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116, blood pressure 94/58, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Normal tone, power and reflexes, no dysmorphic features, normal cardiovascular examination with no murmur, conjunctival pallor
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 96 g/L (110-140); mean cell volume 68 fL (75-87); ferritin 7 mcg/L (15-150)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and obtain a twelve lead electrocardiogram before discharge
Arrange an electroencephalogram and start sodium valproate at an antiepileptic dose
Admit for overnight cardiac monitoring and arrange an echocardiogram in the morning
Give parental explanation with safety advice, correct the iron deficiency, and record an electrocardiogram
Reassure without investigation and review him in the general clinic in three months

subtopic_detail: Persistent watery eye in an infant and the findings that separate it from sight threatening causes
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 4-month-old girl whose left eye has watered since she was about three weeks old. Her mother says the lashes are stuck together with yellow crust most mornings, but the eye looks clear once she wipes it, and the watering has not changed over the past two months.

The baby feeds well, does not screw the eye up in bright light, and her mother has not seen her rubbing it. The left conjunctiva is white and the cornea is clear and of equal diameter to the right. Red reflexes are present and symmetrical, and gentle pressure over the medial canthus expresses a bead of mucoid material.

data_table.Examination: Increased left tear lake, white conjunctiva, clear cornea, corneal diameters equal, symmetrical red reflexes, mucoid reflux on pressure over the lacrimal sac
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer for ophthalmology examination under anaesthesia within one week
Teach lacrimal sac massage and review at the twelve month check
Prescribe chloramphenicol 0.5 per cent drops six hourly for five days
Take a conjunctival swab for chlamydia and start oral azithromycin
Refer for nasolacrimal duct probing on the next available theatre list

subtopic_detail: Umbilical lesion after cord separation and the features that separate a granuloma from a duct remnant
stem:
You are the doctor in a community child health clinic. A 5-week-old boy is brought in because a small lump has appeared where his cord used to be. The cord came away on day 10 and the area has been a little damp on his singlet since.

His mother says there is no smell and the skin around it looks the same colour as the rest of his tummy. He is breastfeeding well and has regained his birth weight. On examination there is a soft pink lesion 4 mm across sitting in the umbilical pit, with no surrounding erythema or induration, and no discharge of urine or faecal material from the site when he cries.

data_table.Examination: Soft pink 4 mm lesion in the umbilical pit with scant serous moisture, periumbilical skin normal in colour and temperature, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Growth: Weight 3.9 kg, back above birth weight since day 12

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Apply silver nitrate to the lesion weekly until it has flattened
Arrange abdominal ultrasound to look for a persistent urachal remnant
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin for two days
Apply table salt to the lesion twice daily and review in three days
Refer to paediatric surgery for excision of an umbilical remnant

subtopic_detail: Asymptomatic labial adhesions in a preschool girl and the threshold for treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3-year-old girl whose mother noticed while bathing her that the opening between her labia looks sealed over. Her mother is worried it will stop her passing urine.

The girl passes a normal forward stream once or twice every few hours, has never had a urinary tract infection, and has no itch, soreness or bleeding. She is toilet trained by day. On examination the labia minora are joined in the midline by a thin translucent line with a small opening anteriorly, the surrounding skin is normal, and there is no bruising, tear or abnormal pigmentation anywhere on the perineum.

data_table.Examination: Thin translucent midline union of the labia minora with a patent anterior opening, normal perineal skin, no bruising or tears
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes, nitrites and blood

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure, advise plain water hygiene, and review at her next visit
Prescribe topical oestrogen cream to the adhesion nightly for two weeks
Separate the adhesion manually in the clinic after topical anaesthetic
Refer to the child protection unit for assessment of possible abuse
Refer to paediatric surgery for separation under general anaesthetic

subtopic_detail: Refusal to weight bear in a toddler with a normal radiograph and normal inflammatory markers
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a 20-month-old boy who has refused to put his right foot down since yesterday afternoon, when he tripped while running on the grass at his older sister's netball game. His mother says he cried for a minute, then went back to playing, but would not stand up when they got home.

He is afebrile, alert and playing on the trolley. He crawls freely and moves the right hip and knee through full range without complaint, but he cries when the lower shin is squeezed. There is no swelling, warmth or bruising, no joint effusion, and no rash. The radiograph of the tibia and fibula reported by the radiologist shows no fracture.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Refuses to weight bear on the right, full painless hip and knee range, focal tenderness over the mid to distal tibial shaft, no effusion, warmth or swelling
data_table.Investigations: C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5); white cell count 9.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0); anteroposterior and lateral tibia and fibula radiographs reported as no fracture seen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange hip ultrasound and admit under orthopaedics for joint aspiration
Discharge with paracetamol and advice to return if still limping in a week
Admit for intravenous flucloxacillin after blood cultures are collected
Request urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the right tibia and knee
Apply a below knee walking cast and arrange fracture clinic review

subtopic_detail: Scarred preputial ring in a school aged boy versus physiological non retraction
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 9-year-old boy whose father reports that the end of his penis puffs up like a balloon when he passes urine, and that this has been happening for about six months. Over that time the stream has become thin and sprays sideways, and twice the tip has been sore enough to keep him home from school.

He has never had a urinary tract infection and is otherwise well. On examination the foreskin will not retract at all. The tip is thickened into a firm pale ring that does not stretch when traction is applied, and the visible glans and surrounding skin are not red or inflamed.

data_table.Examination: Non retractile foreskin with a firm pale thickened preputial ring that does not stretch on traction, no erythema of the glans or shaft, no discharge
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick negative for leucocytes and nitrites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that separation is incomplete and review in twelve months
Prescribe topical betamethasone twice daily to the tip for six weeks
Refer to paediatric surgery for circumcision on the elective list
Prescribe oral cefalexin for seven days and daily saline soaks
Teach gentle daily retraction after a warm bath and review in three months

subtopic_detail: Radio-opaque foreign body ingestion where the number of objects changes the urgency
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 3-year-old boy is brought in two hours after his mother saw him spit out and then swallow some of the small silver balls from his older brother's desk toy. She thinks he swallowed two or three.

He is playing in the cubicle, is not drooling, and has just finished a cup of juice without difficulty. His chest is clear and his abdomen is soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds. The abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects lying in the gastric shadow, stacked against each other with a thin lucent line between them.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 108, blood pressure 96/60, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No drooling, tolerating oral fluids, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Abdominal radiograph shows two round radio-opaque objects in the gastric shadow, apposed with a thin lucent line between them and no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Discharge home with advice to sieve the stools and repeat the film in a week
Give oral polyethylene glycol and repeat the abdominal film in 24 hours
Arrange urgent upper endoscopy for retrieval of both objects tonight
Observe on the ward with four hourly review and a film in the morning
Refer for laparotomy and removal of both objects with bowel inspection

subtopic_detail: Return to contact sport after concussion in a person under 19 years
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14-year-old boy eight days after he collided head to head in a junior rugby league match. He did not lose consciousness but was dazed on the field, was removed from play, and had headache and difficulty concentrating in class for four days.

He has now been free of headache, fogginess and light sensitivity for three full days, has returned to a full school day, and has completed light jogging and stationary cycling without symptoms. His neurological examination including balance testing is normal. His coach has asked you to sign him off for the semi final this Saturday, and his father says he has never had a previous head knock.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, limb and cerebellar examination, tandem gait normal, no neck tenderness
data_table.Timeline: Injury day 0, symptoms resolved day 5, aerobic exercise tolerated days 6 to 8, currently day 8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about returning to play?

options.text: Allow return to contact training now with a full game on the weekend
Arrange a computed tomography head scan before any return to training
