Allow return once he completes a two day graded exercise progression
Withhold competitive contact sport until at least 21 days after injury
Refer for neuropsychological testing before clearing him to play again

subtopic_detail: Choice of imaging for suspected hip dysplasia once the femoral head has begun to ossify
stem:
You are the paediatric outpatient registrar seeing a 6-month-old girl referred because her mother noticed that the skin creases on her thighs do not match. She was born at term in the breech position and had a normal newborn hip examination documented in her blue book.

She is not yet crawling but rolls both ways and sits with support. On examination the left hip abducts to only 45 degrees while the right abducts fully, the left knee sits lower than the right when the hips and knees are flexed with the feet together, and there is no click or clunk on provocative testing. Her leg lengths and spine are otherwise normal.

data_table.Examination: Limited left hip abduction to 45 degrees, asymmetric thigh creases, positive Galeazzi sign on the left, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing
data_table.History: Breech presentation at term, newborn hip examination recorded as normal, no family history of hip disease

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging investigation?

options.text: Arrange static and dynamic hip ultrasound of both hips this week
Arrange an anteroposterior pelvis radiograph and orthopaedic review
Apply a Pavlik harness and review in the orthopaedic clinic in three weeks
Reassure and reassess the hips at the twelve month health check
Request magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under light sedation

subtopic_detail: Nocturnal events in a preschooler where the pattern separates seizure from parasomnia
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 4-year-old girl referred by her general practitioner with a working diagnosis of night terrors. Her parents have kept a two week diary and have filmed several events on a phone.

The diary records six to eight events on most nights, spread from shortly after she falls asleep through to the early morning. Each lasts about 30 seconds and looks identical to the last: she opens her eyes, stiffens her right arm, then cycles her legs and makes a grunting noise. Her parents can rouse her at the end and she talks to them normally before going back to sleep. She is tired and irritable during the day, and her development and examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Normal neurological and developmental examination, no neurocutaneous stigmata, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Sleep diary: Six to eight stereotyped events per night lasting about 30 seconds, occurring throughout the night, with full alertness immediately afterwards

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Reassure, advise a safe sleep environment, and review in three months
Start melatonin 2 mg at bedtime and review the sleep diary in one month
Arrange overnight oximetry and refer for adenotonsillectomy assessment
Refer for polysomnography to quantify arousals from slow wave sleep
Refer for a sleep deprived electroencephalogram and neurology review

subtopic_detail: Bowed legs with a metabolic bone profile that separates nutritional from inherited rickets
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 20-month-old boy referred because his legs have become increasingly bowed since he started walking at 17 months. His family moved to Melbourne from a country with a warmer climate two years ago, his mother covers most of her skin outdoors, and he was breastfed without supplementation until 14 months.

He now drinks about 1.2 litres of cow milk each day and eats little else. He has no family history of bone disease and both parents have straight legs. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, widening at both wrists, and a normal chest and abdomen.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical genu varum, widened wrists, no frontal bossing, no proximal weakness, growth tracking on the 25th centile
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.15 mmol/L (2.20-2.60); phosphate 0.85 mmol/L (1.20-1.80); alkaline phosphatase 1180 U/L (100-400); parathyroid hormone 18.5 pmol/L (1.6-6.9); 25 hydroxyvitamin D 16 nmol/L (greater than 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start colecalciferol and oral calcium with repeat bloods in one month
Start colecalciferol alone and repeat the bone profile in three months
Refer for genetic testing for X linked hypophosphataemia before treating
Refer to orthopaedics for bracing of both legs and monitor his growth
Advise increasing cow milk to two litres daily and review in one month

subtopic_detail: Knee pain in an adolescent where the examination redirects the imaging
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13-year-old boy with three weeks of aching in the left knee that is worse after football training and eases with rest. There was no single injury and no swelling.

He weighs 78 kg and his body mass index sits above the 97th centile. He walks into the room with the left foot turned outwards. The left knee has full range of movement, no effusion, no joint line tenderness and stable ligaments. When you flex the left hip the thigh rolls into external rotation, and internal rotation of that hip is limited to 10 degrees compared with 40 degrees on the right. He is afebrile and systemically well.

data_table.Examination: Out toeing gait on the left, normal knee examination with no effusion, obligatory external rotation on left hip flexion, left hip internal rotation 10 degrees versus 40 degrees on the right
data_table.Growth: Weight 78 kg, body mass index above the 97th centile for age

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the left knee within two weeks
Advise relative rest, ibuprofen and physiotherapy for the knee pain
Arrange left knee radiographs and review in the fracture clinic later
Order pelvis radiographs including frog leg views and refer urgently
Check inflammatory markers and arrange an ultrasound of the left knee

subtopic_detail: Recognising a vascular birthmark in a location that threatens function
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 4-month-old girl whose mother has brought her because of a lump on her eyelid. It appeared as a faint pink patch at about three weeks of age and has grown steadily since.

The lesion is a bright red raised swelling 25 mm across on the right upper eyelid that extends over the lid margin and pushes the lid down so that it covers the upper half of the pupil. It is soft, compressible and not tender, and there is no ulceration or bleeding. She is otherwise well, feeding and growing along the 50th centile, and has no other skin lesions.

data_table.Examination: Bright red compressible 25 mm lesion on the right upper eyelid overlying the lid margin and obscuring the upper half of the pupil, no ulceration, single lesion on full skin examination
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer urgently to ophthalmology and paediatrics for propranolol
Reassure the parents and review the lesion at twelve months of age
Apply topical timolol maleate gel twice daily and review monthly
Refer for pulsed dye laser treatment at the next available list
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the orbit before treatment

subtopic_detail: Investigation after biochemistry confirms a central cause of early puberty
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a girl of 5 years and 6 months whose mother noticed breast development four months ago. Her height has crossed from the 50th to the 90th centile over the past year and her mother has noticed an adult body odour.

She has breast development to Tanner stage 3 and sparse pubic hair. She has no headache, no vomiting and no visual symptoms, and there are no cafe au lait macules on full skin examination and no history of unexplained laughing episodes. Her fundi are normal and her visual fields are full to confrontation.

data_table.Investigations: Luteinising hormone 4.2 IU/L after gonadotrophin releasing hormone stimulation indicating a pubertal response, oestradiol raised for age, thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Bone age 9 years and 6 months against a chronological age of 5 years and 6 months, pelvic ultrasound shows an enlarged uterus with an endometrial stripe

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange a pelvic ultrasound and repeat the bone age in six months
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and pituitary
Measure adrenal androgens and image the adrenal glands with CT
Commence a gonadotrophin releasing hormone analogue immediately
Reassure the family and repeat the growth measurements in a year

subtopic_detail: Vaccinating a child whose food allergy is widely but wrongly assumed to be a contraindication
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 11-month-old boy who is due his scheduled vaccines including measles mumps rubella, and whose mother also wants this season's influenza vaccine given.

At seven months of age he developed widespread hives, vomiting and wheeze within 15 minutes of one mouthful of scrambled egg and was given intramuscular adrenaline in the emergency department. He has avoided egg since. He has no asthma and has had no previous vaccine reaction, and he is well and afebrile today.

data_table.Examination: Well child with clear chest, no rash and no fever
data_table.Immunisation history: Up to date on the National Immunisation Program schedule with no previous adverse events following immunisation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate approach today?

options.text: Refer to a specialist allergy clinic for vaccination in hospital
Give the measles mumps rubella vaccine but omit the influenza one
Give both vaccines today with the standard 15 minute observation
Arrange skin prick testing to each vaccine before administering it
Give each vaccine in graded doses 30 minutes apart in the practice

subtopic_detail: Applying low risk criteria to a transient event in a well infant
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 10-week-old boy born at 39 weeks whose mother brought him in after an episode this afternoon. She says that while he was lying in his bouncer after a feed he went floppy and the skin around his lips turned blue for about 20 seconds, and that he came good when she picked him up and blew on his face.

Nobody gave rescue breaths or chest compressions. He has fed normally since and is now alert and interactive. He has had no fever, no cough and no vomiting, no similar episode before, and his immunisations are up to date. His examination including tone, fontanelle, femoral pulses and a full skin inspection is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, blood pressure within normal limits for age
data_table.Examination: Alert and interactive, normal tone, soft fontanelle, symmetrical femoral pulses, no bruising or petechiae on full skin inspection, normal cardiovascular and respiratory examination
data_table.Observation: Four hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring in the emergency department with no further events

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for 24 hours of cardiorespiratory monitoring and observation
Arrange an electroencephalogram and a brain scan before discharge
Perform a full septic screen including lumbar puncture and admit
Educate the parents, offer resuscitation training and discharge
Arrange a 24 hour oesophageal pH study and start a proton pump drug

subtopic_detail: Sequencing treatment against imaging after an abnormal newborn screening result
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 7-day-old girl recalled after her newborn screening card taken on day three flagged a raised thyroid stimulating hormone. Confirmatory venous blood taken this morning has just been reported.

She was born at term after an uncomplicated pregnancy, is breastfeeding slowly and sleeps through feeds. She is mildly jaundiced, has a large posterior fontanelle and mildly reduced tone, and no goitre is palpable. Her mother has no thyroid disease, has taken no antithyroid medication and has had no iodine containing contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate 44 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 92 mIU/L (1-20 in the first week), free thyroxine 6 pmol/L (10-26), total bilirubin below the phototherapy threshold for age
data_table.Examination: Posterior fontanelle admitting a fingertip, mildly reduced tone, no goitre palpable, umbilicus healing normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Await the thyroid scan result before starting any thyroid hormone
Repeat the venous thyroid function tests in two weeks and review
Commence thyroxine only if the thyroid scan shows no gland present
Refer to paediatric endocrinology for review within four weeks
Commence thyroxine today and arrange thyroid imaging in parallel

subtopic_detail: First line treatment of asymptomatic hypoglycaemia in an at risk newborn
stem:
You are the paediatric resident called to the postnatal ward to see a two hour old boy born at 39 weeks and 1 day to a mother whose gestational diabetes was managed with metformin. His birth weight is 4250 g and he had a good breastfeed at 40 minutes of age.

He is pink and alert with normal tone, is not jittery, and has no grunting, tachypnoea or recession. His axillary temperature is 36.9 degrees Celsius and he is rooting for a further feed. The routine pre feed blood glucose taken by the midwife is 2.2 mmol/L, confirmed on a laboratory sample.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 138 beats per minute, respiratory rate 46 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.2 mmol/L on a laboratory confirmed sample, taken before the second feed
data_table.Examination: Alert, pink, normal tone, no jitteriness, anterior fontanelle soft, cardiovascular and respiratory examination normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give buccal 40 per cent dextrose gel and support a breastfeed
Give a 2 mL/kg bolus of 10 per cent glucose intravenously now
Give a formula top up by bottle and recheck the glucose in one hour
Recheck the blood glucose before the next feed without treating now
Admit to the special care nursery for an intravenous glucose infusion

subtopic_detail: First line drug choice in a generalised epilepsy where one common agent is aggravating
stem:
You are the general paediatric registrar seeing a 6-year-old girl whose teacher has recorded 20 to 30 episodes a day in which she stops mid sentence, stares, and does not respond for a few seconds before carrying on as if nothing happened. Her school work has fallen away this term.

She does not fall, does not jerk and is not drowsy or confused afterwards. When you ask her to blow on a paper windmill for two minutes in clinic she stops and stares for six seconds with fluttering eyelids and a brief upward eye movement. Her development, growth and neurological examination are normal, and an electroencephalogram shows generalised 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background.

data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, calcium and glucose within normal limits
data_table.Electroencephalogram: Generalised symmetrical 3 Hz spike and wave discharges on a normal background, provoked by hyperventilation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Commence carbamazepine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
Commence ethosuximide and review the seizure diary in four weeks
Commence levetiracetam and review the seizure diary in four weeks
Commence lamotrigine and review the seizure diary in four weeks
Arrange brain magnetic resonance imaging before starting treatment

subtopic_detail: Timing of referral for a palpable inguinal testis that has never been in the scrotum
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 14-month-old boy for a routine check. His mother mentions that a doctor told her at the six week check that one of his testes was not down, and she was told it would probably sort itself out.

The right hemiscrotum is small and empty. You can feel a firm mobile testis in the right inguinal canal and can bring it as far as the neck of the scrotum, but it springs straight back when you let go. The left testis sits normally in the scrotum, the phallus is normal with a terminal meatus, and his growth and general examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Empty right hemiscrotum with a palpable testis in the right inguinal canal that cannot be brought into the scrotum, normally descended left testis, normal phallus with terminal meatus
data_table.Growth: Weight and length tracking along the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the parents and review the testis at his second birthday
Arrange an ultrasound of the groin to locate the testis first
Refer to paediatric surgery for orchidopexy without further delay
Arrange human chorionic gonadotrophin stimulation before referral
Refer for karyotype and hormonal testing before any surgical opinion

subtopic_detail: Selecting first line treatment for primary monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7-year-old boy who wets the bed five or six nights a week and has never been dry for longer than a fortnight. He has started refusing invitations to sleep at his cousin's house and tells you he wants it to stop.

He is dry all day, has no urgency or frequency, and does not have to rush to the toilet. He opens his bowels once a day with a soft stool and has never soiled. His growth, abdominal examination, spine and lower limb neurological examination are normal, and his parents say they are willing to be woken at night and to keep a record.

data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis shows no glucose, protein, blood, nitrites or leucocytes
data_table.Examination: Normal abdominal examination with no palpable faecal loading, normal lumbosacral spine and normal lower limb neurological examination

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first line treatment?

options.text: Prescribe desmopressin each night and review him in three months
Advise no drinks after six in the evening and review in three months
Prescribe oxybutynin twice daily and review him in three months
Arrange an enuresis alarm and review him after four to six weeks
Prescribe imipramine at night and review him after four to six weeks

subtopic_detail: Follow up schedule for renal involvement after a childhood small vessel vasculitis
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing a 6-year-old boy who has had a raised purple rash over his buttocks and the backs of both legs for five days, along with sore swollen ankles and tummy pain that comes and goes.

The rash does not fade when you press it and the spots stand up from the skin. His abdomen is soft with no guarding and no mass, his stool has tested negative for blood and his scrotum is not swollen or tender. He is eating and drinking, walking with a limp, and his parents want to know what happens next.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 380 x10^9/L (150-450), haemoglobin 124 g/L (110-145), international normalised ratio 1.0, activated partial thromboplastin time within normal limits, creatinine 34 micromol/L (20-60), albumin 38 g/L (35-50)
data_table.Urinalysis: Blood 1 plus, protein negative, no nitrites or leucocytes

lead_in: What is the most appropriate ongoing plan?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone for one week and then review him
Refer for renal biopsy before the rash begins to resolve
Commence an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor today
Discharge with advice to return only if the rash worsens
Arrange weekly urinalysis and blood pressure for one month

subtopic_detail: Managing blood streaked stools in a thriving exclusively breastfed infant without stopping breastfeeding
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a 7-week-old girl whose mother has noticed streaks of bright red blood and clear jelly like strings mixed through her nappies for the past four weeks.

She is exclusively breastfed, feeds hungrily every three hours and settles afterwards. Her mother reports no vomiting, no fever and no change in the number of nappies. She has dry rough patches on both cheeks that her mother has been treating with a moisturiser. Her weight has tracked steadily along the 50th centile since birth and her abdomen is soft with no distension or masses.

data_table.Examination: Alert and settled, weight on the 50th centile tracking along the same line since birth, soft non-tender abdomen, mild dry eczematous patches on both cheeks, normal perianal appearance
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C reactive protein less than 5 mg/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange flexible sigmoidoscopy before making any dietary change
Exclude cow milk from the mother's diet and continue breastfeeding
Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and stop breastfeeding
Change to an amino acid based formula and stop breastfeeding now
Start a proton pump inhibitor and continue breastfeeding as usual

subtopic_detail: Ordering creatine kinase before genetic testing in a boy with proximal weakness and calf hypertrophy
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 4-year-old boy referred because he falls more than the other children at kindergarten and cannot keep up with them.

He walked at 20 months. His mother demonstrates on her phone how he gets up from the floor: he rolls onto his front, pushes his bottom into the air and then walks his hands up his own thighs to straighten. He goes upstairs one step at a time holding the rail with both hands. His speech is behind that of his older sister at the same age. On examination he waddles when he walks, his calves feel firm and look bulky compared with his thighs, and his reflexes are present but reduced at the ankles. His mother mentions that a maternal uncle used a wheelchair from his teens but nobody ever explained why.

data_table.Examination: Waddling gait, proximal lower limb weakness with normal distal power, bulky firm calves, ankle reflexes reduced, no sensory loss, no spinal deformity or midline skin lesion
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Refer to physiotherapy for gait retraining and review in a year
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the whole spine urgently
Measure vitamin D and calcium and start supplementation if low
Measure the serum creatine kinase as the initial investigation
Arrange dystrophin gene testing as the initial investigation

subtopic_detail: Disimpaction before maintenance in functional constipation presenting as soiling
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a 6-year-old boy whose parents have brought him because he has been having accidents in his underpants most days for eight months. They describe smears and sometimes larger amounts of loose brown material and have been treating him for diarrhoea.

On closer questioning he sits on the toilet properly only every five to seven days, and when he does the stool is so large it has blocked the bowl twice. He hides in the corner of the lounge room when he feels the urge. He passed meconium on the first day of life, his growth has followed the 60th centile throughout, and he has no vomiting, no blood and no urinary symptoms. On examination there is a firm mass in the left lower abdomen that indents under your fingers, his back is normal and his anus is normally sited with normal perianal sensation.

data_table.Examination: Indentable mass palpable in the left iliac fossa, normal spine with no sacral dimple or hair tuft, normally positioned anus, normal lower limb tone and reflexes, weight and height on the 60th centile
data_table.Investigations: Coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A and thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Loperamide for the soiling with a review appointment in one month
An abdominal radiograph to confirm the load before any treatment
An escalating oral macrogol regimen to disimpact, then maintenance
A daily oral macrogol maintenance dose without a disimpaction phase
A sodium phosphate enema on the ward followed by dietary advice

subtopic_detail: Recognising referred hip pathology in an adolescent presenting with knee pain
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar seeing a 12-year-old boy with six weeks of a dull ache in the right knee that has been worse after football training. There was no specific injury.

For the past two days he has not been able to put weight through the right leg at all and has been hopping to the toilet. He has had no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss, and he has not been unwell. His body mass index is on the 95th centile. Examination of the knee shows a full range of movement with no effusion, no tenderness over the joint line and no ligamentous laxity. When you flex the right hip the leg rotates outwards and he will not let you rotate it inwards.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Right knee with full painless range and no effusion, right hip held in external rotation with obligatory external rotation on passive flexion, right leg apparently shortened
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 8.2 x10^9/L (5.0-15.0), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange frog lateral pelvic radiographs and refer to orthopaedics
Arrange knee radiographs and refer to the physiotherapy service
Arrange knee ultrasound and start regular non-steroidal analgesia
Arrange hip ultrasound and review him in the clinic in one week
Arrange blood cultures and start intravenous flucloxacillin now

subtopic_detail: Choosing radiograph over ultrasound for suspected hip dysplasia once the ossific nucleus has appeared
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-month-old girl for her routine check. She was born at 39 weeks in a breech presentation and is the first child in the family.

Her six week check was recorded as normal with negative provocative hip tests. Her mother mentions in passing that her own sister wore a brace on her hips as a baby. Today the skin creases on the back of the thighs are asymmetrical, the left leg looks slightly shorter with the hips and knees flexed, and abduction of the left hip stops at 50 degrees while the right abducts fully. There is no clunk on provocative testing and no pain on movement.

data_table.Examination: Asymmetric posterior thigh creases, limited left hip abduction to 50 degrees, apparent left femoral shortening on the Galeazzi test, no clunk on Ortolani or Barlow testing, normal spine and lower limb tone
data_table.Investigations: Growth and development otherwise age appropriate

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a hip ultrasound and arrange orthopaedic review thereafter
Apply a Pavlik harness and arrange orthopaedic review thereafter
Repeat the clinical examination at the 12 month check up instead
Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of both hips under sedation
Arrange an anteroposterior pelvic radiograph and orthopaedic review

subtopic_detail: Separating suture fusion from positional moulding by ear position and contralateral bossing
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 5-month-old boy whose parents have noticed that the back of his head has looked uneven since about two months of age and has not improved despite them alternating the side he is laid down on.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth and has met his milestones. His head circumference has tracked along the 50th centile since birth. On examination the right side of the back of his head is flattened. His right ear sits further back and slightly lower than the left. The forehead on the left side is more prominent than the right, and there is a firm ridge you can feel running from the back of the skull towards the right ear with a bony fullness behind that ear. He turns his head freely to both sides with no tightness in the neck.

data_table.Examination: Right occipital flattening, right ear displaced posteriorly and inferiorly, contralateral left frontal bossing, palpable ridge over the right lambdoid suture with an ipsilateral mastoid bulge, full passive neck rotation both ways, head circumference on the 50th centile
data_table.Investigations: Development age appropriate, red reflexes present bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for a moulding helmet and review again in three months
Refer to physiotherapy for neck stretches and review in a month
Arrange skull radiographs and review the films in the clinic
Refer to a craniofacial service for urgent specialist assessment
Advise repositioning and tummy time with review in three months
